content: More than 7,000 Kashmir Pandits in Kashmir Valley are on the radar of terrorist networks, with the United Liberation Council (ULC), an proxy of the Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terror outfit, leaking their personal information online. According to reports, the ULC has issued a terror threat against more than 7,000 Kashmiri Pandit workers deployed in the Valley under Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s special package, prompting a high alert across Jammu and Kashmir. The Lashkar proxy, has also leaked personal information of some of the Kashmiri Pandit employees, including their names, home addresses, and vehicle numbers, increasing the severity of the threat, and fermenting an atmosphere of fear among the workers and increased pressure on the administration regarding their safety. In its message, the ULC has opposed arming Kashmir Pandits working the Valley, claiming such measures could make these workers soft targets. Security sources believe the public threats aim to drive a wedge between Kashmir’s local and expatriate communities, particularly Kashmiri Pandits who have returned to the Valley and are employed under government schemes, News18 reported. Further, the public threats issued by proxy groups like the ULC and The Resistance Front (TRF) are believed to be part of a broader psychological warfare strategy by Pakistan’s ISI to distract security forces from protecting personnel, allowing terrorists to establish and activate their secondary networks, they said. As per the report, Pakistan and its terrorist proxies are using diversionary tactics to conceal the activities of around 1,000 terrorists stationed at launchpads near the Line of Control (LoC), who seek to infiltrate into the densely forested areas of Jammu and Kashmir. The terrorists are also attempting to establish a network with their handlers across the border in Pakistan, to leak confidential administrative information, and to carry out lone-wolf attacks against religious minorities and workers from outside the country, the report added.
title: 7000 Kashmiri Pandits receive terror threat! Lashkar proxy leaks private info online, high-alert in Jammu and Kashmir; what we know so far

movement_abstract: 【印度News18报道】印度新闻18日报道，克什米尔山谷地区超过7000名克什米尔班迪特（Kashmir Pandits）成为恐怖网络目标。作为虔诚军（LeT）代理组织的联合解放委员会（ULC）在线泄露了这些在莫迪总理特别计划下部署的班迪特工人的姓名、家庭住址及车牌号等个人信息，引发当地高度警戒。ULC在声明中反对武装在谷地工作的班迪特，声称此举将使其成为软目标。安全部门分析认为，此类公开威胁旨在制造克什米尔本地社区与返乡班迪特群体间的裂痕，属于巴基斯坦三军情报局（ISI）心理战战略的一部分，意在分散印方安全部队对人员保护的注意力，以便恐怖分子建立并激活二级网络。报告指出，巴基斯坦及其代理组织正利用声东击西战术，掩护约1000名部署在实际控制线（LoC）附近发射点的恐怖分子，企图渗透至查谟和克什米尔茂密林区。此外，恐怖分子正试图与巴基斯坦境内的联络人建立网络，以泄露机密行政信息，并针对宗教少数群体及外籍工人发动独狼式袭击。

content: Security agencies in Jammu and Kashmir have been put on high alert following a fresh threat letter issued by the United Liberation Council (ULC), an online proxy front for the banned terror outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba. The public warning directly targets over 7,000 migrant Kashmiri Pandit employees posted in the Valley under the Prime Minister’s Special Package, escalating security concerns across government departments. In a serious breach of confidentiality,the terror outfit released sensitive personal details —including full names, residential addresses, and vehicle registration numbers—to intimidate employees and instil widespread panic. The ULC’s communication explicitly opposes administrative considerations to equip migrant Kashmiri Pandits with light weapons, claiming such measures turn the community into targetable counter-insurgency tools. Furthermore, the outfit attempted to manufacture an ideological divide between non-migrant residents and returning migrant Pandits employed through government schemes, labelling the latter as white-collar operatives serving an external political agenda. Top intelligence sources reveal that the publicised online threats by proxy groups like the ULC and The Resistance Front (TRF) form part of a calculated psychological warfare campaign. Security analysts indicate that Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI) is leveraging these high-profile digital hit-lists to distract law enforcement, forcing security forces to divert personnel towards static protection duties while terror handlers attempt to rebuild ground networks. The diversion tactic is designed to cover the movements of nearly 1,000 terrorists currently stationed across launchpads along the Line of Control, waiting for opportunities to infiltrate dense forest sectors in Jammu and Kashmir . Simultaneously, cross-border handlers are attempting to establish fresh networks of Over Ground Workers (OGWs) to leak confidential administrative data and incite lone-actor targeted strikes against religious minorities and non-local workers.

content: Nurul Arifin: Spionase Modern Berubah Wujud, Indonesia Butuh 3 Pilar Hukum Antispionase Rabu, 02 September 2026 - 17:18 WIB Anggota Komisi I DPR RI dari Fraksi Partai Golkar Nurul Arifin mendorong RUU Antispionase segera ditempatkan sebagai salah satu prioritas dalam Program Legislasi Nasional (Prolegnas).Foto/Tangkapan layar IG @na_nurularifin JAKARTA - Ancaman terhadap kedaulatan Indonesia telah berpindah bentuk secara fundamental, dari spionase konvensional-militeristik menjadi ancaman digital, asimetris, dan multidimensi yang bekerja di area grey zone. Di tengah pergeseran itu, instrumen hukum nasional dinilai masih tersebar, sektoral, dan belum memadai, sehingga Indonesia mendesak untuk membangun satu kerangka hukum terpadu guna menghadapi spionase dan intervensi asing di era digital.Hal itu ditegaskan anggota Komisi I DPR RI dari Fraksi Partai Golkar Nurul Arifin , yang mendorong agar Rancangan Undang-Undang (RUU) Antispionase segera ditempatkan sebagai salah satu prioritas dalam Program Legislasi Nasional ( Prolegnas )."Indonesia membutuhkan kerangka hukum yang modern untuk melindungi kedaulatan nasional dari spionase dan intervensi atau pengaruh asing, dengan tetap menjaga demokrasi, HAM, kebebasan pers, kebebasan akademik, dan due process of law," ujar Nurul Arifin dalam keterangannya di Jakarta, Rabu (2/9/2026).Nurul menjelaskan, spionase hari ini tidak lagi terbatas pada pencurian dokumen fisik atau operasi agen rahasia secara langsung. Ancaman kini bergerak sebagai satu spektrum utuh, mulai dari pengumpulan informasi, penetrasi dan perekrutan sumber, pencurian data hilirisasi dan teknologi strategis, hingga operasi pengaruh (foreign interference) dan perang hibrida. Baca Juga: Mengenal Ikan Robot, Spionase Terbaru Militer Dunia Yang membuatnya lebih berbahaya, kata Nurul, adalah karakternya yang nyaris tak kasat mata. Serangan Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) terhadap Pusat Data Nasional, infrastruktur energi, dan sistem keuangan, hingga operasi cognitive warfare berbasis kecerdasan buatan dan deepfake yang merekayasa opini publik, kini menjadi instrumen yang lazim digunakan aktor asing untuk menembus jantung kedaulatan politik, stabilitas ekonomi, dan kohesi sosial Indonesia. "Ancaman yang paling berbahaya justru yang tidak lagi kita kenali sebagai ancaman," ujarnya. Nurul menambahkan, "Ketika infiltrasi kepentingan asing berulang kali terjadi dan diterima sebagai hal yang lumrah, di situlah kita kehilangan lapis pertahanan paling mendasar."Di sisi lain, perangkat hukum Indonesia, mulai dari KUHP, UU Nomor 17 Tahun 2011 tentang Intelijen Negara, UU ITE, hingga UU Pelindungan Data Pribadi, masih bekerja secara sektoral dan belum memberikan definisi terpadu atas delik spionase modern maupun intervensi asing. movement_abstract: 【印度尼西亚雅加达媒体9月2日报道】2026年9月2日，印度尼西亚众议院第一委员会成员、戈尔卡党党团成员努鲁尔·阿里芬在雅加达发表声明，呼吁将《反间谍法》草案（RUU Antispionase）列为国家立法规划（Prolegnas）的优先事项。阿里芬指出，针对印尼主权的威胁已从传统军事间谍活动转变为数字化、非对称及多维度的灰色地带威胁。现代间谍活动涵盖信息收集、战略技术与数据窃取、外国干预及混合战争，包括针对国家数据中心、能源基础设施和金融系统的先进持续性威胁（APT），以及利用人工智能和深度伪造技术进行的认知战。阿里芬强调，印尼现行法律体系（包括刑法典、2011年第17号国家情报法、信息电子交易法及个人数据保护法）呈碎片化状态，缺乏对现代间谍行为和外国干预的统一法律定义。他主张建立现代法律框架，在保护国家主权的同时，兼顾民主、人权、新闻自由、学术自由及正当法律程序，以应对日益隐蔽且难以识别的外国渗透风险。

content: TEHRAN — Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf has warned that the United States has resorted to a “hybrid war” against the Islamic Republic in an attempt to compensate for its military and diplomatic failures. “The enemy has shown us that, after suffering setbacks on the military and diplomatic fronts, it has added an extensive economic and cognitive warfare campaign to its operations,” Qalibaf said in a video address. He added, “In other words, we are now facing a hybrid war where the naval blockade itself constitutes a form of military warfare. Economic warfare remains their primary focus, reinforced by sophisticated psychological operations.” The Parliament speaker touched upon Washington’s broader objectives behind this strategy, stating: “The enemy’s goal in this hybrid war is to incite domestic unrest and chaos—that is their sinister intention—and in some instances, carry out targeted assassinations. They may even attempt short, limited military strikes to weaken our resolve or compel us to capitulate at the negotiating table.” Qalibaf also warned that Iran will respond militarily if the US intensifies its blockade of Iranian ports. “If they intensify the blockade, we will definitely respond militarily, and everyone will suffer. If the enemy is determined to prevent us from exporting oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be able to export oil,” he asserted. Qalibaf’s remarks come amid escalating rhetoric from Washington. President Donald Trump recently threatened an unprecedented multi-front campaign against Tehran, warning of potential military strikes against Iranian strategic assets and infrastructure if key demands are not met. The military threats coincide with what Trump described as an all-out “crushing economic D-Day” campaign against Tehran. Under the sweeping economic measures, Washington warned international banks, companies, and governments that maintaining trade ties, processing transactions, or facilitating Iranian oil exports would trigger severe secondary sanctions and financial isolation. The US and Israel initiated another round of unprovoked aggression against Iran on February 28, coming approximately eight months after their previous unlawful attacks on Iranian territory in June 2025. However, Iran’s strong military response against Israel and American bases in the region forced Trump to call for a ceasefire, which went into effect on April 8. Despite the truce and a Pakistani-mediated memorandum of understanding on June 17, the US has violated its commitments with new strikes against Iran and the continuation of its naval blockade.

content: TEHRAN – In yet another delusional outburst from the decaying American empire, Donald Trump has once again proven that Washington's leadership has lost all touch with reality. His August 31 declaration that "Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!" represents not strategic analysis, but the desperate hallucinations of a regime accustomed to imposing its will through deception. Nations do not cease to exist because a bankrupt politician declares them so on social media. Iran's ancient civilization has weathered far greater storms than the current Zio-American pressure campaign and will certainly outlast the current crop of Western leaders whose grip on reality grows more tenuous by the day. More concerning is Trump's brazen use of artificial intelligence as an instrument of psychological warfare. The fabricated video purporting to show Kharg Island's destruction, later admitted to be AI-generated by Vice President JD Vance, represents a new low in American propaganda. When Washington presents imaginary destruction as accomplished fact, it reveals its fundamental weakness: the inability to achieve strategic objectives through legitimate means. The Zionist-inspired American regime has long understood the power of spectacle, from Hollywood's vilification of Iran to the systematic erasure of Palestinian identity. But war is less forgiving than electoral theater. Missiles do not disappear because a bankrupt real estate mogul declares the enemy finished. Sovereign nations do not surrender because Washington announces their defeat through artificial images. The contradiction in American policy toward Iran is glaring. If Iran is already "dead," why does Washington continue to warn Tehran about future consequences? Why does the administration still describe Iranian attacks as a serious threat to American forces and commercial shipping in the Persian Gulf? The answer is simple: the battlefield reality contradicts the propaganda. Iran has not only survived Washington's maximum pressure campaign but has demonstrated remarkable resilience. Despite facing the most comprehensive economic warfare in modern history, Iran continues to advance its scientific capabilities, maintain regional influence, and defend its sovereignty. Iran's military capabilities remain formidable, as evidenced by the embarrassing failures of American and Israeli operations against Iranian assets. The Islamic Republic's air defense systems, naval presence in the strategic Persian Gulf, and missile capabilities continue to pose a genuine deterrent to Zionist ambitions in the region. One cannot separate Washington's hostility toward Iran from the corrosive influence of the Zionist lobby on American foreign policy. The relentless push for confrontation serves Tel Aviv's interests far more than America's. Why should American soldiers sacrifice their lives for Israeli security? Why should American taxpayers fund endless conflicts that only benefit the apartheid regime in occupied Palestine? The Iranian people have repeatedly demonstrated their capacity to resist foreign domination. From the 1979 Islamic Revolution to the present, Iran has consistently rejected Western attempts to impose its will. The American war of words against Iran is fundamentally a war against national sovereignty and the right to chart one's own destiny free from imperial interference. Perhaps most disturbing is Washington's callous exploitation of human suffering. Reported casualty figures from American sources have shifted dramatically from tens of thousands to more than 100,000 alleged deaths with little evidence to support these claims. If accurate, these figures represent a humanitarian catastrophe demanding independent verification. If inaccurate, their use as political slogans reduces human tragedy to mere ammunition in Washington's propaganda war. The Islamic Republic has repeatedly called for international investigations into American and Israeli war crimes, including the systematic assassination of Iranian scientists, cyberattacks on civilian infrastructure, and economic warfare that constitutes collective punishment under international humanitarian law. Washington's reckless rhetoric also threatens the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most strategically important waterways. Any serious confrontation in the Persian Gulf would have devastating consequences for regional security and the global economy. These realities cannot be managed through memes, AI-generated videos, or declarations that an entire nation is "dead." The Islamic Republic has consistently demonstrated its commitment to regional stability, unlike the American regime that has left a trail of destruction from Afghanistan to Libya to Yemen. When political leaders become more invested in declaring victory than establishing facts, credibility becomes collateral damage. The United States' strategic asset should be its credibility, yet every false image or exaggerated claim weakens this foundation. Propaganda can shape perception, but perception cannot substitute for strategy. AI can manufacture the image of a destroyed island. Social media can manufacture the appearance of triumph. None of it can manufacture victory. Military power can destroy infrastructure, but it cannot, by itself, manufacture political outcomes. This is a lesson America learned in Vietnam, Afghanistan, and Iraq, and will inevitably learn in its confrontation with Iran. While Washington indulges in fantasies of Iranian collapse, the Islamic Republic continues to demonstrate remarkable resilience. Iran has transformed challenges into opportunities for self-reliance and technological advancement, from nuclear technology to biotechnology, from aerospace to nanotechnology. Iran's political system, grounded in Islamic values and republican institutions, has proven its legitimacy through successive elections and popular participation. The American claim that Iran is a "failed state" ignores the reality of a functioning government that provides services to its citizens, maintains security across its vast territory, and continues to exert influence from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean. The broader issue extends far beyond Iran. The American empire is in terminal decline, unable to accept that the unipolar moment has passed. Washington's desperate attempts to maintain global hegemony through sanctions and military threats reflect not strength but weakness. China, Russia, and the emerging multipolar order represent a future that respects national sovereignty and cultural diversity. Iran will continue strengthening its ties with these powers, reducing its vulnerability to American pressure. The so-called "America First" policy reveals itself as "America Alone," isolated from the global consensus that rejects unilateralism. Trump may dominate the news cycle with a post. He may make an artificial image trend across social media. None of that changes the battlefield reality. Iran will continue its path of dignity, resistance, and development. The Islamic Republic will survive American propaganda, Zionist ambitions, and imperial pressures. Iranian civilization has endured for millennia; it will not collapse because a bankrupt American politician declares it "dead" on social media. The American empire, meanwhile, continues its inevitable decline, hoisted by its own petard of deception and moral bankruptcy. History will judge which civilization truly failed.

content: A small number of private technology firms now build the infrastructure on which both military power and the public’s perception of reality depend. Drawing on a 2025 wargaming experiment at the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College and on the documented information war of the June 2025 Israel-Iran conflict, this essay argues that simulated combat and cognitive warfare increasingly depend on the same technological ecosystem — shared firms, infrastructure, and supply chains — with direct implications for doctrine, training, and mid-sized powers such as Brazil. Power has historically followed infrastructure: control of sea lanes defined the nineteenth century, control of oil and industry defined the twentieth. In this century, the decisive axis has shifted to digital infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI). This is not a future possibility; it is a present condition. Whoever controls information systems can shape more than data: that control increasingly influences perception, behavior, and how populations interpret events. Every advanced AI model depends on a physical layer of semiconductors, data centers, and satellite links, which makes that physical layer, rather than any single algorithm, the true strategic terrain. Washington has increasingly treated China’s technological rise as a hegemonic challenge rather than mere commercial competition, since military capability, industrial autonomy, and normative leadership now converge on control of computing, data, and networks. Between the United States and China — and between the private companies that supply both — lies the central contest of contemporary geopolitics: a competition over semiconductors, advanced computing, and autonomous systems in which the winner sets the terms for every nation that depends on that infrastructure. A relatively small group of private firms now supplies infrastructure once built primarily by states themselves. Palantir, founded in 2003 with early funding from the Central Intelligence Agency’s venture arm In-Q-Tel, operates the Maven Smart System, which processes drone and sensor data for targeting decisions. In July 2025, the U.S. Army signed an enterprise contract with Palantir with a ceiling over ten years, consolidating seventy-five prior contracts and following the earlier Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node (TITAN) award. SpaceX, through its Starshield division, provides the orbital backbone for military communication and target-tracking, using large constellations of small satellites to preserve connectivity under electronic-warfare conditions. Microsoft supplies sovereign cloud infrastructure to the Department of Defense and has tested the augmented-reality Integrated Visual Augmentation System (IVAS) with soldiers in the field. In February 2025, control of the twenty-two-billion-dollar was set to transfer from Microsoft to Anduril Industries — a company founded in 2017 by Palmer Luckey that also develops the Lattice command software and autonomous drone systems. This transfer remained subject to Department of Defense approval. Google supplies data infrastructure to defense agencies through Google Public Sector, but internal opposition has repeatedly constrained that work: in 2018, more than three thousand employees signed a letter opposing Project Maven, several resigned in protest, and Google subsequently declined to renew . Oracle hosts isolated, hardened databases for the U.S. intelligence community. NVIDIA manufactures the graphics processors that underpin nearly every military AI application, from war-gaming simulation to autonomous targeting, while Broadcom supplies the hardened semiconductors and network components behind radar and satellite systems. OpenAI and Anthropic supply the language models increasingly integrated into intelligence analysis, cybersecurity automation, and logistics planning. None of these firms was elected; together they constitute an informal general staff for the defense architecture of the United States and its partners. The economics of AI make reversal implausible. Training a frontier model costs hundreds of millions of dollars, but deploying it costs a fraction of a cent per use, so once built, the capability propagates at near-zero marginal cost. Militaries that adopt AI-assisted planning do not regress to manual methods any more than air forces return to celestial navigation after adopting GPS. Private investment has also outpaced the ability of most legislatures to regulate it in real time. These dynamics mirror earlier arms races — the repeating rifle, the submarine, the atomic bomb — with one structural difference: the firms building the current generation of weapons-relevant technology are civilian, transnational, and often headquartered outside the countries whose forces rely on them. A 2025 at the U.S. Army Command and General Staff College (CGSC) tested whether a large language model could support realistic course-of-action analysis. When given highly detailed, step-by-step instructions, the model systematically favored friendly forces and required constant human correction. When given only the commander’s intent and key tasks, a second instance of the same model produced substantially more realistic assessments. In the wargame’s decisive scenario, a friendly battalion of three companies was tasked with fixing a defending force of more than five companies; the model returned an assessment of friendly remaining at seventy-five percent against an enemy reduced to forty percent, a result the staff initially distrusted but confirmed after review: the model had correctly accounted for the effects of close air support, attack aviation, and artillery that the human planners had themselves underestimated. Similar findings have emerged elsewhere in U.S. professional military education. The College has used AI to reduce the variable space of its 2025 wargames, and the Army War College has used large language models to support Free Kriegsspiel-style adjudication in unclassified scenarios. Across these cases, human oversight remained essential: officers corrected AI-modeled enemy lethality, enforced movement restrictions on logistics nodes, and re-established scenario context after the model lost continuity — with AI augmenting the capabilities of intelligence professionals rather than replacing them, in line with doctrinal norms. The central finding is that excessive procedural detail degrades AI performance by preventing the model from applying its doctrinal knowledge, while clear intent, combined with accurate underlying data, improves it. Writing effective instructions for an AI system is converging with writing an effective operations order, and the resulting bias exposure functions as an informal test of a staff’s own planning assumptions. Simulated battle is one half of this problem; contested perception is the other. The twelve-day war between Israel and Iran in June 2025 provides a documented case of AI-enabled information warfare at scale. A study by the Association, based on 592 fast-checks published by 50 organizations across 23 countries, found that roughly one-fifth of false content examined was generated from scratch using AI, while more than 70 percent was stripped of its original time and place and recirculated as if documenting the current conflict. The researchers assessed that 72 percent of the examined false content could have served Iranian interests, as could 90 percent of the content, a pattern consistent with, though not conclusive proof of, a strategic recalibration by Iran: compensating for the battlefield setbacks suffered by its non-state allied groups, a weakened Hezbollah and a severely debilitated Hamas, by turning to influence operations aimed at the adversary’s morale rather than its decision-making process. The inference remains circumstantial, but the timing and target selection lend it plausibility. Israel’s institutional response illustrates one way to organize against this threat. The IDF’s C4I and Cyber Defense Directorate has restructured to create dedicated AI and spectrum warfare divisions. Within this reorganization, the new Sphera unit consolidates electromagnetic-spectrum operations and strategic communications under a single command — a recognition that the two functions belong to the same battlespace, even as AI-enabled analysis is managed through a separate, parallel structure. This institutional capacity was not built for the Iran conflict alone. A parallel civil-military monitoring structure has taken shape around organizations like FakeReporter, an independent NGO that has operated as Israel’s primary open-source intelligence and disinformation monitoring body since the Gaza war, documenting more than distinct disinformation narratives in that earlier conflict’s first week alone. Israel has also developed a broader distributed monitoring network integrating military and civil society actors, though the precise channels linking NGO findings to military intelligence remain undocumented in open sources. Detection tools nonetheless struggle to keep pace with rapidly improving generation tools — a structural gap documented across the field, not a temporary lag. In this environment, prioritizing response speed — publishing verified information and correcting errors quickly — offers a more sustainable posture than an unwinnable race to detect every fabrication before it spreads, a logic consistent with the approach observed in Israeli information operations. These two cases point to the same underlying infrastructure. The chips and cloud platforms that train a model capable of realistic combat-power estimation are drawn from the same supply chain used to train a model capable of generating synthetic battlefield imagery. Simulated war-gaming and the war for perception increasingly run on a shared technological ecosystem — common cloud infrastructure, common model providers, and, in some cases, the same defense-analytics firms that supply both targeting systems and narrative-monitoring tools. This overlap creates common points of failure: a vendor outage or breach can degrade military planning and public-facing information defenses at once, and it concentrates significant leverage in the hands of a small number of private companies whose commercial incentives do not necessarily align with military doctrine or institutional accountability. For military institutions, this implies that AI competency belongs in doctrine and professional military education rather than in a technology office: officers require the same discipline in writing intent for AI systems that they apply to operations orders, and information-verification capacity requires the same institutional priority as intelligence and fires. For nations without a Palantir, a Starshield, or a leading-edge semiconductor industry, three outcomes are plausible. A small oligopoly of powers could consolidate control over AI and military infrastructure, leaving most states dependent on imported capability. Alternatively, falling model costs and technology diffusion could extend AI-enabled cognitive and combat capability to smaller states and non-state actors, increasing instability. A third path — pursued deliberately rather than by default — involves building sufficient independent capacity in data governance, AI-assisted planning, and disinformation verification to avoid total dependence on great-power infrastructure, without pretending to compete with it directly. This course suits mid-sized states with large domestic data pools and diversified diplomatic ties — Brazil among them — better than it does smaller or more exposed powers. Which path predominates will depend less on the pace of technological change than on sustained institutional investment and doctrinal adaptation, since forces that continue preparing for the previous war risk losing the current one before it is formally declared.

movement_abstract: 2025年，美国陆军指挥与参谋学院开展兵棋推演，测试大语言模型在作战方案分析中的应用。结果显示，提供明确指挥官意图而非繁琐指令可显著提升模型评估准确性，模型在计算空中支援与炮火效应方面优于人工规划。同期，以色列与伊朗爆发冲突，事实核查协会研究显示，约20%的虚假内容由AI生成，超70%为旧内容被剥离时空背景后重新传播。以色列国防军重组C4I与网络防御局，设立专门AI与频谱战部门，整合电磁频谱与战略通信职能，并依托民间组织FakeReporter构建军民融合监测网络。分析指出，作战模拟与认知战日益依赖同一技术生态，包括Palantir、SpaceX、微软、英伟达等少数私营企业的芯片、云基础设施及数据模型。这种重叠导致单一供应商故障可同时削弱军事规划与公共信息防御能力。对于巴西等中等强国，报告建议通过加强数据治理与独立验证能力建设，避免对大国基础设施的完全依赖，而非直接进行技术竞争。

content: Previous articles devoted to special military propaganda in the Soviet Union covered the major military conflicts that influenced the development of this type of military activity. The topic of Soviet propaganda directed at the troops of Nazi Germany and its allies is quite broad, so it will be the subject of a series of articles covering various periods of the war, from its beginning to the Victory Day of May 9. This article is the first in this series. The content of political campaigns against German troops at different periods of the war was structured according to the military and political situation developing at the front, the combat missions being accomplished by Soviet troops, and changes in the enemy's political and morale. To exert ideological and political influence on the enemy, the press, radio (broadcast radio stations and those from the front, domestic and captured), oral propaganda (through loudspeakers and megaphones), and visual propaganda (leaflets, newspapers, brochures, and books) were used.1. Before examining in detail the types and methods of Soviet special propaganda during the Great Patriotic War, it is necessary to understand the organizational structure of this work. Therefore, this article will reveal which specific agencies developed and implemented information and psychological warfare against enemy troops. Red Army soldiers training at the Voroshilov Barracks in Moscow on August 30, 1941. It's important to begin with the fact that the recent Soviet-Finnish War exposed numerous weaknesses in the then-young Red Army. It became clear that it was necessary to summarize the war's results in order to promptly identify and address all errors and shortcomings. To this end, a meeting of the Red Army's command staff was held from April 14 to 17, 1940, under the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) to summarize the experience of combat operations in Finland. 2. The meeting yielded a reliable picture of what was happening. At this meeting, in his speech on April 17, Stalin explained why studying the experience of the Soviet-Finnish War was a priority. Here are two important quotes from this speech: …keep in mind that during the entire existence of Soviet power, we have never fought a real modern war. Minor episodes in Manchuria, at Lake Khasan, or in Mongolia are nonsense; they are not war, they are isolated episodes in a strictly limited area. Japan was afraid to start a war, we didn't want that either, and a small test of strength in that small area showed that Japan had failed. They had two or three divisions, and we had two or three divisions in Mongolia, the same number at Lake Khasan. Our army has never fought a real, serious war. A civil war is not a real war, because it was a war without artillerywithout aviationwithout tanks, without mortars. Without all that, what kind of serious war is this? - I.V. Stalin. …our modern Red Army was shelled on the fields of Finland – that was its first baptism — I.V. Stalin3 Speech by I.V. Stalin at a meeting of the Red Army's command staff to summarize the experience of the Winter War (excerpts). April 17, 1940 (RGASPI, F. 558, Op. 11, D. 1124, L. 23, 35) The second outcome of the meeting was the proposal by Deputy People's Commissar of Defense G. I. Kulik to elect a commission to summarize the council's proposals, as well as to comprehensively analyze the military operations against Finland and formulate specific proposals for each individual area. The commission was established and began its work on April 19, 1940. It included K.E. Voroshilov (chairman), I.V. Stalin, G.I. Kulik, L.Z. Mekhlis, E.A. Shchadenko, and other representatives of the central military department. However, most of the commission's members had been direct participants in the Winter War. These included the combined arms, air force, technical troops, armored vehicle, political work, and other subcommittees. Each was required to submit practical recommendations on its specific area to the USSR People's Commissar of Defense by the following day. Due to the abundance of problems identified, for some, the deadline was extended until April 21. 4. After all subcommissions presented their findings at the plenary session on April 21, I.V. Stalin proposed creating a special "narrower commission" to address issues not previously considered. Meetings of this special commission continued from April 23 to May 14, 1940. 5. In the context of this article, the most interesting is the report of the head of the Political Directorate of the Red Army, L. Z. Mekhlis, on military ideology from May 10, 1940, in the part concerning the informational and psychological influence on soldiers and the population of Finland. Lev Zakharovich Mekhlis This report outlined the key areas for improving Soviet special propaganda, taking into account all the mistakes of the past war. The full text of the report can be found in open sources, but I will provide the key excerpts necessary for understanding the topic. The study of the armies of potential adversaries and possible theaters of military operations is completely unsatisfactory, and the available intelligence data is too classified and is not made available to the command staff,— L. Z. Mekhlis. A deeply ingrained, harmful prejudice holds that the populations of countries entering war with the USSR will inevitably, almost en masse, rebel and defect to the Red Army, and that workers and peasants will greet us with flowers. This false belief stems from ignorance of the actual situation in neighboring countries. The war in Finland demonstrated that we hadn't conducted political reconnaissance in the northern regions and therefore didn't know what slogans to bring to these populations or how to work among them... We need to know the lives and interests of the populations of each country. — L. Z. Mekhlis It must be said that we have made more than one mistake in the area of political study of the enemy and have made limited progress in working among the enemy's troops and population. It was only in early 1939 that foreign-language newspaper editorial offices were introduced, but they are still far from meeting the requirements, as they lack writers with a sufficiently good knowledge of the language, everyday life, history and the culture of the respective countries. If you want to defeat your enemy properly, you need to know him well... Therefore, you must carefully study and understand the strengths and weaknesses of all the armies of neighboring countries, including small ones. — L. Z. Mekhlis6 Following the meeting, the subcommittee on party and political work in wartime, in the section devoted to work among enemy troops, adopted a number of decisions of great practical significance for the formation of a special propaganda structure. Thus, point 4 stated: “In order to provide organizational support for political work among the enemy troops and population, create departments for work among the enemy troops and population in the political departments of all border districts and armies.”. A group of Soviet soldiers walks along the shore of the Kola Bay. 1941. Other points also discussed establishing a military registry for individuals proficient in foreign languages, assigning them to editorial offices of foreign newspapers based on their knowledge of a particular language, and holding periodic meetings to exchange experiences and improve their skills. Furthermore, a decision was made to issue a manual on organizing political work among enemy troops in peacetime. 7. As early as July 1939, foreign-language newspaper editorial offices were established in a number of border military districts as training centers, where editorial staff were required to accumulate information about the neighboring country, study its strengths and weaknesses, select facts for propaganda, and also improve their experience in the field of publishing printed materials for soldiers and the population of a potential enemy (that country). A total of 24 editorial offices were created. A special instructor was assigned to manage them, and later a group of instructor-translators was formed. In April 1940, the group was reorganized into a special department for managing foreign-language publications. Each of the department's senior instructors oversaw newspapers in a specific foreign language and studied the respective countries and their armies. Battle for the village. 1941 Finally, in August of the same year, a special department for propaganda among the enemy troops and population was established on the basis of this department within the Main Directorate of Political Propaganda of the Red Army (GUPPKA). 8It was headed by Major Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev, who already had experience conducting special propaganda in battles with the Japanese at the Khalkhin Gol River in 1939 and with the Finns on the Karelian Isthmus in 1940. Major General Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev. Photo from his 1981 book "Insight" It was the seventh department, and hence its common name, the 7th Department. It was tasked with studying the political and morale of army personnel and the population of foreign countries, and preparing to conduct propaganda and agitation among them with the aim of undermining their morale. Highly educated specialists, scientists, and educators from institutes of the USSR Academy of Sciences, graduates of state universities, and postgraduate programs at military academies, fluent in German, Finnish, Romanian, English, Persian, Arabic, Japanese, and other foreign languages, were selected and appointed to the department.9. Following the creation of the Seventh Department within the Main Directorate of Political Propaganda of the Red Army, similar departments were established in the political directorates of the following border districts: the Leningrad, Western, and Kyiv Special, Odessa, Transcaucasian, Central Asian, and Transbaikal Military Districts, and the Far Eastern Front. Furthermore, the political departments of the armies within these districts established propaganda units for enemy troops and the general population, and the position of senior instructor for propaganda among enemy troops was added to the staff of each division's political department.10. Naturally, such a system needed to be staffed with qualified personnel. This work began as early as May 1938, when the first census of career political workers proficient in foreign languages and capable of conducting propaganda among enemy troops and the general population was conducted. These political workers, who were in the Red Army reserves, were periodically called up for training sessions. The military department at the 2nd Moscow State Pedagogical Institute of Foreign Languages (since 1942, the Military Institute of Foreign Languages (VIIL)) played a major role in training special propagandists. It was called the forge of the USSR's special propagandists. The military department at the Moscow Institute of Oriental Studies also played a major role. There, students took short but informative courses on conducting political work among enemy troops and the population.11Captured enemy documents and existing propaganda publications often served as teaching aids. The Lesnoye Sanatorium in the city of Stavropol on the Volga (now Tolyatti), where the Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages, established at the 2nd Moscow Pedagogical Institute of Foreign Languages, was evacuated by ship by order of October 10, 1941. Photo from 1941 Students of the Military Faculty of Western Foreign Languages in Stavropol-on-Volga, 1942. Photograph from the collection of the Togliatti Museum of Local History. On October 12, 1940, GUPPKA issued Directive No. 267, which described the experience of working among enemy troops and populations in past battles, and also defined new methods and directions for conducting ideological work in relation to enemy troops.12Unlike other countries, where psychological warfare departments were independent or part of the intelligence services, the 7th Departments, as organs of ideological struggle, became part of the military-political apparatus. It must be said that within the political agencies, they felt rather out of place in their functional responsibilities, often encountering skepticism, and at times even sabotaging their activities.13. At that time, there were still quite a few Soviet soldiers and commanders who seriously doubted even the slightest success of this difficult and dangerous task. Officially, the special propagandists were said to be engaged in decomposing enemy troops. Many front-line soldiers, hearing this, said, "Fascists decompose only in the ground." 14. Thus, the tasks of the seventh department (directorate) of GUPPKA included: 1. Development, publication and organization of distribution of propaganda materials (leaflets, slogans, newspapers, brochures) among the armies and population of enemy countries;2. Guidance of front-line and army special propaganda agencies and assistance in decomposing the enemy’s troops and population;3. Development and implementation of special information and propaganda operations among enemy troops at the front and the population in the rear;4. Conducting a daily study of the political and moral state of the personnel of the armies and the population of enemy countries, the nature and system of their ideological processing;5. Collecting information about the effectiveness of our propaganda;6. Selection, training and distribution of special propagandists who speak the relevant foreign languages;7. Generalization and dissemination of best practices in information warfare in its information bulletins and in collections of experience in political work among the enemy troops and population15. Excerpts from one of the 7th Department's "Exchange of Experience" bulletins. September 25, 1943. Photo from the Russian Ministry of Defense website. The operational apparatus for special propaganda included the seventh departments of the front (district) political directorates, the seventh sections of the army political departments, and senior instructors of the corps and division political departments for work among enemy troops and the population. The seventh departments of the fronts and border military districts also operated foreign-language newspaper editorial offices and radio broadcasting offices. 16. Each element of the special propaganda system had its own operational scope. Thus, the front political directorates served as the link between the 7th Department of the GUPPKA and all subordinate structures, ensuring a continuous exchange of information between the special propaganda leadership and those working on the ground. Furthermore, the front political directorates provided all possible support to the army political departments. For example, they instructed and dispatched special propaganda teams equipped with mobile printing presses, powerful sound amplification stations, photo laboratories, and other front-line propaganda equipment. They also carried out extensive work on the timely delivery and distribution of propaganda materials among enemy troops and civilians. This was accomplished primarily by frontline aviation. This required constant coordination with air force headquarters. They also carried out extensive work on training special propagandists, as well as working with prisoners of war to instill in them an anti-fascist ideology and further involve them in propaganda work against the enemy.17. Interrogation of a captured German. July 1941. As for the army's political departments, their important task was to collect and systematize reliable information about the opposing enemy forces and disseminate it to higher authorities. Overall, the army's political departments were distinguished by their efficiency and were able to quickly adapt their propaganda in content, forms, and methods based on the constantly changing combat situation. Their primary task was to provide comprehensive assistance and maintain constant contact with the divisional political departments. In turn, the divisional political departments operated, as they say, "on the ground" and in a more targeted manner. Officially, they were represented only by a senior instructor for work among enemy troops and the population, but since one person could not carry out all the work, several individuals with the necessary skills were assigned to assist the instructor. This created a unique department. It addressed the task of maximally weakening the combat capability of enemy units engaged in battles against a given division in a given sector of the front. At this level, the most common tool used was operational propaganda (that is, propaganda aimed at specific enemy military formations, whose situation was comprehensively studied at the divisional political department level).18. Senior Lieutenant P.I. Nikitin drops leaflets on enemy troop positions using a mortar of his own design. 1942. The publication of leaflets in foreign languages was handled by the Military Publishing House of the USSR People's Commissariat of Defense, which included a department for fulfilling special orders under the 7th Department (Directorate). The Moscow-based Iskra Revolutsii printing house, capable of typesetting and publishing printed materials in 60 foreign languages, was assigned to the 7th Directorate from the USSR Foreign Publishing House. The printing plant of the Pravda Publishing House of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) was also involved in the production of the most important and high-circulation propaganda materials. 19. One of the first Soviet propaganda leaflets for the Germans. A Russian translation is included below. Leaflets with similar content were almost entirely ineffective. In addition, on the eve of the war, military districts sent many civilian specialists (journalists, philologists, historians, German language teachers and others) to training camps fleet and into ground military units for use according to their specialty. Upon completion, they were warned that in the event of war, they would be called up again. 20This was also necessary to staff the system with valuable personnel, which, however, was constantly in short supply. As mentioned above, the main document regulating the activities of special propaganda was Directive No. 267. It was written in the spirit of socialism and Lenin's ideas that when the enemy army and the population, through information provided by the Soviet Union, understand the senselessness of war for the working people, they will immediately protest against their government and express sympathy for the Red Army. 21. The objective class position of capitalists is one thing. They fight for themselves. Soldiers are proletarians and peasants. That's different... their class interests are against war! That's why they can be enlightened, persuaded,— V.I. Lenin22 This was the basis of the "gold standard" of Soviet political propaganda directed at enemy troops in the pre-war period. Back then, no one understood that the Soviet Union would be confronted with soldiers raised from childhood to believe in their exceptionalism and the superiority of their nation over all other nations on the planet. In early May 1941, the People's Commissar of Defense demanded that the 7th Department of the GUPPKA, headed by Mikhail Ivanovich Burtsev, prepare a report on the political and moral state of the countries bordering the USSR and their armies. A few days later, such a report was prepared and read out. 23But there was one important nuance. The report contained very little information about the situation in Germany. The reason for this was that, at that time, Germany was not among the Soviet Union's most likely adversaries. This was especially influenced by the non-aggression pact between the USSR and the Third Reich in 1939. Political Commissar I.I. Petrov conducts propaganda work on German positions using a primitive tin pipe. North Caucasus Front, 1942. As a result, the German-language newspaper's editorial office in the Leningrad Military District was liquidated. Furthermore, only one or two German publications were subscribed to for research into the situation in Germany. A major drawback was the fact that the Soviet leadership prohibited the translation of German articles and books critical of our country. 24, even to structures for which this was a direct part of the work. All this together made it impossible to see the real processes taking place in Germany in the pre-war period and to form a true picture of the enemy, and at the same time to develop methods and arguments for informational and psychological influence on the future enemy based on current data. Among the potential adversaries being studied were countries located on the southern borders of the USSR (Iran, Afghanistan, India, and Turkey). Propaganda theses had already been prepared for these countries, exposing the colonial nature of the British imperialists, and some printed materials had been prepared. 25. Photo taken during the Battle of Smolensk, 1941 Thus, on the eve of the Great Patriotic War, the special propaganda agencies lacked complete and up-to-date information on the Third Reich and its allies, but were preparing to wage psychological warfare against entirely different countries. Furthermore, among all the employees of the 7th Departments, there was a critical shortage of people with a high level of German proficiency. More often than not, those who spoke the language only spoke it colloquially, not to mention the new military terms and ranks that had emerged in Nazi Germany. Only after the aforementioned May 1941 report was the 7th Department of the GUPPKA tasked with filling this gap and preparing a report on the situation in Germany in the shortest possible time. 26The report systematized all available relevant data on the Third Reich. But it was, of course, insufficient to fully reflect reality. Nevertheless, based on available sources, it was noted that the German army was undergoing extraordinary moral and political preparation for war. Their army was assessed as strong, well-disciplined, and well-armed. However, the report again erroneously concluded that it would be easy to convince German soldiers that this war was inadvisable for them. The report was distributed to the Red Army's political organs for review. 27. By the time Nazi Germany invaded the USSR, many special propaganda efforts had to be implemented on the fly. Thus, on June 22, 1941, two sections were formed within the 7th Department of the GUPPKA: the first for conducting information and psychological warfare against Germany and its allies, and the second for propaganda work among the populations of occupied countries and territories.28. Of fundamental importance was the decision of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) on June 25, 1941, to establish the Bureau of Military-Political Propaganda. This was a collegial body created to centralize the direction of all propaganda efforts against the enemy and the populations of the territories they had captured. The 7th Department became the working body of this Bureau. 29. Resolution of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) "On the Creation of the Soviet Bureau of Military-Political Propaganda." June 25, 1941 (Original. RGASPI, Fund 17, List 163, D. 1316. L. 183) The Bureau included: the head of the GUPPKA, L. Z. Mekhlis, his deputy, D. Z. Manuilsky, professor and specialist in propaganda, V. S. Kruzhkov, head of the press department of the People's Commissariat of Foreign Affairs, P. G. Palgunov, and deputy people's commissar of foreign affairs, S. A. Lozovsky (on July 2, the director of the Marx-Engels-Lenin Institute under the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks), M. B. Mitin, was also included in the Bureau).30L. Z. Mekhlis became the head of the Bureau. At the meetings, the fundamental directions and content of all special propaganda were determined, leading general political materials for the enemy troops and population were approved, and joint activities in the matter of special propaganda of such bodies as TASS, the Soviet Information Bureau, the USSR Radio Committee, state publishing houses and others were coordinated. 31. Another important agency for special propaganda was the Soviet Information Bureau (Sovinformburo), established on June 24, 1941, by a joint resolution of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Council of People's Commissars. Information transmitted through the Sovinformburo was often used in the preparation of leaflets for enemy soldiers (for example, the information leaflets "International Information"). Resolution of June 24, 1941 of the Central Committee of the All-Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) and the Council of People's Commissars on the establishment of the Soviet Information Bureau (Sovinformburo) This information was of even greater importance for the residents of the occupied eastern territories of the USSR, who were cut off from receiving News about the progress of the war. Therefore, in 1942, a directive was issued requiring every partisan detachment to receive Sovinformburo reports, record them, and reproduce them as leaflets for subsequent distribution among Soviet citizens remaining in enemy-occupied territory. In this way, people cut off from information about the state of the war and constantly subjected to massive fascist propaganda and lies could learn the truth and maintain contact with their country. 32. Thus, the structure of the Soviet Union's special propaganda agencies targeting the enemy troops and population at the start of the Great Patriotic War can be represented in the following diagram. The diagram of the Soviet Union's special propaganda apparatus at the start of the Great Patriotic War In conclusion, it can be concluded that by the beginning of the Great Patriotic War, the structure of the apparatus of special propaganda had already been created, which, nevertheless, during the course of the war will undergo some necessary changes due to the increase in the scale and effectiveness of this work. However, this work began too late, preventing the necessary experience from being accumulated. Furthermore, due to unjustified restrictions on the study of information materials from the Nazi bloc countries, by the outbreak of the war there was no true picture of the processes taking place in Germany and its allies. This led to the Red Army's ignorance and misperception of the enemy soldiers' morale and psychological state. This resulted in failures in conducting special propaganda against the enemy during the initial period of the war. Naturally, the forced, constant retreat of Soviet troops during that difficult period contributed to the failures in disseminating propaganda against German soldiers. The next article will examine in detail the initial successes and failures in conducting political work among enemy troops. NOTES: 1 N.N. Bernikov. movement_title: 苏联建立第七局构建卫国战争初期对敌宣传体系
movement_abstract: 1940 年 4 月至 5 月，苏联红军总政治部在总结苏芬战争经验后，由斯大林主持成立特别委员会，决定建立针对敌军的特种宣传体系。1940 年 8 月，红军总政治宣传局（GUPPKA）下设第七局，由米哈伊尔·布尔特塞夫少校领导，负责研究敌国政治心理、制定宣传策略及培训外语宣传员。该体系在列宁格勒、西部等边境军区及方面军政治部设立对应机构，并依托莫斯科第二外语师范学院等机构培养专业人才。1941 年 6 月 25 日，联共（布）中央成立军事政治宣传局，第七局作为其执行机构，统筹塔斯社、苏联新闻局等媒体资源。尽管体系架构已成型，但因战前对德国情报研究受限、德语人才短缺及误判德军士气，导致卫国战争初期对德宣传效果不佳。1941 年 6 月 22 日战争爆发后，第七局迅速调整，设立针对德国及其盟友的专门部门，并配合游击队利用苏联新闻局信息在占领区开展反法西斯宣传。

author_name: By John Murray, Dr. Elise Annett, and Dr. James Giordano
content: that a central challenge of cognitive warfare is governing the relationship between institutional cognition and an operational environment in which informational, behavioral, and social dynamics evolve continuously and often independently of military decision timelines. To meet this challenge, we propose that future command architectures should emphasize and integrate mechanisms for the adaptive synchronization of human judgment, AI, and the cognitive ecosystem being engaged. This approach augments extant theories of command by recognizing that operational advantage emerges from maintaining temporal alignment between institutional decision-making and the environment in which decisions are executed and incur effects. One method of constructing such an architecture is to reconsider the roles of humans and AI across the decision cycle. If a temporal gap arises because human-paced observation, decision, and execution cannot keep pace with an environment that continues to evolve in the interim, the relevant question becomes which functions must remain human and which can be delegated to AI systems better capable of synchronizing with the cognitive environment. This reframing shifts the challenge from one of tempo alone to one of function reallocation. We posit that the resulting approach entrusts speed-bound functions to AI systems operating under human direction while preserving human judgment, accountability, situational interpretation, and . . This figure consists of two panels depicting a decision cycle along a left-to-right temporal axis. Red segments denote machine-executed functions and blue segments denote human judgment and authority. Dotted vertical lines mark points of ecosystem sampling and downward arrows indicate human discretion exercised over machine-executed functions. The current model (top) confines machine execution to the front and back ends of the cycle, whereas the proposed model (bottom) relocates the human to a supervisory position above the cycle. Figure 2 illustrates both a current and proposed model of human-machine teaming with two panels depicting a decision cycle (i.e., observe, orient, decide, act) along a temporal axis. In doing so, Figure 2 contrasts the current distribution of engagement with the proposed reallocation of human and machine function across the decision cycle. In the regnant loop, machine systems perform the front-end functions of the observe and orient stages by analyzing the operational environment and processing the resulting data for human interpretation. At the back end of the decision cycle, they execute the functions of the action stage by implementing orders issued by human decision-makers. Between these nodes, humans sustain a continuous arc of involvement. Consequently, ecosystem sampling occurs only at the boundaries of these stages, such that institutional understanding is dependent upon a small number of episodic observations acquired early in the cycle. As the cycle advances at human tempo, assessments generated upon initial observation risk losing relevance before decisions can be executed. The proposed model addresses this misalignment by relocating human involvement from within the decision cycle to a supervisory position across it. Here, the human directs and bounds machine systems that execute functions at a tempo the human observer could not achieve unaided. As noted, the vertical arrows indicate how human discretion is exercised continuously over machine function by establishing command intent, parameters, and engagement criteria within which sensing, orientation, and execution proceed. Because these functions are no longer rate-limited by human throughput, the cognitive ecosystem is sampled at a higher frequency, as indicated by the increased density of sampling lines beneath the observe, orient, and act stages. Institutional understanding under this model thereby tracks the evolving environment rather than capturing a series of static snapshots. Decision authority, however, remains a wholly human function in both configurations. As illustrated in the lower panel of Figure 2, the reintroduction of direct human control at the decisional point functions as a guardrail, preserving human judgment, accountability, and responsibility for the use of force even as other functions are executed at machine speed. Delegation of the decisional point to machine interfaces would achieve synchronization at the cost of accountability for the use of force, which we regard as an . The operational implications of this analysis extend beyond the optimization of decision speed and refinement of existing C2 processes. Cognitive environments should therefore not be regarded as static operational conditions to be episodically observed and acted upon. Instead, the object of decision evolves continuously through (1) persistent human interaction, (2) algorithmically mediated information exchange, and (3) increasingly autonomous computation. The operational relevance of any decision is therefore determined both by its velocity and by the extent to which institutional cognition remains synchronized with the evolving . Consequently, temporal synchronization should stand as a complementary principle of military decision theory that extends Boyd's OODA construct. Whereas Boyd demonstrated that adaptive orientation and competitive tempo are central to operational advantage, we argue that this understanding should be broadened to recognize cognition as a biopsychosocial and institutional process in which operational consequences recursively shape future decision-making. Within this framework, the ongoing evolution of the cognitive ecosystem during the execution of each decision cycle emerges as an additional operational variable. Decisional superiority will thus depend increasingly upon preserving coherence between institutional understanding and an operational environment in constant flux. AI assumes importance within this context because it enables persistent observation, continuous contextual integration, predictive analysis, and adaptive decision support across . Properly governed, these capabilities position human-AI teaming to sustain alignment between evolving operational conditions and institutional understanding while preserving the indispensable human roles of judgment, strategic reasoning, ethical deliberation, accountable command, and missional responsibility. Within this paradigm, human cognition and AI are best regarded and engaged as reciprocally complementary capabilities within an adaptive . More broadly, we perceive that this relationship reflects an evolution in the character of command. As military operations become increasingly data-intensive, distributed, and AI-enabled, command advantage will derive less from accelerating individual decision cycles in isolation than from the sustained governance of cognition across interconnected human-machine . Accordingly, future C2 architectures should increase computational speed while preserving alignment among command intent, institutional understanding, computational processes, and environmental change. We believe that decision superiority in AI-enabled warfare will increasingly depend upon this capacity for synchronized cognition and therefore regard temporal synchronization as an essential element of cognitive governance through which military organizations can integrate and sustain AI while preserving accountable human authority. The views and opinions expressed in this essay are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the United States government, Department of War, or the National Defense University. Mr. John Murray is a Research Intern in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare at the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and a graduate candidate in the Master of Public Administration program at Auburn University. Dr. Elise Annett is a Research Fellow in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University. Dr. James Giordano is Head of the Center for Strategic Deterrence and Weapons of Mass Destruction Studies of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and serves as NDU Special Advisor to the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War (CBRN).
title: Decision Advantage in Cognitive Warfare, Part 2
movement_title: 美国国防大学提出人机协同认知同步指挥架构
movement_abstract: 美国国防大学国家战略研究所研究人员约翰·默里、伊莉丝·阿内特和詹姆斯·吉奥尔达诺提出，认知战的核心挑战在于治理机构认知与持续演变的作战环境之间的关系。文章建议未来指挥架构应强调并整合机制，以实现人类判断、人工智能与认知生态系统的自适应同步。该方案主张将受速度限制的功能委托给人工智能系统，同时保留人类在判断、问责、情境解释及决策权威方面的核心作用。研究对比了当前模型与提议模型：当前模型中人类处于决策循环内部，导致环境采样频率低且易滞后；提议模型将人类置于监督位置，通过设定意图和参数持续指导机器执行，从而在保持人类问责的前提下实现高频环境采样。文章指出，决策优势将取决于机构理解与动态环境之间的连贯性，时间同步应作为军事决策理论的补充原则。在人工智能赋能的战争中，指挥优势将源于对互联人机系统的认知持续治理，而非单纯加速单个决策循环。

author_name: By Dr. James Giordano and Dr. Robert Schmidle
content: Every competitive or conflictive human activity wields some form of power in attempt to affect . Diplomacy seeks to influence it through politics; economic sanctions seek to modify it through the distribution and access of goods; military operations seek to compel it through the threat or use of force; and information operations seek to shape it through exerting influence upon thought, attitudes, values and emotion. In all cases, whether acting upon policy makers, civilian populations, warfighters, and/or their commanders, all such strategic endeavors ultimately engage and operate through the human nervous system. Thus, the brain serves as the mediator of all enterprises of cooperation,or . Cognitive warfare certainly operates in and upon psychological and social dimensions of human action, but differs from historical forms of influence in the increasing ability to understand and exploit the neural substrates and mechanisms that contribute to, if not directly subserve thought, emotion, judgment, and . Contemporary neuroscience provides an iteratively expanding set of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) data of the biological “terrain and conditions” in which cognitive warfare could be . We opine that the emergence of the brain-as-battlespace can be seen as a significant evolution in tactical nuance and strategic competition, as near future conflicts are likely to be defined and determined by who best employs such ISR to understand and influence the cognitive processes that shape human perception and action. Neuroscientific studies have demonstrated that cognition occurs through dynamic interactions among distributed, networked systems of the brain, which coordinate activity to continuously integrate internal and (for overview, see DiEuliis and Giordano). As schematically depicted in Figure 1, several neural systems are particularly relevant to cognitive warfare. Particularly, the salience network (which involves the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex) functions to identify information deemed important for survival and action. The default mode network supports self-referential thought, identity formation, memory integration, and narrative construction. Executive control networks (of the prefrontal cortex) are involved in planning, judgment, behavioral regulation, and decision-making; and limbic structures (e.g., the amygdala, hippocampus, and fornix) contribute to memory consolidation, threat detection, emotional processing, and affective learning, all of which evolved to support adaptive survival. : Diagrammatic representation of major functional networks in the human brain. Note that while defined aggregates of neural nodes and assemblies subtend types of cognitive functions and activities, there is some overlap of different networks’ involvement of brain structures and regions. Human cognition relies upon mental heuristics, biases, assumptions, and predictive mechanisms that frequently substitute accuracy for . These adaptive features can be targeted as exploitable vulnerabilities, and cognitive warfare seeks to identify these substrates and leverage such susceptibilities. One of the more influential models in contemporary neuroscience is predictive processing and coding theory, which establishes that the brain functions as an active prediction . Accordingly, the brain continuously generates representations of reality and compares incoming information against those expectations such that perception becomes an act of prediction. Thus, individuals actively filter incoming information according to dispositions formed by prior experiences, extant beliefs, emotions, expectations, and sociocultural frameworks. When incoming information confirms dispositional biases and expectations, cognitive “flow” is consonant and perceptions remain stable; when information conflicts with expectations, a condition of cognitive dissonance occurs, and existing schemas of reality must be modified, and/or incoming information (and decision trajectories) must be adapted. This reflects the well-known , and expands the construct to entails prior dispositions and biases, and the interpretive function of consequential effects of behavior (viz., a ; see Figure 2). This process is fundamental to understanding cognitive warfare.
