Iterative experience(s) establish dispositional cognitions (i.e., biases) against which cognitive engagements of present factors are compared and appraised (via Bayesian dynamics) to influence initiation, extent and type of observation(s) and evaluative orientation(s). Relative valence of orienting processes as relevant to current factors, and reflective of prior value-based (cognitively biased) recollections (casuistically) inform and afford purchase to decisional options (that are weighted against prior experiential cognitions/memories, and their attendant emotional register) to (1) predict possible outcomes of different action effects and trajectories, and (2) compel action selection and execution. The (immediate and latent) consequences of action(s) are cognitively appraised relative to cognitive and emotional valences of prior experiences and actions. Consequences that are aligned with prior biases and expectations are positively reinforced, while those that are not prompt discordance. Additional details in text. Influence operations succeed because information (positively or negatively) interacts with pre-existing cognitive architectures. Narratives that align with existing beliefs (i.e., which are cognitively consonant) can propagate rapidly. Information that challenges core constructs, values and/or identities (i.e., which are cognitively dissonant) may be rejected regardless of objective accuracy. Thus, successful cognitive engagement depends upon (1) understanding how brains construct reality, and (2) by controlling the information itself. Trust determines whether information is accepted, rejected, amplified, or ignored, and thus one of the most important variables in cognitive warfare. Neuroscientific studies have demonstrated that feelings of trust occur through interactions of the brain’s mechanisms involved in social affiliation, group membership, cooperation, empathy, and collective . Humans exhibit strong tendencies toward in-group preference and out-group disfavor, and these tendencies may be amplified during periods of uncertainty, perceived threat, or social instability. Identity-based narratives, memes and semiotics exert influence because they engage these neural systems, and adversarial cognitive operations can exploit identity dynamics by targeting perceptions of belonging, legitimacy, victimization, grievance, and collective . The objective is to alter the social and emotional frameworks through which reality is interpreted, and in this way, affect individual and collective action. Neurocognitive processes can be targeted indirectly or . Most current cognitive warfare activities operate indirectly, by manipulating socio-environmental inputs via information ecosystems (e.g., digital media, social networks, algorithmic recommendation systems, news platforms, entertainment channels, and interpersonal communication) to influence neural processing to affect behavior “downrange.” Emotional content activates attentional systems; threat-related information engages defensive circuitry; social validation or disruption differentially activates reward networks; and narratives shape memory consolidation. With robust and/or repeated exposure, these effects accumulate such that beliefs become reinforced, attitudes become entrenched, and behavioral tendencies can become . This approach is a subtle, yet powerful feature of cognitive engagement, as it exploits natural neurocognitive mechanisms via indirect means that can be difficult to detect and directly attribute. Although indirect approaches to cognitive warfare are currently predominant, emerging technologies are increasingly enabling more direct assessment and potential modulation of neural activity. For example, advances in multimodal neuroimaging (e.g., convergent use of functional magnetic resonance imaging [fMRI], functional near infrared imaging [fNIR], magnetoencephalography [MEG], high-density quantitative electroencephalography [qEEG]) now afford ability for increasingly detailed observation, analyses and correlation of brain structure and functions. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) afford tools for sophisticated communication between neural systems and computational platforms, and neural decoding methods have made it possible to identify brain nodes and networks involved in perception, attention, intention, emotional state, and decision-making that could be targeted and modulated using ever more specific drugs, toxins, microbes, and devices (e.g., directable sonic and/or electromagnetic ). While limitations remain, these developments illustrate a notable trend toward increasing ability to assess, access and affect neurocognitive processes. Tactically and strategically, this affords capability for more diversified, and thus greater means of influence. The convergence of neuroscience, behavioral science, and computational analytics is transforming understanding and accessibility of human cognition at scale. Historically, neuroscientific research has focused upon individuals, with studies conducted in controlled environments. While valuable, these approaches can be inadequate for understanding how cognitive processes occur and manifest effect in large populations, and/or how collective behavior arises from individual . However, as we have , big data methods and technologies are affording capabilities to accumulate, assimilate, synthesize and analyze a huge amount of vastly different types and levels of information. Artificial intelligence systems can analyze big datasets to identify behavioral patterns, cognitive/emotional tendencies, preferences, vulnerabilities and volatilities, and do so in ways that enable individual-to-group and group-to-individual comparisons and norming. For example, machine learning systems are capable of integrating biological, psychological, social, cultural, economic, and informational variables simultaneously to identify patterns, correlations, and predictive relationships within datasets. The resulting capability is referred to as population . Population neuroanalytics enable improved understanding of neural, psychological, and behavioral processes at scale by identifying recurring patterns and relationships between neural mechanisms, psychological tendencies, social interactions, and collective action(s). While totally accurate (viz., “perfect”) prediction remains unrealistic, ever more sophisticated probabilistic models are now achievable. A next step beyond population neuroanalytics is development of synthetic cognitive modeling. Advances in computational neuroscience, agent-based modeling, machine learning, and digital-twin technologies are feasible for creating virtual representations of individuals, organizations, and populations. Of course, such models do not replicate actual brains, but instead afford simulacra of cognitive and behavioral tendencies based upon known relationships among neural, psychological, sociological, cultural, and environmental variables; the strategic utility of these systems is their ability to evaluate possible futures. Indubitably, all models possess limitations, and human behavior remains inherently complex, adaptive, and often unpredictable. Yet even imperfect predictive capability can afford significant strategic advantage, as synthetic cognitive environments may become indispensable tools for operational planning, deterrence and defense. To wit, synthetic cognitive modeling can provide valuable capabilities within the cognitive domain, given that such models may enable identification of several factors and functions, as summarized in Table 1. • Emerging social tensions • Declining institutional trust • Radicalization pathways • Information contagion dynamics • Social fragmentation indicators • Cognitive resilience factors • Decision-making vulnerabilities • Behavioral responses to crises In effect, the convergent use of big data techniques and tools, and AI enables far more nimble and thus functionally adaptive cognitive engagement, to instantiate a shift from mass persuasion toward precision influence. In this light, near future cognitive operations could be likened to precision-guided weaponry directed against specific targets rather than generalized assault. However, target specificity does not negate the viability or value of more broadly directed targeting. Indeed, the cognitive condition of populations can be a critical strategic variable and leveraging factor. Historically, the extrapolation of individual data to collective relevance has been difficult, given that no two brains are identical. Individuals differ genetically, developmentally, culturally, socially, and experientially. Moreover, collective behavior emerges through interactions among individuals rather than simple aggregation of individual traits. This complexity has limited attempts to extrapolate directly from neuroscience to population behavior. But the aforementioned scientific and technological developments are reducing, if not overcoming many of these impediments; and thus, the “brain-as-battlespace” of cognitive warfare is poised upon a cusp of capability. Throughout history, military power has depended upon understanding critical domains of engagement and effect. To be sure, the aforementioned convergence of neuroscience, big data, AI, biotechnology, and information technology creates a new engagement environment that we believe could be regarded as the milieu of neurocognitive strategic competition. Currently, states that successfully integrate these disciplines could acquire unprecedented capabilities to understand and shape human thought and behavior. The implications extend beyond military operations. Political stability, economic confidence, social cohesion, and national resilience all depend upon such cognitive factors. Accordingly, we argue that cognitive security must become a central component of national security. To remain apace of, if not preferably ahead of peer-competitors’ and adversarial developments, we advocate that the DoW should establish an interdisciplinary and operationally focused . Toward such an enterprise, the following lines of effort are proposed: 1. , to develop methods and improved tools to assess cognitive vulnerabilities and resilience across military forces, governmental institutions, and critical populations. 2. , toward advancing understanding of relationships among neural architectures and mechanisms, cognitive processes, behavioral dynamics, social cohesion, and strategic stability. 3. to create systems capable of monitoring evolving cognitive and emotional trends that are relevant to national security. 4. to develop technologies that enhance decision-making while preserving human judgment and ethical oversight. 5. aimed at identifying methods to strengthen resistance against manipulation, misinformation, coercion, and adversarial influence. 6. to monitor global developments in neuroscience, neurotechnology, AI-enabled behavioral systems, and related dual-use capabilities. 7. to develop rigorous methodologies for measuring cognitive effects and evaluating operational outcomes. 8. ensuring responsible development and use of cognitive-security capabilities. Toward achieving these ends, we offer the following recommendations: 1. The DoW should establish a permanent cross-functional organization integrating expertise from neuroscience, behavioral science, biotechnology, AI, strategic deterrence, and military planning. 2. A dedicated intelligence effort should continuously monitor foreign developments in neurotechnology, computational neuroscience, cognitive warfare, AI-enabled behavioral analytics, and related dual-use capabilities. Particular attention should focus upon activities conducted by China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea. 3. The Department should establish secure infrastructures capable of integrating behavioral, informational, sociological, and neurocognitive datasets while maintaining appropriate legal and ethical safeguards. Such architectures will be essential for future cognitive-security operations and analyses. 4. Training, education, leader development, and force-preparation programs should incorporate cognitive-security principles. The objective should be development of cognitively resilient personnel, organizations, and populations capable of recognizing and resisting adversarial influence efforts. 5. Long-term investment is required. Short funding cycles are insufficient for sustained advancement in neuroscience and technology, big data, and AI. A dedicated research portfolio should be established comparable to historical investments in nuclear deterrence, cyber security, and biodefense. The future of strategic competition will be defined and determined by the ability to understand, influence, protect, and defend the human cognitive processes that shape perception, judgment, decision-making, and behavior. Advances in neuroscience are revealing the neural substrates that are involved in and subserve thought, emotion, and action. Concomitant advances in big data and AI are enabling unprecedented capacity to examine relationships between individual cognition and collective behavior. Taken together, these developments have established cognition as a domain of tactical accessibility, strategic relevance and operational viability and value. Adversaries recognize this reality and are actively pursuing capabilities designed to exploit cognitive vulnerabilities, manipulate perceptions, degrade trust, and influence thought, emotion and . The U.S. cannot afford to regard such developments as merely academic or theoretical but instead should acknowledge and respond to such advancements as emerging risks and threats to national security. Thus, the challenge and opportunity for DoW is to strengthen the scientific, technological, operational, and ethical foundations necessary to successfully secure and protect the neurocognitive domain. Indubitably, success of an enterprise of this magnitude will necessitate sustained investment, interdisciplinary collaboration, strategic foresight, and whole-of-nation . As previous generations developed doctrines for nuclear deterrence, and biological and chemical weapons governance and control, we opine that it is now vital to develop a coherent doctrine of cognitive security and neurostrategic competition. For in this emerging environment, strategic advantage will increasingly belong to those who most effectively understand and protect the biological, psychological and social dimensions that influence human thought, emotion, judgment, and action. The views and opinions expressed in this essay are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the United States government, Department of War, or the National Defense University. Dr. James Giordano is Head of the Center for Strategic Deterrence and Study of Weapons of Mass Destruction, and Program Lead for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University. He is also Professor Emeritus of Neurology, Biochemistry, and Ethics at Georgetown University Medical Center. Dr. Robert Schmidle (LtGen, USMC, ret) is a Professor of Professional Practice in the Irregular Warfare Center at the Arizona State University.

movement_abstract: 美国国防大学国家战略研究所詹姆斯·吉奥尔达诺博士与罗伯特·施米德尔博士发表文章，提出将认知安全确立为国家安全核心组成部分。文章指出，随着神经科学、大数据与人工智能的融合，大脑已成为新的战略竞争领域，即“神经认知战略竞争”。对手正积极利用神经技术、计算神经科学及AI行为分析系统，针对人类认知漏洞进行操纵，以影响感知、判断及行为。文章建议美国国防部（DoW）建立跨职能常设组织，整合神经科学、行为科学、生物技术及AI专家。具体行动包括：开发评估认知脆弱性与韧性的工具；建立监测全球神经技术及AI行为系统发展的情报机制，重点关注中国、俄罗斯、伊朗及朝鲜的活动；构建安全基础设施以整合多源数据；将认知安全原则纳入人员培训与部队准备；设立长期研究投资组合以支持相关技术发展。文章强调，未来战略优势将取决于对生物、心理及社会维度的理解与保护能力，需制定类似核威慑的连贯认知安全学说。

content: The contemporary information environment is characterized by unprecedented levels of connectivity, exposure, and competition for human attention. While information has become abundant, the cognitive capacity required to process it remains limited. This article argues that information overload can generate cognitive fatigue by overloading attention, degrading memory, and reducing decision-making quality. These effects create vulnerabilities that may be exploited within the cognitive dimension of conflict, not necessarily by altering beliefs directly, but by diminishing the capacity for critical information processing. Drawing upon research on attention, cognitive fatigue, memory, and decision-making, the article examines how excessive information exposure can affect individual and collective cognitive performance. It concludes that cognitive readiness should be treated as a component of societal resilience and proposes cognitive defense measures designed to preserve cognitive effectiveness in increasingly saturated information environments. In contemporary information environments, strategic effects can be achieved not only through persuasion or coercion, but also through saturation. When individuals are exposed to an overwhelming volume of information, their ability to process, prioritize, and make decisions may deteriorate. In this sense, information overload is more than a byproduct of the digital age; it represents a potential vulnerability that can be exploited within the cognitive dimension of conflict. The scale of today’s information ecosystem is unprecedented. Hilbert and López estimated that, between 1985 and 2007, global telecommunication by approximately 28 percent annually, while broadcasting capacity increased by 6 percent per year. This expansion was driven by the rapid diffusion of digital technologies, including personal computers, smartphones, and internet connectivity. Nearly two decades later, the trend has accelerated. According to the DataReportal 2025 Global Overview Report, more than six billion people — approximately 73 percent of the world’s population — , while 5.66 billion actively participate in social media platforms. The significance of these figures extends beyond connectivity. Social media users collectively spend consuming, sharing, and reacting to information. Such sustained exposure places increasing demands on human attention and cognition. As , attention can be overwhelmed, manipulated, or redirected, generating cognitive stress and reducing individuals’ capacity to process information effectively. This emerging reality raises an important strategic concern. If information can be used not only to influence perceptions but also to exhaust cognitive capacity, then cognitive readiness becomes a critical element of societal resilience. This article argues that developing cognitive readiness is essential to mitigate the effects of cognitive fatigue generated by information overload and to preserve decision-making capacity in increasingly contested information environments. The central question guiding this discussion is straightforward yet consequential: What happens when a society becomes cognitively exhausted? To address this question, the article first examines the scale of contemporary information exposure and the growing demands it places on human attention. It then discusses the relationship between information overload, cognitive fatigue, and decision-making performance, highlighting how excessive informational stimuli can degrade individual and collective cognitive capacity. Finally, the article argues that cognitive readiness should be understood as a critical component of societal resilience and proposes measures to strengthen the ability of individuals and institutions to operate effectively in increasingly saturated information environments. The contemporary information environment is characterized by an unprecedented level of connectivity and continuous exposure to digital content. According to the , more than six billion people — approximately 74 percent of the world’s population — are connected to the internet. This represents an increase of nearly one billion users compared to the previous year, demonstrating the rapid expansion of digital access across societies. At the same time, social media platforms have become central nodes of information consumption, reaching approximately 5.79 billion users worldwide, equivalent to 69.9 percent of the . The significance of these figures lies not only in the number of connected individuals but also in the amount of time devoted to digital engagement. Collectively, internet users spend an estimated on average. In 2025,spend approximately 2 hours and 23 minutes per day interacting with digital platforms. In at least twenty countries, daily social media use exceeds the global average, further intensifying exposure to continuous information flows. As a result, a substantial portion of the world’s population remains connected to an environment characterized by permanent streams of news, entertainment, advertisements, social interactions, and algorithmically curated content. This level of exposure represents a significant departure from previous communication eras. Individuals are no longer exposed to information at discrete moments through newspapers, radio broadcasts, or scheduled television programs. Instead, smartphones and digital platforms provide a persistent connection to a virtually uninterrupted information ecosystem. The competition for attention has consequently become a defining feature of the contemporary information environment, with governments, corporations, media organizations, and other actors simultaneously seeking to influence what people notice, believe, and remember. The strategic implication is clear: Before information can influence attitudes or behaviors, it must first compete for limited human attention. Understanding the scale of this exposure is therefore essential to understanding how cognitive fatigue emerges and why cognitive readiness has become increasingly important for both individuals and societies. Attention is arguably the most valuable resource in the contemporary information environment. While the volume of available information continues to expand, the human capacity to process it remains limited. This imbalance creates a vulnerability that can be exploited within the cognitive domain. As , cognitive warfare seeks to influence perceptions, attitudes, and behaviors. Achieving this objective first requires gaining access to an individual’s attentional resources. Information therefore becomes not only a means of communication but also a tool for capturing, directing, or manipulating attention. Lindsay as the flexible control of limited cognitive resources, enabling individuals to prioritize relevant information while suppressing competing stimuli. Because these resources are finite, increasing informational demands reduce the ability to focus, evaluate information, and make sound judgments. Attention therefore acts as a bottleneck in human information processing. Grigsby et al. as an important cognitive vulnerability. Rather than persuading a target directly, adversaries may achieve strategic effects by overwhelming attentional capacity. Under such conditions, individuals struggle to distinguish relevant information from noise, prioritize competing demands, and maintain situational awareness. Herbert Simon’s that “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention” remains particularly relevant in contemporary information environments. As the volume of available information exceeds human processing capacity, attention becomes an increasingly scarce strategic resource. As information volume exceeds processing capacity, attention becomes fragmented and cognitive resources become increasingly strained. In this sense, information saturation is more than a communication challenge; it is a mechanism capable of generating cognitive fatigue and reducing cognitive resilience. If attention is a finite cognitive resource, sustained demands on attention inevitably affect cognitive performance. In contemporary information environments, individuals are continuously exposed to large volumes of information competing for limited attentional capacity. When the volume, complexity, and frequency of incoming information exceed an individual’s ability to process them effectively, attention overload emerges. This condition is not merely a form of distraction; it is a precursor to cognitive fatigue. Giordano that cognitive overload means: “toward degrading information processing and decision-making capacity”. Because cognitive resources are limited, every additional informational demand requires greater mental effort to maintain focus, process content, and update situational awareness. As this effort becomes prolonged, individuals find it increasingly difficult to distinguish relevant signals from background noise, sustain concentration, and allocate attention efficiently. Borragán et al. as a state resulting from increased cognitive load over a limited period while processing ongoing cognitive demands. Their experimental findings suggest that fatigue is driven less by the complexity of a task than by the continuous mental effort required to sustain information processing. In other words, cognitive fatigue emerges not only from difficult tasks, but also from persistent exposure to cognitive demands without adequate recovery. This phenomenon has important implications for decision-making. Steward and Chib that cognitive fatigue plays a critical role in effort-based decisions, influencing the willingness of individuals to invest cognitive resources in analytical tasks. As fatigue increases, people become less inclined to engage in effortful reasoning and more likely to rely on simplified judgments, heuristics, and intuitive responses. From the perspective of cognitive warfare, this dynamic is strategically significant. Influence does not necessarily require persuading a target audience to adopt a particular narrative. It may be sufficient to degrade its capacity for critical information processing. By saturating the information environment with excessive, repetitive, contradictory, or emotionally charged content, adversaries can increase cognitive load and accelerate the onset of fatigue. The objective is not simply to shape what people think, but to impair how effectively they think. Consequently, cognitive fatigue should not be viewed solely as an individual psychological condition. In highly connected societies, persistent exposure to overwhelming information flows can produce collective effects, reducing a population’s ability to evaluate information critically, identify manipulation, and sustain informed decision-making. Cognitive fatigue therefore represents not only a human-factor challenge but also a strategic vulnerability within contemporary information environments. Attention and memory are closely interconnected cognitive functions. Information that does not receive sufficient attentional resources is less likely to be effectively encoded, stored, or retrieved. Consequently, when attention becomes overloaded, memory performance declines. According to Lindsay,by allocating limited cognitive resources to relevant information. In contemporary information environments, where individuals constantly alternate between messages, notifications, and digital platforms, attention becomes fragmented, and memory formation suffers. Information overload further amplifies this problem. Excessive information can overwhelm working memory, making it more difficult to distinguish relevant content from irrelevant stimuli. As a result, individuals may retain isolated facts while losing the broader context necessary for accurate interpretation. This has important implications for cognitive warfare. Memory supports situational awareness by connecting past experiences with present circumstances. When memory processes are degraded, individuals become more vulnerable to misinformation, repetition effects, and rapidly changing narratives. Rather than replacing memories, information saturation can create uncertainty about what information should be retained, trusted, or recalled. In this way, degraded memory becomes another pathway through which information overload weakens cognitive resilience. The cumulative effects of attention overload, cognitive fatigue, and memory degradation ultimately converge in the decision-making process. Because decisions depend on acquiring, processing, retaining, and evaluating information, disruptions in these cognitive functions directly affect judgment and performance. Simon observed that an abundance of information creates a poverty of attention,to operate under conditions where available information exceeds their capacity for evaluation. Under these circumstances, individuals are more likely to simplify complex problems, ignore relevant information, or rely on cognitive shortcuts. Roetzel that information overload emerges when information demands exceed processing capacity, reducing the ability to identify the optimal course of action. Instead of producing better decisions, excessive information often generates uncertainty, hesitation, and diminishing analytical returns. Cognitive fatigue intensifies this problem. As mental resources become depleted, individuals become less willing to engage in effortful reasoning and more likely to depend on heuristics, emotional reactions, and simplified narratives. For cognitive warfare practitioners, these effects present a strategic opportunity. By increasing information noise and cognitive strain, adversaries can shape the conditions under which decisions are made rather than the decisions themselves. When attention is saturated, memory fragmented, and fatigue present, the quality of both individual and collective decision-making deteriorates, reinforcing the importance of cognitive readiness in contested information environments. Cognitive warfare is often associated with influencing perceptions, beliefs, and behaviors. However, influence may also be achieved by degrading the cognitive functions that support critical thinking and decision-making. Rather than convincing individuals to adopt a specific narrative, adversaries can seek to reduce their capacity to process information effectively. The Russia–Ukraine War illustrates this challenge. Markova et al. high levels of news-related addiction, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and psychological distress associated with continuous exposure to war-related information. Their findings suggest that prolonged exposure to intensive information flows can contribute to cognitive and emotional exhaustion, reducing the ability to critically evaluate information. In this context, information overload functions as a force multiplier. By increasing information noise, fragmenting attention, and accelerating cognitive fatigue, it can reduce critical processing and create conditions that make individuals more susceptible to manipulation, misinformation, and influence operations. Cognitive warfare therefore targets not only what people think, but also their ability to think effectively. Figure 1. From Information to Objective of Cognitive Warfare Source: authors If information overload represents a cognitive vulnerability, cognitive readiness should be viewed as a form of defense. Drawing inspiration from public health, societies should promote principles of cognitive hygiene aimed at reducing unnecessary cognitive strain. These measures may include encouraging healthy information-consumption habits, limiting exposure to continuous information streams, promoting periodic disconnection from digital media, and fostering the use of reliable information sources. At the individual level, Arnold et al. specific training to reduce and prevent information overload. At the institutional level, governments and defense organizations should consider developing Cognitive Readiness Programs, comparable to existing physical and mental readiness initiatives. Such programs could provide training in attention management, recognition of information overload, and responsible information consumption practices. They could also support the development of indicators capable of identifying emerging patterns of cognitive fatigue within organizations and populations. Strengthening cognitive readiness will not eliminate information overload, but it can increase resilience against its effects. In increasingly contested information environments, protecting cognitive performance may become as important as protecting information itself. The contemporary information environment presents a paradox: never before have societies had access to so much information, yet the human capacity to process it remains fundamentally limited. As information exposure increases, attention becomes overloaded, cognitive fatigue accumulates, memory processes degrade, and decision-making quality declines. These effects create vulnerabilities that can be exploited within the cognitive dimension of conflict. Cognitive readiness is therefore essential to prevent and mitigate the effects of cognitive fatigue caused by information overload and to preserve decision-making capacity in saturated information environments. Information superiority alone is no longer sufficient. In the digital age, cognitive endurance may be equally important. The central challenge is not merely protecting societies from false information but preserving their ability to think critically under conditions of continuous information pressure. Indeed, the question for the twenty-first century may no longer be who controls information, but who can remain cognitively effective despite its abundance.

content: TOKYO, Aug 31 — Japan’s defence ministry requested a record budget of ¥8.9 trillion (RM220 billion) todayas Tokyo looks to artificial intelligence to speed up decision-making in the face of a tense security environment. The final budget reportedly could reach ¥10 trillion as Tokyo undergoes a sweeping upgrade of its defence in order to navigate growing tension with neighbours such as China, North Korea and Russia. The latest request focuses on countering “new ways of warfare”, with an emphasis on the use of AI, drones and standoff missiles. Under the request, the ministry hopes to implement an AI-powered decision support system. It also wants to procure low-cost drones that can work in tandem with long-range missiles to neutralise enemy assets. The ministry said it plans to develop underwater-launched hypersonic missiles and establish a new unit to bolster defences against cognitive warfare, a growing threat aimed at shaping public opinion through disinformation campaigns and other operations. The budget request for the fiscal year starting from April 2027 highlights the latest step by Japan to boost its military to meet the volatile geopolitical reality, gradually shedding its traditional pacifist stance that limited the use of force purely for self-defence. China’s rapid military expansion and North Korea’s steady development of missiles and nuclear weapons have pressed Japan to shore up its defence. Russia’s war in Ukraine has fuelled worries among Japanese policymakers that a similar conflict could erupt in East Asia, considering China’s mounting pressure on Taiwan and its escalating territorial disputes with Japan. — AFP

Shaun Neil, information warfare branch chief for the National Guard Bureau, attended a roundtable discussion focused on the future of training in the National Guard psychological operations officer community in Arlington, Va., Aug. 21, 2026. The changes to their training are designed to enhance readiness and interoperability and strengthen defense cooperation within the organization. (Photo Credit: Sgt. 1st Class Daisy Broker) VIEW ORIGINAL FORT BRAGG, N.C. — Eight Army National Guard information operations officers graduated from a newly developed Psychological Operations Qualification Course July 24 at the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School, marking a significant milestone in Army transformation. For the first time, Soldiers from all three components — Regular Army, National Guard and Army Reserve — are training together to combat modern cognitive warfare threats. As adversaries increasingly rely on sophisticated disinformation campaigns and information warfare to undermine global stability, the Army recognized a need for a unified response. The new integrated training model ensures that Army psychological operations and information operations professionals across the Total Army share a common baseline of skills and strategic understanding required to counter these evolving nonkinetic threats on the battlefield. "The Army National Guard's information warfare transformation is fundamentally prompted by the need to stay ahead of our adversaries' ever-changing threats through continuous innovation," said Brig. Gen. Isaac Martinez, assistant director of the Army National Guard for aviation, intelligence and information. Martinez explained that the constant threat of adversarial action drives changes to information operations, creating a need for Guard officers who can conduct rapid, strategic analysis and act accordingly. "Graduation from the 10-week pilot program at the U.S. Army John F. Kennedy Special Warfare Center and School is part of the National Guard's modernization effort in information warfare by introducing psychological operations officers to the Army National Guard landscape to conduct information warfare overseas," said Maj. Shaun Neil, information warfare branch chief for the National Guard Bureau. Despite conducting information operations for more than 20 years in support of conventional and special operations, this effort will close the Guard’s gap between planning and execution. "Historically, military information operations have suffered from technological operational delays," Martinez said. "Strategic planners would design operational packages and then wait on specialized execution groups to implement them." In the swiftly shifting space of digital information, these delays often rendered tactical responses obsolete before they could be fully deployed. "The course aims to prepare cross-functional leaders who can address planning and execution simultaneously, supporting faster decision-making on the battlefield," said Col. Kirsten Roy, commander of the Expeditionary Military Intelligence Brigade and Information Forces Modernization lead for the National Guard Bureau. Roy emphasized that this approach is fundamental in an environment where fast decision-making can determine mission success or failure. Developing leaders capable of managing planning and execution in real time is essential. "Speed is critical to mission execution," Roy said during a recent roundtable discussion about the Guard's broader modernization efforts. "The newly structured training has undergone two iterations and empowers officers to consolidate a wide array of previously disjointed capabilities, including intelligence gathering, data analysis, cyber warfare and electromagnetic warfare, and integrate them with psychological operations units. These newly minted officers are comprehensively equipped to implement the changes required to operate at the speed that modern, digital-first threats demand."
title: New PSYWAR course strengthens Guard capabilities

content: That’s the effect on me of this week’s UK Cabinet Office proclamations about families needing to lay in several days of food, water and energy supplies, in case of disasters. Those disasters are? A cyber-attack on our national systems by a hostile foreign power; or a disruptive, extreme weather event, whether water or heat. Not to forget the collapse of food supply chains or the next pandemic. Did I mention autonomous robots and super AIs? A deep horn sounds, warning that the UK Government ’s War Book is to be restored. This is a so-called “secret” document (not really, if it’s being trumpeted in UK Government’s comms) that lays out how all sectors of society are to coordinate themselves when these islands are under attack. READ MORE: Andy Burnham's PR bung for Sainsbury's hides a big, fat nothing The bit that concerns us punters is the stacking of tins, water barrels, batteries and wind-up radios. Otherwise, we leave the deep state to manage the crisis, exercising executive powers on our behalf against the declared enemy (seemingly and equally, Gaia or Vladimir Putin). I was struck by the year in which the War Book, in place since 1911, was stood down: 2004. A few years after 9/11 in Manhattan, a year before 7/7 in London – both blowbacks from the far-off second Gulf War. Putin was in Kyiv that year, campaigning for a pro-Russian presidential candidate. Yet still, it felt stable enough for the British state to go for peacetime contingency rather than war-fighting – that is, dropping its right to conscript citizens, intern them for refusing, ban industrial strikes. (I managed to get a book out that year too, titled – of all things – The Play Ethic. Blithe days). The current chat around the geopolitical watercoolers of London is that, given the perceived threat levels, an updated War Book is now required. Including those emergency executive powers? It’s all sotto voce at the moment. Someone you can rely on to say the quiet part loudly is Paul Mason, a man of the left but recently an enthusiastic advocate of strengthening the British military. His recent paper is explicit. The problem with the 2004 Civil Contingencies Act, replacing the War Book, is that it “cannot compel citizens to do military service; nor can it ban strikes or other industrial action”. Mason wants us to agree our position on consenting to the use of such emergency powers now, in peacetime and democratically, ahead of it being imposed when we suddenly have to deal with “kinetic war”. Good luck with getting that debate, Paul. Across major recent polling by YouGov and Ipsos, only around 6% to 11% of Britons state they would actively volunteer to fight if the UK faced an imminent military invasion – 41% report they wouldn’t take up arms under any circumstances. Draft agers (18- to 40-year-olds) state they would actively refuse conscription even in the event of a global war; this outnumbers those who say they would willingly accept a call-up. And apparently the most common reason for refusing service (21%) is an unwillingness to risk your life in order to defend corrupt elites and politicians. Another soldier-tastic source is Wilton Park’s recent report on UK “preparedness”. They’re candid about how they need to get a grip on recalcitrant minds. “Framings such as ‘we are at war’ are unlikely to prompt action”, they write. “More tangible entry points, such as climate resilience or emphasising the impact of real cyber attacks, such as those on Marks and Spencer or Jaguar Land Rover, could serve as testing grounds for models later applicable to defence…’Multi-hazard’ framing may be more accessible to the public than a single abstract national security narrative.” This explains the shenanigans behind this week’s stories. It’s associating the return of the War Book, and the militarised society it implies, with domestic resilience against the consequences of climate catastrophe, or the activity of criminal networks. Going in via the latter softens acceptance for the former. Sunset lights the sky over a Moscow district in Moscow, Russia (Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP) Mason is big on the Russian state’s perpetration of “cognitive warfare”. Which, says Nato, “disrupts individual perception, erodes psychological certainty, creates social polarisation, and degrades the democratic resilience of the state”. Isn’t the War Book story at least an attempt at “cognitive defence”? One of the suggestions from the Cabinet Office is the production of a booklet or pamphlet, summarising what’s expected of “prepared” families and communities. It’s on the model of a Swedish publication, sent to all homes, titled “In case of crisis or war”. I downloaded it – and most of one’s fluffier assumptions about Scandinavian life are stripped away immediately by the cover, which has a Swedish woman soldier grimly standing athwart the homeland, rifle at the ready. She’s defending a kindergarten scene; above them, bunting on one side, a fighter plane on the other. Page five is straightforward: “If Sweden is attacked, we will never surrender. Any suggestion to the contrary is false.” This is clearly a response to Russian disinformation strategies. But it’s also an expression of what the Swedes call Total Defence (Totalförsvarsplikt), which under Swedish law involves every resident from 16 to 70. This includes gender-neutral military draft (värnplikt) for 18-year-olds, as well as non-military civilian service (civilplikt) in sectors like emergency rescue and electricity supply; also, general workers to maintain everyday social functions. Preparedness is treated as a basic civic virtue, rather than fringe survivalism. (Denmark, Finland and Estonia – the latter two sharing borders with Russia – also take this approach). Is all this really coming our way? I have an oblique take on “preparedness”, given my involvement with democratic innovation through the Alternative Global and Spring. There is so much “resilience” and “capacity” being developed in ecologically minded communities all over the world. But most of them would fastidiously distinguish their notion of communal readiness for an implacably worsening climate situation from military concerns about threats to “critical social infrastructure.” Take the Lifehouse movement, based on the book of that title from techno-anarchist Adam Greenfield, and Jem Bendell’s Deep Adaptation network. Both propose setting up local initiatives which can be a material resource of skills, tools, supplies and deliberation, as the shocks of climate collapse multiply. Their belief is that such strengthening of capacity is intrinsically worth doing, involving a revaluation of the priorities in your personal and communal life – regardless of how much it protects you from a worsening climate. The lifehouse that helps you to deeply adapt to ever-tougher circumstances is attractive. It goes along with the current resistance to the heedless expansion of AI data centres and wind farms. But I have severe doubts that there are enough levels of trust, in the not-exactly-Scandinavian social fabric of these islands, for such resistance and autonomy to be put to national service. Could and should the Scottish Government distinguish itself from the militarisation of daily life implied by our submission to a “War Book”? The Scottish Government (Image: Jane Barlow) Because the geopolitics are not locked down. For one thing, our enemy may not be as implacable as he is often rendered. There’s a thousand deaths a day of Russian soldiery in Ukraine (Nato estimating that overall casualties – killed, wounded, and missing – are 1.2 million to 1.4m). With their war economy on shaky ground, indy-minded Scots should be readying themselves for Russia’s implosion as much as its expansion. I end this piece no less terrified than when I started. It feels like a degradation of the quality of our lives together, in the early 21st century - to reorder our relations and priorities according to the threat of war, at many different levels. Surely we have enough imagination and vision, even amidst the general exhaustion, to yearn and plan for much more?
title: As UK resurrects its War Book, would militarisation of our daily lives hold?

movement_abstract: 【英国《卫报》2026 年 8 月报道】英国内阁办公室近期发布声明，要求家庭储备数日食物、水和能源，以应对网络攻击、极端天气、供应链崩溃及大流行病等潜在灾难。此举标志着自 2004 年废止的《战时法案》（War Book）可能恢复。该法案曾赋予政府在战时征召公民、拘留拒服兵役者及禁止罢工等紧急行政权力。分析人士指出，当前舆论倾向于将军事动员与气候韧性及网络防御相结合，以降低公众对‘战争’叙事的抵触。威尔顿公园报告建议采用‘多灾害’框架替代单一国家安全叙事，以提升公众接受度。作为参照，瑞典推行‘总体防御’制度，法律规定 16 至 70 岁居民均有义务参与军事或民事服务，并分发《危机或战争指南》。然而，英国民意调查显示，仅 6% 至 11% 的民众愿在面临入侵时主动参战，41% 表示绝不拿起武器，年轻群体对强制征兵持强烈反对态度，主要理由是不愿为腐败精英冒险。尽管苏格兰政府面临是否区分自身与军事化日常生活的抉择，但英国政府正试图通过认知防御手段，将社会准备度转化为国家防御能力。

content: Forget “Let’s go fly a kite” from Mary Poppins. The song from Disney’s movie sends spirits soaring, but in Israel, post-October 7, 2023, kites are not symbols of innocent childhood fun. They have transformed from symbols of freedom into weapons of physical and psychological warfare. It’s evil, but brilliant. In 2018, first kites, then helium balloons, and later even condoms were attached to incendiary devices and explosives and left to float across the border into Israel. In a couple of particularly twisted cases, falcons were attached to burning devices and let loose to die on Israeli territory. It was eco-terrorism and scorched earth policy at its worst, destroying thousands of dunams of agricultural land, woods, and nature reserves, along with much of the wildlife that lived there. But only Israel was blamed, because it retaliated. As a PR ploy, it’s stunningly simple. When you place the image of kite-flying kids next to an image of a soldier, Hamas wins, and Israel loses. If Israel takes action, it is a brutal army; if it refrains from action, it will be portrayed as weak. Either way, it provides more fuel for future violence that serves Hamas and Islamist terrorism so well. And it didn’t stop there, as we now know. The March of Return was a declaration of intent, not a mere slogan. On October 7, 2023, thousands of Hamas-led terrorists invaded southern Israel, murdering, mutilating, raping, and carrying off captives. Communities were set on fire, homes were burned with families tied up inside, partygoers at the Supernova music festival and elsewhere were hunted down and killed wherever they sought shelter. Some 1,200 were murdered, and 251 were abducted to Gaza, of whom only 168 survived. The terrorists were so proud of their deeds that they boasted about them in real-time, recording rapes and murders on GoPro cameras and sharing images of death and destruction on social media, in some cases streaming it directly to the victims’ own friends and family to intensify the terror and pain. If you want to understand why, for Israelis, kites symbolize innocence lost, consider what happened to the annual “Kites for Freedom” festive event at Kibbutz Kfar Aza. For 15 years, local residents would send a message of peace and hope over the border to their neighbors in Gaza. In 2023, that year’s Kites for Freedom event was scheduled for October 7, the Jewish festival of Simchat Torah, but terrorists invaded the kibbutz in the early hours of the morning. Among the 60 members of Kibbutz Kfar Aza killed that day was Aviv Kutz, the founder of Kites for Freedom, who was murdered in his home with his wife and three children. Their bodies were found embracing each other on a bed in the safe room of their home. An entire family wiped out. In a statement this week, Hamas reportedly claimed the kites were just “children’s toys” from Gaza refugee camps and warned Israel against taking threatened actions. But these “toys” were attached to strings – in some cases 4 km.-long – and decorated with threatening slogans in Arabic. Mary Poppins it ain’t. It’s child abuse. Follow the thread, and it will lead you back to a Hamas terrorist, yet again shielding behind children. The world media, fed by reports from Gaza, is full of sob stories of poor refugee children just trying to have fun and are now being threatened by Israeli might. That Israeli children are learning to be wary of kites and balloons, which might be attached to explosive devices, does not seem to bother even those who profess to care for human rights. The trauma of Israeli children doesn’t count. PRESIDENT ISAAC HERZOG, visiting the South this week, met with residents to discuss their fears, and stressed that maintaining peace and security was the responsibility of not just the State of Israel but also of the international community. On Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz both declared that a return to the pre-October 7 days of the Gaza kite campaign would not be tolerated. On Monday, Israel reportedly gave a three-day ultimatum via the US-led international Board of Peace in Gaza that the kite launches be halted or that Gaza would face expanded targeted strikes. Katz declared that “a balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone.” Disturbingly, however, there are still drones carrying drugs and weapons that manage to cross the border from Egypt and Jordan into Israel. It does not take many steps to go from kite-running to arms-running and full-blown attacks. It’s been suggested that the kites might be employed without explosives or incendiary devices at this stage to gauge their range and where they land. One thing is clear: The kites are not toys; they’re a test, trying to ascertain at what point, and how, Israel will respond. The Foreign Ministry posted a message on X in different languages, including Farsi, saying: “Even a child’s toy can be turned into a weapon by Hamas… We will not tolerate attacks on civilians.” On Tuesday, the Board of Peace ordered that the kites be stopped but reportedly also warned Israel against taking action. DR. RON SCHLEIFER, an international expert on psychological warfare, says the use of the kites is an example, par excellence, of “an offensive strategy that operates in small steps.” “It’s called conditioning. The whole idea is that you don’t create havoc for a small step because you’ll look ridiculous… This is what Hamas is trying to achieve. “According to the doctrine of revolutionary warfare, every asset is dedicated toward victory, and that includes human lives – all human lives. The end justifies the means. It’s for the cause, and the cause is always ideological.” Schleifer acknowledges the intense inherent difficulties in explaining the situation to the world, which sees the Israeli army threatening Gazan children “playing” with kites. “It’s a very sophisticated trap. Their [Hamas] photographers are in the field and sharing the images with the international media, Reuters, AFP, etc. to see Israel’s response. Whatever the IDF does, it will not be good. “If it doesn’t respond, it will be stupid, and in the Middle East it will be well understood as a sign of weakness. If it acts against the children, it will be even worse. They are managing to put the IDF – their enemy – on the horns of the dilemma.” He supports the view of Netanyahu and Katz to treat every kite as a serious threat, and he is encouraged that Israel is “at last learning to understand the language of the Middle East.” “We saw what happened in 2018 with the March of Return when the kites became balloons and gradually turned into grenades and RPGs,” he says. “It’s genius.” There is no easy answer to the kites blowing in the wind, but there are certain actions that can be taken, according to Schleifer. Primarily, “Israel needs to turn to UNICEF [the United Nations children’s fund] and other children’s rights and human rights organizations in the West and show how Hamas shamelessly is exploiting children, not for the first time. You can also show the photos of the [Palestinian] children wearing [mock] explosive belts.”
title: My Word: The 'fight or flight' kite dilemma - opinion

content: August, 28, 2026 - 10:54 Politics news TEHRAN (Tasnim) – The IRGC Intelligence Organization said the US, the Zionist regime and their allies have acknowledged the failure of a strategy based on military strikes to undermine the Islamic Republic and are seeking to destabilize Iran through psychological, economic and security operations. Politics In a statement, the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps Intelligence Organization said assessments by US intelligence agencies indicate that Iran has moved beyond the stage of simply preserving its existence and has maintained its asymmetric capabilities, while also strengthening its national resilience and retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz. According to the statement, US intelligence assessments further indicate that Iran is no longer merely responding to attacks but is moving toward greater strategic initiative and increasing its ability to influence the timing, location and costs of war and diplomacy. The IRGC Intelligence Organization said a joint committee involving US, Israeli and British intelligence services, along with some anti-Iran opposition figures, had acknowledged the failure of the strategy of seeking regime change through military strikes. It said information obtained by the organization showed that the enemy is now updating that strategy. Under the new approach, limited periodic attacks would be maintained alongside the activation of crisis-generating centers, psychological warfare, efforts to create turmoil in currency and financial markets, and counter-security operations. The statement said the objective is to prevent the consolidation of domestic stability and Iran’s recovery of regional and extra-regional power by seeking to transform the “idea of resistance” into one of dependence, turn indigenous defense capabilities into dependent capabilities, and shift the country from a revolutionary approach toward a passive one. The IRGC Intelligence Organization also said it had recently detected and monitored a Mossad project aimed at creating a secret, dedicated structure to exert pressure on Iran from within. It said the structure’s tools included establishing links with dissident groups, conducting acts of sabotage and using harmful local operatives. The organization identified seven main areas of the enemy’s current efforts: - Undermining the role of the Strait of Hormuz in Iran’s national security;- Preventing Iran from repeating regional military action;- Portraying the Resistance Axis as having limited capabilities;- Imposing a maritime blockade;- Eroding national unity while promoting dissatisfaction, polarization and exaggerated portrayals of differences;- Exaggerating and exploiting domestic weaknesses, shortages and limitations;- Encouraging people to take their grievances to the streets. The statement said the main focus of the current strategy is to “disrupt stability and reduce the national resilience of Iranians” through cognitive warfare designed to generate fear and uncertainty. At the same time, the IRGC Intelligence Organization pointed to significant domestic constraints facing the US, including the dismissal, demotion or removal of more than 23 military commanders and dozens of political and intelligence officials opposed to the US administration, the negative effects of Iran’s regional actions on US economic indicators, declining popularity of US President Donald Trump, uncertainty over political support for the Israeli regime, and limitations on the US military’s ability to provide offensive and defensive combat support against Iran. The statement said the IRGC Intelligence Organization has consequently prioritized maintaining permanent military intelligence and readiness, countering actions that could undermine domestic calm, solidarity and cohesion, preventing hostile intelligence services from conducting security operations inside Iran and along its borders, and remaining vigilant against “neo-Daesh” elements and networks cooperating with terrorist groups. content: Iranian threats against American and Israeli leaders have expanded beyond presidents, military commanders, and senior policymakers to include members of their families. The immediate question is how much of the rhetoric represents psychological warfare and how much reflects preparations for actual operations. For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org Iranian state television broadcast a three-minute video this week targeting Barron Trump, the 20-year-old son of US President Donald Trump. Titled “Where To Kill Barron Trump?” the video purported to show information about locations associated with him, his security arrangements, and his movements. Produced by media affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and aired on Iran’s Channel 3, the footage claimed that a $10 million bounty had been offered for his killing. The purported bounty and alleged surveillance have not been independently verified, and no public evidence has emerged linking the broadcast to an operational Iranian assassination team. The US Secret Service said Tuesday that it was aware of the footage and investigates anything that could be perceived as a threat to its protectees, while declining to discuss protective intelligence. Screenshot of channel 3's video explaining how to kill Barron Trump. (credit: Screenshot/X/@GhorbaniiNiyak)Barron Trump assassination threat flanked by threats to Melania, Netanyahu familyThe Barron Trump video followed an earlier production released by the IRGC-affiliated Tasnim news agency focusing on First Lady Melania Trump. That broadcast, reportedly titled “Where to Kill Melania Trump?” presented alleged details about her movements and potential weaknesses in her security. Reports about the Melania video did not indicate that a comparable multimillion-dollar bounty had been offered. On Monday, Aug. 24, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu added another allegation. “Iran targeted one of my sons. Iran tried to kill, to murder one of my sons,” Netanyahu told Israel’s Channel 14. Netanyahu did not initially identify whether he was referring to Yair or Avner Netanyahu or say when or where the alleged attempt occurred. Newsmax reported Wednesday that Yair Netanyahu, the prime minister’s 35-year-old elder son, was the alleged target. Citing an unnamed US law enforcement source familiar with the matter, the outlet said Israeli intelligence learned in December 2025 that suspected Iranian operatives were in the Miami area conducting surveillance of his home and movements. Israeli officials alerted US authorities and instructed Yair Netanyahu to leave Florida immediately, according to Newsmax. He reportedly returned to Israel without collecting his belongings and has remained there. US and Israeli authorities have not publicly confirmed his identification as the alleged target or the operational details in the report. Israeli media had previously reported that the security establishment had known about the alleged threat for months and that details were subject to military censorship. Iran’s mission to the United Nations did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. Netanyahu made the disclosure while responding to reports that the Shin Bet security agency had declined to provide protection for political rival Gadi Eisenkot ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election. Netanyahu said the alleged threat against his son demonstrated that security protection was “not a luxury” and that appropriate protection should be provided to every candidate for prime minister. Iran has a documented history of pursuing targets overseas. In 2022, the US Justice Department charged IRGC member Shahram Poursafi with attempting to arrange the murder of former US National Security Adviser John Bolton. Prosecutors said the operation was likely intended as retaliation for the January 2020 killing of IRGC Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani. European governments have also accused Iran of using criminal networks as intermediaries. Sweden’s security service has accused Tehran of using criminal groups to target Israeli and Jewish interests, while the British government sanctioned the Swedish-based Foxtrot network in 2025 over attacks allegedly carried out on Iran’s behalf. In June 2026, the UK joined 22 other countries in condemning Iranian state-linked attacks, intimidation, kidnappings, and assassination plots overseas. A British parliamentary briefing published that month said UK security agencies had tracked more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots during the preceding year and identified dissidents, journalists, Israelis, and Jews among Iran’s targets. The current US-Israeli war with Iran may have increased Tehran’s incentive for retaliation. The conflict began with large-scale strikes on Feb. 28 that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and senior Iranian military officials, expanding the list of figures Iran may seek to avenge. Daniel Byman, a professor in Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service with a concurrent appointment in its Department of Government, told The Media Line that the escalation had increased Iranian incentives for retaliation. He cautioned against treating every public threat as evidence of an imminent attack. “The current war has greatly increased Iran’s motivation for different forms of terrorism, including assassinations,” Byman said. “Iran attempted several plots in the past in response to the killing of figures like Qasem Soleimani, and the scale of the US and Israeli killings in Iran is far, far greater than what we saw in the past.” He pointed to a possible countervailing factor: “US and Israeli operations also demonstrate a thorough penetration of Iranian intelligence networks. It is possible that the networks used for foreign assassination attempts are also penetrated...” Byman said he could not know that for certain. Open threats decrease likelihood of success, lead to increased security“Highly publicized plotting, such as videos regarding the president’s family, are more likely intimidation and trolling attempts, as this will lead to increased security, making an actual plot harder,” he said. Public threats, though, are only one part of Iran’s evolving overseas model. Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher in the Iran and the Shi’ite Axis Program at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), said the scale of Iran’s losses means the drive for retaliation is unlikely to disappear even if diplomacy eventually reduces the military confrontation. “The Iranians are now in the revenge business,” Citrinowicz told The Media Line. “This is not something that is going away. The Iranians, regardless of what will happen in terms of an agreement, yes or no, will seek revenge for Khamenei, I think, for the foreseeable future.” Citrinowicz said Iran’s increasing reliance on criminals and other intermediaries offers Tehran deniability but also creates vulnerabilities. “Their modus operandi is very unique. They are using third-party elements because they want to create a distance between them and the operation itself,” he said. “The good thing for them is that they’re distancing themselves from any activity that happens. The bad thing is that you’re hiring people that are not experienced in this kind of work, and the signature they create helps local authorities discover that,” Citrinowicz said. “I’m not underestimating their ability to do things, but I think the modus operandi is helping security services to track what the Iranians are trying to do,” he added. Byman reached a similar conclusion from a different angle. “Iran’s shift to using criminal networks makes detection harder in some ways, but these networks are also more likely to betray Iran and are more amateurish,” he said. “Most of these plots fail, but at a relatively low cost to Iran.” Outsourcing allows an operation to be disrupted without exposing large numbers of Iranian intelligence personnel or directly linking Tehran to an attack. Irina Tsukerman, president of Scarab Rising, said the distinction between propaganda and operations is not absolute. She spoke to The Media Line before Wednesday’s report identified Yair Netanyahu as the alleged target. “Given Iran’s established record of surveillance, kidnapping plots, assassination attempts, and planned attacks against Israelis abroad, Netanyahu’s claim is plausible enough to warrant serious attention, although there is not enough public information to determine how advanced the alleged operation became,” Tsukerman told The Media Line. She cautioned that sophisticated-looking targeting videos are not proof of physical surveillance or an active assassination cell. “Some information presented in state media may originate from social media, commercially available databases, hacking, open-source research, exaggeration, or fabrication, so the existence of an elaborate video does not demonstrate that an assassination team has been deployed,” she said. The danger, Tsukerman argued, can develop after the material is released. “Criminals can respond to the prospect of money, ideological sympathizers can volunteer assistance, and Iranian intelligence can later identify useful individuals who began acting without receiving instructions from Tehran,” she explained. “Under those circumstances, propaganda can become part of an operational environment even when the original broadcast was produced primarily for intimidation.” That distinction also complicates the frequently used concept of Iranian “sleeper cells.” Tsukerman said the term can suggest organized teams living covertly in Western countries while awaiting direct instructions from Tehran. Recent investigations instead point to looser systems in which intelligence officers, criminals, locally recruited individuals, foreign nationals, and other intermediaries perform separate tasks. Such networks can still leave detectable traces. Surveillance of a target, unusual financial transfers, recruitment attempts, weapons acquisition, and communications with known Iranian intermediaries can form an identifiable pattern when intelligence and law enforcement agencies combine information across jurisdictions.
title: Iranian assassination threats blur theater and action with videos, plots, and propaganda - analysis

content: ERBIL, Kurdistan Region - The spokesperson for Iran’s armed forces on Wednesday threatened journalists working for several Persian-language media outlets abroad, describing them as “soldiers” of Israel and the United States and saying they could be treated as military targets. Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi made the remarks during a visit to Defa Press, a media outlet linked to Iran’s defense establishment, explicitly naming Iran International, BBC Persian, Manoto and Radio Farda and accusing their employees of working on behalf of Tehran’s enemies. “Media outlets such as BBC, Iran International and Radio Farda are directly connected to [the Israeli intelligence agency] Mossad, the [US’s Central Intelligence Agency] CIA and hostile intelligence organizations, and receive their operational direction and support from them,” Shekarchi said. “Those who work for these outlets are considered soldiers of Zionism and the criminal [United States of] America, and they could even be included in the military target bank, because from our perspective, these are not media organisations.” The remarks represent an unusually direct threat against journalists working for Persian-language media outside Iran and come amid the continuing conflict between Tehran and Washington. Iranian authorities have for years portrayed Persian-language broadcasters based overseas as part of a wider foreign campaign against the Islamic Republic, often framing their reporting as part of a wider psychological warfare or a national security threat. Moreover, Iran has previously used financial pressure against journalists working for Persian-language broadcasters abroad. In 2017, Iranian authorities imposed an asset-freezing injunction on 152 current and former BBC Persian staff and contributors, preventing them from buying, selling or inheriting property in Iran. Journalists inside Iran have also repeatedly been detained over their work, particularly during periods of unrest and political crisis. Earlier this month, Iranian photojournalist Yalda Moaiery was sentenced to 15 years in prison under legislation introduced after the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June of last year. The charges included giving interviews to media deemed hostile by the authorities and providing photographs to organizations linked to the US and Israel. Reporters Without Borders said 16 journalists had been detained in Iran so far this year. Iran has also detained foreign and dual nationals on espionage and national security charges. Western governments and rights groups have repeatedly criticized such arrests as politically motivated, allegations Tehran denies. BBC Persian and other outlets have previously reported pressure on journalists’ relatives inside Iran, while Tehran has imposed legal and financial restrictions on journalists working for foreign-based Persian-language media. Shekarchi’s Wednesday remarks however, go further by placing media workers directly within the language of military targeting, blurring the distinction between journalism and participation in hostilities.
title: Iran threatens journalists at Persian-language outlets abroad as ‘military targets’
