movement_abstract: 【台湾自由时报2026年8月25日报道】美国联邦通讯委员会以国家安全为由禁止进口中国制人形与四足机器人，并主导'矽盛世'倡议，联合24国整合芯片、算力及关键矿产供应链，将中国排除在核心AI生态之外。中国在上海世界人工智能大会期间推动成立'世界人工智能合作组织'，吸纳俄罗斯、巴西等29个创始成员，总部设于上海，旨在建立以主权国家为核心的多边治理平台抗衡美国。台湾立法院已通过《人工智能基本法》，数发部推出风险分类框架，AI产品与系统评测中心利用本土语料检验模型对繁体中文及社会脉络的理解。文章指出，台湾虽处于全球先进芯片供应链核心，但在联合国及美国主导的AI治理机制中缺乏正式席位。建议台湾整合本土语料库，建立符合民主法治的模型评测制度，将硬件优势转化为标准制定与治理影响力，以应对美中两强在技术、制度与规则层面的全面竞争。

content: Pouria Zeraati, an Iranian dissident who was living in London, spent nearly two years collecting evidence that the regime in Tehran had dispatched agents to silence him. He received harassing messages almost daily, by phone and e-mail. Masked men staked out his home and stalked his wife on the street. A stranger warned him on Telegram that he had been offered money to harm him. Zeraati reported each threat to the British police, who assured him that he was safe. But he grew worried that his life was in danger. “I felt as though I was my own detective, prophesying my assassination,” he told me. Zeraati, who is thirty-eight, had arrived in England in 2007 to study mechanical engineering. After graduating, he was hired as a reporter for Manoto, a Persian-language television channel based in London that, at the time, was one of the most-watched in Iran. He quickly rose to prominence with an opinionated style that he modelled after anchors he admired on Fox News and CNN. In 2022, Zeraati started hosting a Friday-night program called “The Last Word” at Iran International, a satellite channel that was attracting attention among Iranians for its scathing coverage of the regime. Zeraati and I first met over dinner in late 2022. He was polished and charismatic, with dark-brown hair slicked into something approaching a quiff. He told me that his program was reaching people via satellite inside the country, where the government’s censorship had nearly eliminated independent media. Iran International was launched in 2017 with funds from Saudi-British investors. The channel, which is banned inside Iran, refuses to disclose its private donors. And that refusal has given rise to suspicions that the network is part of a media campaign to bolster the Iranian government’s opposition. When I met Zeraati, the “ Women, Life, Freedom ” protest movement had erupted across the country after the death in custody of Mahsa Jina Amini, a twenty-two-year-old woman who had been detained and beaten by the police for reportedly exposing her hair. Zeraati and his colleagues’ broadcasts featured interviews with anti-regime activists and Israeli officials, and a steady stream of videos from street demonstrations: women burning their hijabs, police beating university students, and crowds shouting “Death to the mullahs’ regime!” In a post on Twitter, Zeraati called for “the destruction of a murderous regime that kills worshippers and children.” He later told me, of Iranian officials, “I don’t bother to hide what I really think of them.” The Iranian government saw Iran International’s coverage as evidence that the channel and its anchors were weapons in an information war. The country’s intelligence minister, Esmail Khatib, accused the station of being a “terrorist organization.” He said it was operating as an extension of a coördinated “influence operation,” backed by the regime’s regional enemies, to erode confidence in Iran’s government and incite violence at home. Fars News Agency, which is affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, created a poster that said “ WANTED: DEAD OR ALIVE ,” beneath head shots of Zeraati and four other anchors. U.K. police deployed armored vehicles to Iran International’s office in Chiswick after they discovered threats against its staff. Photos of Zeraati’s residence were posted on social media. His wife was followed to her gym by two men on a motorbike who told her, in Farsi, that she and her husband would be killed. Police installed alarms in the couple’s home and moved them temporarily to a safe house. Zeraati and his wife stopped doing many of their usual activities, such as trips to the grocery store and dinners out with friends. But he didn’t tone down his messaging. In early January, 2023, Zeraati called the regime “the Islamic Republic of filth” after it executed two protesters. His posts about Reza Pahlavi , the son of the deposed Shah of Iran, veered toward adulation. Zeraati endorsed Pahlavi as “a mature political leader whom Iran needs today,” and his social-media accounts featured photos and videos of crowds greeting the former Crown Prince in Oxford, Brussels, and Jerusalem. Zeraati also flew to Israel and filmed an interview with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In the segment, Netanyahu spoke directly to the Iranian people, praising the ongoing protest movement, and he challenged the country’s leaders to “let your people go.” Viewership of Zeraati’s program soared; so did the number of threats. Soon after, a pair of men wearing medical masks arrived outside Zeraati’s home in Wimbledon. They carried a bat and scissors. His wife filmed the men from their balcony. A neighbor, who spotted the men lingering in a garden behind Zeraati’s building, notified the police, who arrived and arrested them. Investigators later discovered that the intruders were Romanian nationals. One of them, a twenty-two-year-old named George Stana, had travelled to England weeks earlier. Messages recovered from his phone showed that an anonymous handler, nicknamed Em, had directed him to the address. “His flat is number 5,” Em wrote. “Make sure he is alone. Hope you do it today.” Shortly after the police disrupted the plot, they released Stana, who flew back to Bucharest. But he returned to London a year later, to finish the operation. He stayed in a hotel room with two other Romanian men who had also been enlisted for the job. During the next few weeks, Stana’s sister, Florina, wired the group money to pay for SIM cards, clothing, lodging, and a blue Mazda. The team made a series of short trips to Zeraati’s home to scope out his neighborhood and study his movements. On a Friday in March, 2024, at around 3 P.M. , Zeraati was leaving home for his weekly commute to Iran International’s studios. As he walked to his car, a nineteen-year-old Romanian man, Nandito Badea, came up to him and asked him for “three pounds.” At the same time, another Romanian, David Andrei, approached Zeraati from behind. One of them grabbed Zeraati while the other plunged a knife into his right leg three times. The two men ran, laughing, to the blue Mazda that was waiting for them, and Stana, who was driving, sped away. Zeraati lay collapsed in the street. Neighbors who overheard the scuffle arrived to help. A construction worker fashioned a tourniquet out of a tool belt to stanch Zeraati’s bleeding. Meanwhile, the three Romanians ditched the van, chucked their clothing into a garbage bin, and ordered a taxi to Heathrow Airport. They boarded a flight to Geneva and then another to Bucharest. The plot against Zeraati is part of a widening campaign by the Iranian government which involves hiring criminals—Russian mobsters, Hells Angels bikers, and even Swedish teen-agers—to attack its detractors and sow fear among Iranians in exile. Because these operations draw from the criminal underworld, the Iranian regime can deny any involvement. “Hired criminals are cheap, and they know how to blend in,” Colin Clarke, the executive director at the Soufan Center, a global-security think tank, told me. “And Iran doesn’t seem to care if these guys get caught or can’t get the job done.” Even a foiled plot can spread fear among the diaspora. “Sometimes terrorism isn’t about body counts. It’s about who is watching.” The Iranian regime has been killing troublesome exiles since the Islamic Revolution, in 1979. Its agents have been accused of murdering dozens of people living abroad. One of the most dramatic attacks took place in Berlin in 1992, when Iranian agents gunned down a group of Kurdish opposition leaders while they were dining at a Greek restaurant. Police arrested the murder suspects. German prosecutors said that the men were sent by senior members of the Iranian regime, including the Supreme Leader. Later, an international arrest warrant was issued for Iran’s intelligence minister, Ali Fallahian. The German prosecution ushered in a period of relative quiet. The pace of plots picked up in 2009, following nationwide protests against the regime. Authoritarian governments “fear their own people,” Ray Takeyh, an expert on Iran at the Council on Foreign Relations, told me, and that fear “becomes much more acute during periods of vulnerability.” Iran has increasingly relied on hybrid threats as it has confronted a series of of humiliations: a U.S. drone strike, in 2020, that killed Qassem Suleimani , the leader of Quds Force, I.R.G.C.’s élite special-forces-and-intelligence unit; another wave of nationwide protests in 2022; the near-destruction of Iran’s overseas proxies; and an almost uninterrupted cycle of attacks from Israel and the United States since last June. “The more setbacks Iran experiences at home and in the region, the more attractive these fairly cost-free operations become,” Matthew Levitt, a senior fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, told me. Levitt maintains a digital map that tracks Iranian-backed plots abroad since the country’s revolution. Over the past five years, he has recorded more than two hundred—nearly double the number documented from 1979 to 2021. Many have targeted dissidents or journalists whom the regime accuses of aiding its enemies and fomenting unrest in Iran. “Unless Western governments find a real way to increase the costs, the regime will continue to get away with kidnapping, conducting surveillance, and ultimately trying to murder people on their soil,” Levitt told me. One such operation was foiled in 2021, when a team of gunmen, including a member of the Hells Angels, used an encrypted-messaging service called Sky E.C.C. to orchestrate the assassination of two Iranians living in Maryland. Federal prosecutors said that, at the behest of the Iranian government, the attempted murder was coördinated by a serial criminal named Naji Sharifi Zindashti, who lives in Tehran. The U.S. Treasury Department and British officials imposed sanctions on Zindashti and his associates for directing “heinous operations” against Iranian dissidents. The hits, which were never carried out, were consistent with a growing trend of Iran-hired “groups trying to murder U.S. residents on U.S. soil,” Suzanne Turner, the assistant director of the F.B.I.’s Counterintelligence Division, said. In 2022, an Azerbaijani man armed with an AK-47 arrived at the Brooklyn home of an Iranian American activist, Masih Alinejad, with orders to kill her. The would-be assassin was arrested by police and led investigators to two members of a Russian mob network who had enlisted him on behalf of Iran. Law-enforcement agents in Europe began to notice a similar pattern: a court in Germany convicted a man of trying to burn down a synagogue in the city of Bochum in 2022. He was sent by a former Hells Angels member who lived in Iran. In 2023, a Chechen-born man flew to London and filmed the exterior of Iran International’s newsroom headquarters. He was arrested by the police and convicted of spying for a terror plot against the network. “Criminals can obtain false documents, cross borders, rent safe houses, arrange cars, move money, and disappear,” Phillip Smyth, a researcher who tracks Iran’s proxies, told me. The use of local criminals, who don’t have any affiliation with Iran, forces European governments to “invest more in domestic security,” and demonstrates that “any crook can wreak havoc” in diaspora communities, Smyth said. The tactic also makes it difficult for investigators to link the plots to the Iranian regime. According to Western governments, the operations are coördinated by agents in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its Ministry of Intelligence. The United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Union have sanctioned members of a specific I.R.G.C. unit, known as 840, that has a long history of ordering covert operations in Europe. One of the more elaborate assassination-for-hire schemes unfolded in 2024, when the regime allegedly tried to target an Iranian dissident who was living in Haarlem, in the Netherlands. The dissident, Siamak Tadayon Tahmasbi, had been accused by Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence of directing terrorist plots tied to Israeli intelligence. That March, Tahmasbi noticed strangers loitering around his apartment building. He notified Dutch police, who gave him a personal alarm that he could use to call them. He also installed a hidden camera near his back door. For weeks, he barricaded himself inside his apartment, smoking cigarettes and drinking black tea to stay awake. “I could not take my eyes away from the surveillance screen,” he told me. “My life depended on it.” Finally, in June, a pair of men broke into Tahmasbi’s yard wielding guns and a large hammer. He pressed his panic button to summon the police, who arrived within minutes and arrested the intruders. Dutch intelligence later said that the two men were likely hired by the Iranian government to kill Tahmasbi. One of the suspects was a Tunisian French man who was already wanted for an attempted murder in Spain. According to the police, he had shot a former politician—an outspoken critic of Iran’s regime—in the jaw, months earlier, on the streets of Madrid. (Spain’s high court has since charged eight people, including the Tunisian French man, with terrorism.) The Dutch police assigned round-the-clock bodyguards to protect Tahmasbi and began shuttling him through a series of safe houses. “It’s an unofficial prison,” Tahmasbi told me from one of his locations. “But a happy one.” He was content knowing he had helped to unravel a multiyear, international operation designed to kill him and others. Today, such plots appear to be proliferating. Since 2022, counterintelligence officials have identified more than twenty Iran-backed operations that targeted U.K. residents, including Iranian reporters working for Persian-language outlets in London. “There are hundreds of journalists here doing a job that the Iranian authorities hate,” Fiona O’Brien, the regional director for Europe and Central Asia at the Committee to Protect Journalists, told me. Dozens of exiled Iranians have described to me how violence and harassment have upended their lives and the lives of their families in Iran. “They have been coming after our relatives and our elderly parents, and putting pressure on them to stop us from doing our work,” Behrang Tajdin, a journalist at BBC Persian, told me. “It is becoming more and more aggressive.” Sima Sabet, an independent journalist, told me that she had moved more than six times since 2022, when she learned that police had foiled a plot by Iranian agents to kill her using a car bomb. “I feel like a fugitive in a town I have called home for more than two decades,” she said. Even now, she avoids public transport and covers her face when walking through her neighborhood or a local park. “It is an alienating existence. This is what my enemies wanted for me,” she said. “Anyone who is against them is against God. We are infidels. It is acceptable to eliminate us.” But she continues to publish programs, on YouTube and her social-media accounts, which include more than one million followers. In June, I visited Iran International’s headquarters, in North West London. From the outside, the building looks like a bunker, camouflaged amid a block of nondescript offices. It has fences and a long black barrier on one side, designed to block vehicles from ramming into the building. Security cameras stared down at me as I crossed through two checkpoints and stepped into an air-lock-style vault to get to the building’s lobby. Inside the office, producers toggled dials in a control room that looked out onto a vast studio. Tall monitors, stationed in hallways and kitchens, reminded staff members to report suspicious activity to the company’s security team. Two adjoining spaces on the ground floor served as a newsroom filled with desks. A wall of muted screens flashed headlines in Farsi about ongoing peace negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Iran International employs about seven hundred people who work in bureaus around the world. In the past decade, it has emerged as one of the most influential and popular media channels in Iran. It is beamed into living rooms via satellite dishes, which millions of Iranians use to skirt the government’s media censorship. The channel’s sources of funding are opaque. Iran International’s parent company, Volant Media, is controlled by a wealthy Saudi businessman, Adel Abdulkarim Alabdulkarim. In December, Volant Media received about eight hundred and seventy million dollars in a “debt-for-equity” swap with its anonymous shareholders so it could reduce debt the channel had accrued since it started broadcasting. In response to questions from The New Yorker , Iran International declined to disclose its donors. In a written statement, the channel dismissed the suggestion that “hidden hands” were directing its newsroom as “mere speculation.” “The claims that we are funded or directed by state actors (from anywhere) are false. Such claims echo a long-running disinformation campaign aimed at discrediting the network and increasing the security risks faced by our journalists and staff,” the statement said. The Financial Times reported this year that Volant Media is owned by an offshore company whose owner has alleged ties to the Saudi government, which has advocated for regime change in Iran and sanctions against the country. The financial affiliations have prompted speculation, especially through strands of the Iranian diaspora, who accuse some of its journalists of exaggerating the level of support for figures in the opposition and of advocating for war. In 2023, Iran’s government reportedly demanded that the Saudi Kingdom tone down the station’s reporting during negotiations aimed at reducing tension between the two countries. The channel’s support for Iran’s opposition turned more brazen in December, when the Islamic Republic faced another wave of demonstrations across the country. As the unrest spread, Iran International’s anchors amplified the messaging of Reza Pahlavi, the son of the deposed Shah, urging protesters to “plan for the revolution” and stay in the streets “until Israel attacks.” Soon after, in January, security forces massacred thousands of Iranian protesters with military-style weapons. In the days that followed, Iran International broadcast harrowing testimony from survivors who spoke about the violence. Its anchors argued passionately for a foreign intervention that would allow protesters to oust the regime under Pahlavi’s leadership. “After all the blood we have shed,” one newscaster said, “we cannot possibly settle for anything short of a complete overthrow.” The programming featured appearances from American senators, including Lindsey Graham , who promised “help is on the way” and called the end of the Islamic Republic “a godsend to America.” One commentator suggested on Twitter that the United States should use atomic weapons: “Trump or Truman Plus?” the post said. “Maybe this is the ultimate solution to defeat the devil.” Iran’s military called the coverage “psychological warfare” designed to brainwash ordinary Iranians and “help the goals” of the U.S. and Israel. “If support for this vile and satanic media continues, those who collaborate with it will be added to the Islamic Republic of Iran’s target list,” the military said in a statement. Iran’s state media, in turn, has waged a sophisticated propaganda campaign, publishing a barrage of content and misinformation meant to sway public opinion of the wider war and diminish its government’s losses. The regime’s charges that Iran International functions as a tool of its rivals may be legitimate, but that doesn’t justify eliminating its correspondents abroad. This year, the Iranian government froze the bank accounts and seized assets belonging to more than a hundred Iranians who are living overseas, including dozens of staff members and associates of Iran International. In the past year, the channel’s legal team has documented an “alarming and unprecedented escalation” in threats against hundreds of the staff’s family members in Iran, many of whom government authorities have threatened to imprison or kill unless their relatives stop working. “Essentially, everyone working at Iran International has been designated as a Mossad agent, which makes them terrorists who are killable on sight,” Mark Stephens, a British lawyer who represents the channel, told me. In April, two men and a sixteen-year-old boy in an S.U.V. hurled a burning container toward the newsroom’s entrance. They were chased by police, who were stationed nearby. The assailants have been charged with arson and the “intent to endanger life.” To protect against terror attacks, the newsroom’s director, Aliasghar Ramezanpour, reorganizes his staff’s schedule every week. He varies the times at which shows are taped. Journalists rarely gather outside office hours, aside from an annual holiday, which has been attended by armed guards. Such security precautions are not conducive to an active social life. One forty-year-old anchor told me that it was too risky to meet anyone she didn’t already know. “I’ve accepted that romantic relationships are not for this lifetime,” she said. “I’ll find someone special in the next one.” Iran International’s staff are trained to avoid hacking attempts and cyberattacks, which have recently become more frequent and more sophisticated. During my visit, Ramezanpour showed me a fake account on WhatsApp that had used his name and photograph to send an impersonation of his voice to colleagues and sources, asking them to join an “important meeting.” One recipient, Darya Safai, was an Iranian-born politician in Belgium whom the regime tried to kidnap in 2025. When I called her to confirm the hacking attempt, Safai told me that she, too, was recently impersonated on WhatsApp by a fake account, which sent a message to the former Prime Minister of Belgium, Sophie Wilmès. Ramezanpour has worked with security advisers and European intelligence agencies to relocate staff members across Europe. In the past year, I met with several journalists who had been forced to leave their homes or move to new cities or countries. The morning I visited Iran International, Ramezanpour had discovered that another reporter had been added to a purported hit list. “He is working from home this week,” he told me. “For the time being, we control every aspect of his life.” I told him that, a few days before my visit, I had attended a hearing for a Greek man who was charged with spying on a journalist from Iran International using a camera hidden in a sock. “The threat is always there,” Ramezanpour told me. “This regime will not stop trying as long as our lights are on.” He was reassured, at least, that nearly every plot to harm his staff had been disrupted by police. The Islamic Republic’s campaign in Europe poses a challenge to Western governments. Experts say that the attacks are intended not to be too bloody or sensational, lest they provoke an aggressive response. “Torching Jewish ambulances, or even stabbing a journalist in London—these incidents don’t quite rise to the same level as blowing up a bus or an embassy,” John Jenkins, a former U.K. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, told me. But each case demands attention from European and British police and intelligence agencies, which are already dealing with a range of similar threats from other autocracies such as China and Russia. Even as Europe uncovers more instances of Iran directing foreign criminal networks, the cases remain difficult to spot and tedious to litigate. “Investigating a single case in Europe or Britain’s legal system can take months or even years in courts,” Jenkins told me. “In the meantime, Iranian operatives have evolved their playbook into something else.” In 2024, Western intelligence officials started gathering evidence that gangs in Scandinavia were subcontracting local teen-agers to carry out Iranian directives. That year, a fourteen-year-old boy was arrested in connection with a shooting at the Israeli Embassy in Stockholm. Months later, a pair of Swedish teens travelled to Denmark and threw hand grenades near the Israeli Embassy in Copenhagen. The two teen-agers were sentenced to more than a decade in prison for terrorism and attempted murder. According to Swedish intelligence, the plot was ordered by a gang called the Foxtrot Network, which has been behind a wave of violent crime in the country. The network is led by Rawa Majid, known as the Kurdish Fox, who is believed to be residing in Iran and taking orders from the Iranian government. The U.S. Treasury and British officials froze the assets of Majid and his gang last year. Swedish intelligence officers told me that Iran’s new reliance on local teen-agers helps create additional layers of separation between its operatives and the criminals they hire. One officer described the tactic as a “cutout of a cutout.” Young recruits “raise their hands for easy money without any knowledge of what they are involved with,” he said. Many of the teen-agers were recruited via messaging apps such as Telegram and Snapchat. Magnus Ranstorp, who oversees terrorism research at the Swedish Defence University, in Stockholm, told me that Iran’s covert campaign had turned Sweden into “a theatre for hybrid threats,” as operatives in the country use “social media to trawl for anyone who might be up for doing” their dirty work. “The Iranians have a lot of assets in Sweden, which can operate relatively freely and at low cost,” he said. The pattern has extended across Europe over the past year amid the ongoing war with the United States and Israel, which eliminated most of Iran’s senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei . Its stores of ballistic missiles and attack drones have been degraded. In response, the regime appears to have orchestrated a string of attacks against dissidents and Jewish and American targets in Europe, according to American officials. Many of the suspects are young, under the age of eighteen, Adrian Shtuni, an associate fellow with the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism, told me. Shtuni said that the regime’s message to Western countries was hard to miss. “Iran is clearly stating ‘We are still here. And we can hit you wherever we want, whenever we want. And we can use your own hands to do it.’ ” Smyth, the researcher, told me that with young people recruited online “handlers do not need to explain the ideology behind an operation, or even the identity of its intended victim. The pitch can be remarkably simple: ‘I’m offering you cash. Here is the lie as the cover.’ ” He pointed to a recent case in France, where police arrested three teen-agers for attempting to bomb a Bank of America office in Paris. Police told French media that one of the boys, aged sixteen, was hired over Snapchat by an anonymous figure, who had offered him several hundred euros to place a package outside the bank. The Snapchat recruiter claimed that the parcel contained “fireworks” that were intended to frighten a girlfriend who had cheated on him. French investigators said that the package contained a homemade bomb. “These kids are often disaffected loners,” Smyth said. “They don’t ask a lot of questions before they agree to something.” The plot was allegedly directed by the leader of an Iranian-backed militia, which has claimed a string of terror attacks in Europe as part of the Islamic Republic’s retaliation for the war with the U.S. and Israel. Zeraati managed to survive his injuries and returned to hosting his weekly program. But he now lives in Israel, where he works from a television studio. The move, along with the favoritism he has shown toward Netanyahu, has invited speculation about his independence. But he told me that he was convinced that nowhere in Europe was safe to live. Even the United States no longer felt like a viable refuge. “I won’t take any more chances,” Zeraati told me on a video call from the terrace of his new home, where he has continued to broadcast his disdain for the regime. His Instagram profile recently featured a series of A.I.-generated videos in support of the U.S. and Israeli bombardment. One clip shows President Donald Trump playing poker while Netanyahu plays pool in the domed shrine of the former Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, which is rebranded as “Tehran Casino.” Nine months after his attackers escaped to Romania, two of the men, George Stana and Nandito Badea, were extradited back to Britain. (Andrei was held in Romania for proceedings there.) Details of the operation, which emerged during the trial, including cellphone data and CCTV videos, revealed more than a year of coördination in the lead-up to the attack. A binder of charts illustrated dozens of text exchanges and money transfers that funded eight missions to Zeraati’s house. According to investigators, the plot was linked to Edgar Hakkopian, an Iranian businessman living in London, who was granted citizenship by the British government years before. Police connected Hakkopian to Hemroc Ltd., a company that transferred the equivalent of more than a hundred thousand dollars to Stana’s sister, to finance the operation. Both Stana and Badea denied any knowledge that Iran had ordered the attack. Stana told the court that he had travelled to Britain to make money doing odd jobs, like construction and painting houses, and then was enlisted to spy on Zeraati. He was unfamiliar with Zeraati’s work, and unaware that the Iranian government was targeting him. The handlers who hired him told him to slap Zeraati “across the face because he had slept with somebody else’s wife,” Stana said in court. His lawyer argued that he was “used as a disposable tool” by criminals. “Mr. Stana was useful to others for the conduct that they had intended, but he himself did not know the use to which he was being put,” his lawyer said. “He is functionally illiterate. He is not aware of current affairs, let alone current affairs involving foreign actors.” After deliberating, the jury returned guilty verdicts against both men. On a recent afternoon, I made my way through central London to the Old Bailey, the central criminal court. I walked through the building’s marble halls to courtroom No. 1, where the judge in the men’s case, Bobbie Cheema-Grubb, was scheduled to deliver her sentence. The sword of justice was affixed, in a jewel-studded scabbard, over the judge’s bench. A smattering of reporters had assembled in the pews. Three officers escorted Stana and Badea into the courtroom. Stana wore a white T-shirt with a cross pendant that matched a tattoo under his left ear. Badea sported a button-up shirt, wire-rimmed glasses, and cropped hair. Both men bowed their heads toward a Romanian-speaking interpreter who stood between them and translated the proceedings. Cheema-Grubb called the operation to stab Zeraati “a targeted, organized, and funded act of serious violence carried out for reward.” She acknowledged that both Romanians came from disadvantaged backgrounds, which may have made them more susceptible to recruitment. But she was certain that Stana was aware that the plot against Zeraati “was not conventional criminality but an operation being conducted on behalf of a foreign power.” She sentenced him to twelve years in prison, and Badea to eight. Zeraati watched the sentencing, which was live-streamed, from his home in Israel. He told me that he was encouraged by the outcome of the trial. “I am not concerned with how many years these guys get locked away—they were disposable agents,” he told me. It was more important to him that the judge had made clear that Iran was behind the attack. The trial had reignited his fury at the regime and at the British police who had failed to prevent the operation. He was still recovering from the harm it had caused him and his family. But he held on to some hope that he would return to his life in London. Ten days after the Romanians were sentenced, the British government announced that it would include the Revolutionary Guard on a list of organizations that threaten its national security. Maybe now Zeraati would consider moving back to the city he had called home for almost two decades. “This might change things,” he said. ♦
title: Iran Is Using Foreign Criminals to Attack Its Critics Overseas
movement_title: 伊朗招募外籍罪犯在英实施暗杀反政府人士行动
movement_abstract: 【美国《纽约客》2026 年 8 月报道】2024 年 3 月，伊朗国际电视台主持人 Pouria Zeraati 在伦敦遭三名罗马尼亚籍男子持刀袭击，致其腿部重伤。调查显示，该行动由伊朗情报机构策划，通过中间人招募并资助外籍罪犯实施暗杀。袭击者包括 George Stana 和 Nandito Badea，二人于 2025 年被引渡回英受审，分别被判刑 12 年和 8 年。伊朗政府长期利用犯罪网络针对海外异见人士，手段包括雇佣俄罗斯黑帮、瑞典青少年及摩托车帮派成员。2022 年以来，西方情报机构已识别超 20 起针对英国居民的伊朗支持行动。伊朗革命卫队第 840 部队被指协调此类行动，旨在制造恐惧并削弱流亡群体。英国政府于 2026 年 8 月将伊朗革命卫队列入国家安全威胁组织名单。伊朗国际电视台因报道反政府内容，其员工及家属在伊朗境内面临资产冻结、监禁威胁及人身安全风险。该台总部位于伦敦，拥有约 700 名员工，通过卫星向伊朗境内传播，资金来源涉及沙特投资者。伊朗军方称该台为‘心理战工具’，并威胁将合作者列入暗杀名单。

content: On Friday, July 31, the Japanese government formally launched its National Intelligence Bureau (NIB), among the first of several steps to reform Japan’s intelligence capabilities. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who has pursued programmatic expansion of Japan’s defense capabilities since she came into office in the fall of last year, has identified intelligence as a key strategic priority. Proponents of these reforms argue that they are critical for Japan to contribute more actively to the U.S.-Japan alliance and address shared security priorities. Critics point to concerns that the establishment of the NIB does not fully address the causes of Japanese intelligence weakness and that this expansion may decrease oversight and pose a threat to civil liberties at home. The success or failure of Japan’s intelligence expansion will depend largely on whether the Takaichi administration is able to pass other relevant policies, including an anti-espionage law, and whether it establishes a foreign intelligence service. Still, while the NIB is only a first step in reforming Japanese intelligence capabilities, its establishment signals commitment to engagement with the alliance and a desire to adapt to the changing geopolitical system. For Japan’s security partners, these reforms offer an opportunity to provide input on the development of an intelligence community that is more effective, more easily integrated into collaborative defense efforts, and better prepared to address pressing security issues. Why Centralize Japan’s Intelligence?The Takaichi administration’s efforts to establish a robust intelligence capacity are just one aspect of Japan’s new defense policies. Only a few days after her premiership began, Takaichi announced her intention to reach a defense budget of 2 percent of GDP in FY 2026, a full year ahead of the original FY 2027 target. She also accelerated the revision of Japan’s three strategic documents—the National Security Strategy, the National Defense Strategy, and the Defense Buildup Program—which are now expected to be released by the end of 2026. These revised documents are expected to outline significant changes, including expansion of Japan’s human and technological defense base, increased integration and cooperation with allies and partners, and a focus on medium- to long-term conflicts and new forms of warfare. The administration has also strongly reiterated its commitment to working with the United States and other partners to maintain geopolitical stability in the Pacific. The current state of Japan’s intelligence community, however, poses challenges to achieving these goals due to the decentralized structure of the Japanese intelligence community and weak information security policies. Japanese intelligence has been decentralized since it was dismantled by the Allied occupation following the end of World War II. Provision of foreign intelligence under the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty in combination with domestic mistrust of state surveillance disincentivized conversations about intelligence. While many Japanese organizations maintained intelligence capabilities for their own purposes, they were discouraged from information sharing due to bureaucratic rivalries. A lack of anti-espionage laws outside of the Japan Defense Agency meant leaks were common. The result was a collection of disconnected intelligence islands with no pilot organization to guide broader intelligence policy or to ensure important information was shared quickly and with relevant decisionmakers. Japanese leaders have long been aware of the problems with the country’s intelligence capabilities, and Takaichi’s new policies are the latest iteration in a pattern of attempted reform over multiple decades. By the 1990s, Japan was working to expand intelligence-gathering technologies and to streamline intelligence administration and information security. The NIB’s predecessor organization, the Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office (CIRO), was established in 1986 and grew in personnel, budget, and responsibility from the mid-1990s onward. In 2013, the Japanese government passed the Designated State Secrets Law, a policy that serves as Japan’s first equivalent to a classification system and allows designation of certain information as “state secrets” that are legally protected. New security clearance legislation passed in 2024 focused on the protection of information deemed critical to economic security. Despite these changes, major structural problems remained. Chief among these, and the issue which the current reforms attempt to address, was a general lack of clarity regarding organizational structure. Centralization of intelligence capabilities occurred within ministries but rarely addressed conflicts over turf between them. CIRO, which served as a de facto center of intelligence for the cabinet, did not have authority over other intelligence teams in other organizations. This precluded clear and rapid intelligence communication at the national level. In an international system that increasingly relies on swift, coordinated responses, decentralized information is a clear liability. Without timely and targeted intelligence, it is difficult for policy planners to make decisions about the best course of action, especially in times of crisis. Problems with stovepiping and information sharing between the U.S. intelligence agencies, for example, famously hindered efforts to track al-Qaeda operatives prior to 9/11. On the Japanese side, decentralized information sharing obstructed early government responses to the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster. This is of particular concern to Japanese leadership given escalating tensions with China and ongoing concern over North Korean nuclear capabilities. In particular, use of “cognitive warfare” weaponizing social media, AI, and disinformation to manipulate public opinion is of key concern for Japanese planners focused on counterintelligence. Japanese Intelligence in 2026The first two bricks in Takaichi’s path toward greater intelligence capacity—the launch of the NIB and the establishment of the National Intelligence Council (NIC)—are designed specifically to overcome these challenges. The NIB replaces CIRO, inheriting CIRO’s approximately 730 employees, and is led by the former head of CIRO. However, the NIB has been elevated in both authority and importance. It has the legal mandate to compel Japan’s ministerial intelligence wings to share information and centralizes and assesses incoming information. Intelligence synthesized by the NIB is then also shared with the National Security Secretariat to inform defense and economic security policy decisions. The NIB will be overseen by and serve as the secretariat to the new NIC, which also met for the first time on July 31. The NIC is chaired by the prime minister, and its members include the chief cabinet secretary, the foreign and defense ministers, the chair of the National Public Safety Commission, and other key cabinet members. The council will oversee all foreign intelligence, as well as any information considered crucial for national security. The clear structural result of the establishment of these two organizations is a concrete centralization of power over intelligence in the hands of the prime minister’s office. Proponents of this change have praised it as an important initial step in clarifying intelligence processes, establishing a clear chain of command, and ensuring that information reaches key policymakers in a timely manner. The establishment of the NIC and the NIB has the dual benefit of creating greater clarity on how to cooperate with partners on intelligence and increasing ally confidence in Japanese intelligence capabilities. While the establishment of the NIB has been seen by its supporters as a clear step forward for both Japan’s intelligence capacity and its ability to contribute meaningfully to regional defense, its critics have raised doubts about both the effectiveness and legitimacy of these reforms. In terms of structure, the bureau’s role is ultimately one of coordination, rather than production, of intelligence. While it coordinates the government’s intelligence activities and provides analysis to the prime minister, it does not have the authority to guide intelligence organizations regarding how or what to gather, and it cannot recruit foreign agents, significantly guide counterintelligence, or conduct covert operations. Both Japanese minority parties and the public have also voiced concern that centralizing power over intelligence in the prime minister’s office could allow the government to infringe on citizens’ constitutional rights. Finally, as part of a larger diplomatic campaign to paint Japan as engaging in new militarism, China has framed Japan’s turn toward intelligence as a clear indicator of its push toward greater military assertiveness. The Future of Japanese IntelligenceThe establishment of the NIB represents a clear first step in addressing the problems that have traditionally plagued Japanese intelligence: For the first time in postwar history, authority has been centralized, at least nominally, in one organization, which in turn can mandate information sharing between existing intelligence organizations. If successful, this should make it possible for timely and relevant intelligence to reach policymakers when they need it most, and could significantly increase Japan’s ability to make foreign policy and participate in security coordination with partners. If additional positive steps are taken, Japanese intelligence expansion is likely to increase interoperability and ease of coordination with partners and may even make inclusion in broader multilateral intelligence-sharing organizations possible in the long term. However, the NIB alone is not enough to fully rehabilitate Japan’s intelligence community. Several major issue areas remain. Japan’s lack of a foreign intelligence service represents a significant weakness in Japanese capacity. Additionally, Japan’s lack of strong legal repercussions for leaking of sensitive information represents a hurdle to inclusion in intelligence sharing. Both of these issues have been acknowledged by the Takaichi administration, which has announced its intention to pass anti-espionage legislation by the end of the year and to pursue the establishment of a fully fledged foreign intelligence service some time in 2027. These reforms also have strategic implications for the United States and other Japanese security partners. The process of Japanese intelligence reform creates an opportunity for the United States and other partners to help shape the future trajectory of Japanese institutions and practices in ways that enable greater cooperation. Japanese policymakers have already privately sought input from partners on intelligence reforms: For example, U.S. and Australian intelligence officials have reportedly offered input on technology and interoffice information sharing, and the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service discussed how to improve intelligence sharing during his most recent visit to Tokyo. The United States, Australia, and others seeking stronger defense coordination with Japan would be wise to continue to engage Japanese policymakers and to focus not only on information sharing, but on advice regarding institutional structure, how to design robust rules in support of information security, and personnel recruitment and training. Direct engagement during development offers the opportunity to help build a Japanese intelligence community that avoids common pitfalls and is better equipped to gather intelligence on its own. While stronger Japanese intelligence capacity already offers significant benefits to regional security, the United States should also focus on how to increase Japanese inclusion in cooperative intelligence. Clear guidelines for Japan during this period regarding the requirements for entering broader intelligence-sharing organizations would allow Japan to think about its potential role in these institutions and ensure that it builds intelligence capacity that meets the requirements of these potential partners. Japanese inclusion in the Five Eyes has often been raised as a possibility, but the United States should also consider creating or expanding other institutions. For example, intelligence sharing within the Quad might offer new opportunities for cooperation and coordination in the Pacific. Timing is key. Japanese intelligence development—and defense expansion in general—has been progressing at a rapid rate. The current moment offers the United States an opportunity to contribute to Japanese intelligence rules and structures. Once established, they will be less flexible and difficult to change. Now is the time for the United States and other parties interested in defense cooperation with Japan to deepen consultation and coordination in order to ensure Japan is best equipped to contribute to regional security and to the maintenance of a rules-based international order. Deirdre Martin is deputy director of the Japan Chair at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, D.C.
title: The Implications of Japan’s New National Intelligence Bureau
movement_title: 日本正式设立国家情报局推进情报体系集中化改革
movement_abstract: 【美国战略与国际研究中心网站7月31日报道】2026年7月31日，日本政府正式设立国家情报局（NIB），取代原有的内阁情报调查室（CIRO），继承约730名员工。首相高市早苗将情报能力建设列为战略优先事项，旨在解决二战后日本情报体系分散、信息孤岛及缺乏反间谍法等问题。NIB被赋予法律授权，可强制各部委情报部门共享信息，并负责汇总评估情报供国家安全保障会议决策。同日，由首相主持的国家情报委员会（NIC）首次召开，统筹所有对外情报及国家安全关键信息。此次改革标志着日本战后首次实现情报指挥权的集中化。尽管支持者认为此举将提升日美同盟协作效率，但批评者指出NIB仅具协调职能，无权开展海外间谍活动或秘密行动，且权力集中可能引发对公民权利的担忧。高市政府计划于年内通过反间谍法，并拟于2027年建立独立的外国情报机构。美国、澳大利亚及德国等盟友已就技术共享与机构架构提供建议，未来日本情报体系改革将影响其在五眼联盟或四方安全对话等多边机制中的参与度。

content: 인천공항 활주로에 K2 흑표 전차와 K21 보병전투차가 전개되고, 김포공항 앞 롯데몰에는 바리케이드와 철조망이 설치된다. 반포 한강공원에는 천궁 미사일 포대가 숨어 있다. 장갑차 수십대가 홍대입구를 거쳐 성수동을 향해 움직인다. 시내 한복판에서 공포탄이 터지고, 잠실 종합운동장엔 수십명의 병사들이 치료를 기다리며 쓰러져 있다. 여의도 공원에는 AH-64E 아파치 가디언 공격헬기가 착륙한 뒤 미사일을 장전하고, 사당역 사거리 공영주차장에선 K2 전차가 급유를 하고 정비를 받는다. 제2차 한국전쟁을 다룬 비디오 게임 ‘콜 오브 듀티: 모던 워페어 사’의 한 장면이 아니다. 실제로 얼마 전 끝난 군사 훈련을 마치 한국에서 일어난 것처럼 상황을 그대로 옮긴 것이다. 바로 지난 5일부터 14일까지 대만을 뒤흔든 ‘한광(漢光) 42호’ 훈련이다. 대만 각지에서 동시다발적으로 열린 한광훈련의 현장을 직접 체험한 내용과 현지 군사 전문기자·군사 전문가와 인터뷰한 내용을 바탕으로 필자는 이 훈련이 우리에게 어떤 교훈을 줄지에 대해 얘기하고자 한다. 전시작전통제권 전환을 앞두고 을지 자유의 방패(UFS) 훈련을 축소해서 진행했던 우리의 모습과, 2027년 중국의 대만 침공설에 대비하는 그들의 모습이 너무나 달랐기 때문이다. 한광훈련은 대만의 대표적인 군사훈련이다. 올해까지는 중국의 상륙작전을 봉쇄하고 격퇴하는 시나리오로 진행됐다. 하지만 중국 해군의 급격한 성장과 군사력 강화, 그리고 우크라이나 전쟁은 한광훈련의 시스템과 내용을 송두리째 바꿨다. 기본적으로 상황설정이 달라졌다. 중국이 대만을 침공하려고 선전포고를 하고 병력을 동원하는 시나리오 대신, 우크라이나 전쟁에서 러시아가 그랬던 것처럼 중국이 ‘회색지대 전략’으로 수개월동안 대규모 군사훈련을 진행하고 대만 주변 근해를 봉쇄하며 대치하던 도중, 급작스럽게 훈련 병력이 기습 공격을 하는 상황을 상정했다. 이 때문에 모든 훈련의 목표는 현실적이면서도 절박했다. 중국의 강력한 군사력이 대만 본토에 상륙하는 것을 완벽하게 막지 못한다는 상황을 전제하면서, 중국 인민해방군의 대만 상륙이 곧 전쟁의 종결이 되지 않도록 처절한 저항을 준비하는 것에 가까웠다. 우선, 수도 타이베이(臺北) 시내를 봉쇄하고 차단하는 실전적 시가지 방어 훈련이 곳곳에서 진행됐다. 타이베이로 진입하는 최단 경로인 단장(淡江)대교나, 쑹산(松山)공항 앞 지하차도 등과 같은 곳에 중국군의 기갑부대나 공중 강습 부대가 확보하려 할 경우를 대비해 파괴하기 힘든 장애물과 바리케이드를 설치했다. 대만 전역에선 기동 중인 지상장비와 항공기들이 ‘공격 후 전투력 보존’을 최우선으로 삼았다. 타이베이와 가까운 타오위안(桃園) 교외의 사찰 근처 주차장에 별안간 대만 육군의 CM-32 윈파오(雲豹) 장갑차 여러대가 드론 경계자세를 취하더니, 미국제 허밋(HEMTT) 급유트럭이 주차장에 들어왔다. 급유트럭이 급유 준비를 마치자 중국 공군의 공습을 피하려고 건설자재로 덮여 있던 M1A2T 에이브럼스 전차가 튀어나와 빠르게 급유를 마치고 자리를 빠져나왔다. 헬기도 상황은 비슷했다. 한국으로 치면 일산 호수공원이라 할 수 있는 산주후 생태수변공원(山豬湖生態親水公園)의 풀밭엔 별안간 UH-60 블랙호크 기헬기가 비상 급유탱크와 몇 개의 박스를 빠르게 떨구고 사라졌다. 곧 지상에서 안티드론 건과 소총으로 무장한 병사들이 물자를 수습하고 AH-64E, UH-60, OH-58D 카이오와 정찰헬기가 풀밭에 내려앉았다. 지상 병력들은 능숙한 동작으로 헬기에 급유하고 70㎜ 하이드라 로켓, AIM-92 스팅어 공대공 미사일을 장전했다. 급유와 무장 장착을 마치는 시간은 불과 7분 남짓. 중국군이 헬기 기지를 공습하고 추적하는 상황을 가정해 야전 기지인 전방 무장·연료 재보급소(FARP·Foward Ammo and Refueling Post)를 운용했던 것이다. 미사일 부대 훈련의 취재는 정말 까다로웠다. 대만 공군은 텐공(天弓)-3 지대공 미사일과 슝펑(雄風)-3 초음속 지대함 미사일을 한광훈련 때 각지에 전개했는데, 불과 두 시간 남짓한 시간마다 미사일 포대를 설치했다가 철수하길 반복했기 때문이다. 너무 빨리 움직여 몇 번 취재에 허탕을 쳤다. 이 모든 것이 다 중국의 우세한 미사일 전력과 공군력이 공격하는 상황에도 반격을 위해 생존해야만 하는 냉엄한 현실이 반영됐다. 한 가지 특이한 점은 대만 국방부는 한광훈련에서 단 한 발의 실탄도 쏘지 않았다는 사실이다. 한광훈련 기간 동안 미사일을 발사하지도 않았다. 실탄을 사용하지 않아 중국이 훈련에 대해서 반발하는 명분도 줄이고, 실탄 사격을 배제한 대신 실탄을 제외한 보급·이송·기동·점령·장비 조작에 집중했다. 총격이 필요한 상황이 있을 땐 공포탄을 사격했다. 실탄을 사용한 실무장 훈련은 실전 연습에는 좋지만, 안전관리에 따른 비용과 어려움이 늘 따른다. 시내 곳곳은 물론 항만과 공항이 운영 중인 상황, 무엇보다 민간인이 길을 걷거나 일을 하는 도심지에서 작전해야 했기에 공포탄만 사용하는 훈련을 진행할 수밖에 없었다. 하지만 실탄 사용훈련보다 훨씬 더 중요한 것은 위기에 대응하고 인원을 배분하는 실무적 작업이다. 가령 8월 11일 타이베이대학 강당 인근에서 진행된 전투부상자처치(Tactical Combat Casualty Care·TCCC)훈련의 경우 전투 중 부상자 발생, 부상자 엄호, 부상자 분류·응급처치 훈련을 진행했다. 실제로 TCCC 훈련에 필수적인 대량출혈환자 지혈, 기도확보, 순환관리, 저체온증 예방 관련 조치를 시늉이 아니라 실제로 하는 것을 확인할 수 있었다. 환자만 가짜일 뿐, 군복을 잘라서 출혈점을 찾거나 기도확보 조치가 이뤄졌다. 훈련 과정을 참관하는 부분에서 놀라웠던 점은 예비군의 적극적 참여였다. TCCC의 경우 의무 지휘관을 제외한 대부분이 예비역이 참가했는데, 실제 병원에 근무 중인 인원을 활용해 실전성을 극대화한 것은 물론 의료인의 현장 지식과 의무 사관의 야전 응급처치 지식을 공유하는 모습도 보였다. 여기다 야전 지휘관이 임기응변을 강조해 상부 지시 없이 실행하라고 강조한 점도 놀라웠다. 대만 국방부는 이번 훈련을 ‘유상정, 불극투(有想定, 不劇透)’라고 설명했다. ‘상황 설정은 있지만, 핵심은 알려주지 않는다“는 뜻이다. 지휘부가 언제 어떤 위협이 훈련 상황에 부여할 것인지 알리지 않기 때문에 훈련 인원이 알아서 대응하는 과정을 연습할 수 있었다. 중국군이 참수작전 등 지휘부를 궤멸해도 각 야전부대에서 계획에 따라 작전하는 능력을 키우려는 목적이었다. 대만에서도 한광훈련에 대한 비판여론이 상당했다. 국민의 생명을 지키는 훈련이지만, 불편함을 호소하는 시민들은 대만에도 있었다. 대만 현지 언론인 EBC의 20일 기사 에 따르면 대만 공군이 수변공원에서 대공 미사일 포대를 전개했는데, 시민이 자전거를 타고 난입해 물병을 던지고 난동을 부렸다. 중국 대응훈련에 대비한다며 10일과 13일 7개 현(縣)의 무선통신망을 끊은 뒤 긴급신고를 유지하는 훈련을 벌였는데, 시민들이 이에 대해 불만을 나타냈다. 훈련 과정 동안 사고도 났다. 5일 훈련 첫날 F-16V 전투기가 야간에 출격하려다 활주로를 이탈했고, M60A3 TTS 전차의 비상탈출 해치가 떨어져 시민이 주운 일도 있었다. 민간 화물차가 포탄을 옮기다가 48발의 포탄이 도로 밖으로 굴러 떨어져 폭발물처리반(EOD)이 출동한 아찔한 사고도 있었다. 이런 사고 때문에 중국은 한광훈련을 조롱했고, 대만 내부에서도 정치적 논쟁거리가 됐다. 중국 매체는 한광훈련 동안 숏츠(Shorts) 영상으로 대만군이 실전에서 싸우지 못할 것이라고 비아냥거렸다. 중국 네티즌은 대만군을 딸기군으로 놀리는 댓글을 올렸다. 대만의 야당인 국민당은 한광훈련이 도심지 한복판에 전차와 장갑차를 동원하고, 공포탄을 쏜다며 ‘훈련은 가짜고, 진짜는 계엄’이라며 민진당 정부를 비난했다. 그렇지만 대만군의 선택은 ‘훈련의 전면적 공개’였다. 대만은 이번 훈련에서 최초로 부대 동행기자(Embedded Media) 제도를 채택해 언론이 대만군의 훈련을 직접 따라다니면서 취재하는 것을 허용했다. 다만 취재 영상과 기사는 보안 검토 후 다음날 보도하는 방식이었다. 부대 동행기자에 뽑히지 않은 기자와 시민도 훈련 과정 동안 전면적으로 취재할 수 있었다. 차단선이나 단속 없이 모든 부대 훈련에 대해 사진을 찍고 영상을 올릴 수 있도록 허용했다. 외국인인 필자에게 대만군 방첩 담당자는 “훈련 사진은 찍을 수 있으나, 작전 지역이나 전개구역은 보안을 지켜달라”며 짧게 당부할 뿐이었다. 대만군이 한광훈련을 단순한 전투기술의 연마가 아닌 일종의 중국을 상대로 한 인지전(Cognitive Warfare) 수단으로 삼았기 때문이다. 대만 시민이 직접 훈련 현장을 방문해 사진과 영상을 찍고 소셜미디어(SNS)에 올리면 중국 측이 만드는 한광훈련 비판 영상이나 조롱 영상을 반박할 수 있었다. 다만 동행기자에 제외된 미디어가 선발 과정의 불공정성을 제기하고, 대만 국방부가 동행기자 미디어에게 제공한 정보나 자료로 후속 보도를 준비하는 과정에서 미디어 간의 갈등도 있었다. 이번 한광 42훈련에서 대만이 준비하고 작전한 내용은 우리에게도 시사하는 바가 매우 크다.UFS 훈련은 구조적으로 ‘각본 있는 훈련’에 가깝다. 사전에 정해진 시나리오에 따라 각 부대가 역할을 수행하고, 통제부가 상황을 부여해도 그 범위와 시점이 예측 가능하다. 대만의 '유상정, 불극투’ 방침대로 시나리오는 주어져도 그 세부 전개는 예측 불가능해야만 한다. 더 심각한 문제는 올해 UFS 훈련이 도널드 트럼프 미국 대통령의 일방적 지시로 후반부 반격 연습이 취소되고, 야외기동훈련(FTX)도 대폭 줄었다는 사실이다. 한국군 4성 장군(한미연합군사령부 부사령관)의 미래연합사 사령관 역할 수행 연습도 취소됐다. 전작권 전환을 위한 완전운용능력(FOC) 검증에 직접적 영향을 미치는 사태다. 대만은 오히려 반대로 움직였다. 각본을 없애고, 시간을 늘리고, 민간을 끌어들이며, 통신 마비 환경을 스스로 만들었다. 훈련은 하나의 시나리오를 연습하는 것이 아니라, 예상하지 못한 상황에 대응하는 능력을 키우는 것이다. 한국군은 전작권 전환을 앞둔 시점에, 연합훈련 축소를 외부 변수로만 받아들이면 안 된다. 오히려 이 상황이 한국군 독자적 실전 훈련 체계를 강화해야 할 계기로 삼아야 한다. ☞저자 소개=김민석은 미국에 본사를 둔 에비에이션 위크(Aviation Week)의 한국 특파원 겸 한국국방안보포럼(KODEF) 연구위원이다. 여러 매체에서 방위산업·국방 전문가로 활동하고 있다. 저서로 방위산업 투자 안내서인 『K-방산에 투자하라』가 있다.

movement_title: 台军实施“汉光42号”演习强化城市防御与认知战能力
movement_abstract: 【韩国《航空周刊》特约记者金民石报道】2026年5月5日至14日，台湾地区举行“汉光42号”军事演习。此次演习针对中国“灰色地带”策略及2027年潜在冲突，调整作战想定，不再预设中国正式宣战，而是模拟在长期封锁后遭遇突袭。演习重点转向城市防御与生存能力，在台北市区、机场及交通枢纽部署K2坦克、装甲车及天弓-3、雄风-3导弹系统，并实施快速机动与伪装。为应对中国火力优势，台军强调“攻击后战力保存”，在野战基地进行7分钟内完成直升机加油与武器挂载的演练。演习全程未发射实弹，仅使用空包弹，重点演练战术战伤救治（TCCC）及预备役动员。台军首次引入“有想定、不剧透”机制，赋予前线指挥官临机决断权，并开放媒体全程随行采访，将演习作为认知战手段以反击外部舆论。期间发生F-16V战机滑出跑道、坦克舱盖脱落及弹药散落等事故，引发岛内政治争议及中国舆论嘲讽。分析指出，与韩美联合演习缩减形成对比，台军通过去脚本化、延长时长及引入民间要素，强化应对突发状况的实战能力。

content: Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said this following the Ukraine–Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) summit in Kyiv on August 23, according to an Ukrinform correspondent. ““I would say that right now the military assessment and security assessment are quite clear: NATO is working well. Russia’s assessment of NATO’s power and strength is at a level where they know — it is not worth attacking. This means that NATO and European countries can feel confident; there is no direct threat... But the Russians are doing everything they can to make everyone worry about them rather than Ukraine,” Michal said. In his assessment, Russia is likely to carry out more hybrid attacks across the European Union, and everyone should therefore remain vigilant. Michal noted that Putin had previously been a “grandmaster of cognitive warfare,” convincing everyone that he would be in Kyiv within three days. But now the ports of Primorsk and Ust-Luga are burning, as are facilities in major cities protected by layered air defenses, as well as warehouses and other targets. Thus, Putin’s “cognitive warfare” is falling apart, the prime minister stressed. Read also: Russia launches new wave of sabotage at arms factories across Europe – media But, he added, a question arises — one that his Finnish colleagues usually ask: what will a rat do when it is cornered? And no one has a good answer to that. Michal therefore believes that more should be invested in defense, as well as in Ukrainian technologies and the defense industry. Partners, including Estonia, are doing so, including through drone agreements. The Estonian prime minister stressed that although Putin is now “in trouble with his cognitive warfare — he is losing, while Ukraine is gaining momentum,” this momentum must be maintained, and “we must give everything we have and bring Ukraine into the EU and NATO.” “Ukraine’s future is in the European Union and NATO. And we must continue to push in that direction,” Michal said. He criticized those who believe that sanctions may not be sufficiently effective and that it would be more beneficial to lift them and do business with Russia. The Estonian politician said he was convinced that there was “not a single healthy part” of the Russian economy now, but Russia’s economy was still large enough that pressure had to continue: keeping assets frozen, pursuing “shadow fleet” vessels, and “fighting everyone who has been involved in the conflict on Russia’s side.” “The message is quite clear: stay in Russia, wait for the tribunal,” Michal told Russians. As previously reported, several heads of state and government arrived in Kyiv on National Flag Day and ahead of Independence Day. The leaders of Ukraine, Denmark, Latvia, Lithuania, Estonia, Finland, and Norway took part in the Ukraine–Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) summit, while Sweden joined online. movement_title: 爱沙尼亚总理称俄认知战失效并呼吁加速乌入约
movement_abstract: 【乌克兰乌克新闻社8月23日报道】8月23日，乌克兰 - 北欧 - 波罗的海八国（NB8）峰会在基辅举行，乌克兰、丹麦、拉脱维亚、立陶宛、爱沙尼亚、芬兰、挪威领导人出席，瑞典线上参会。爱沙尼亚总理克里斯滕·米哈尔在会后表示，北约运作良好，俄罗斯已评估认为攻击北约得不偿失，欧洲暂无直接威胁，但俄可能增加针对欧盟的混合攻击。米哈尔指出，普京曾被视为“认知战大师”，但当前普里莫尔斯克和乌斯季卢加港口、受多层防空保护的城市设施及仓库等目标遭袭，显示俄认知战正在瓦解。他警告需警惕“困兽之斗”风险，主张增加国防投入，支持乌克兰技术及国防工业，包括无人机协议。米哈尔强调乌克兰未来在于加入欧盟和北约，必须维持当前势头。他批评解除制裁论调，认为俄罗斯经济已无健康部分，但体量仍大，需继续冻结资产、打击“影子舰队”及制裁冲突参与者，并警告俄方等待法庭审判。

content: 立法院外交及國防委員會邀請外交部長林佳龍（右）、僑委會委員長徐佳青（左）報告「外交與僑務協同培育青年國際視野之執行成效與多語布局」，並備質詢。（記者羅沛德攝） 中共對台滲透收買不斷，民進黨立委林楚茵今（19）日揭露，有海外台僑社團遭滲透，將僑團名單洩漏給中國。僑委會委員長徐佳青也證實，洩漏名單一事「已有聽說，並在調查中」。立法院外交及國防委員會今日邀請外交部長林佳龍、僑務委員會委員長徐佳青報告「外交與僑務協同培育青年國際視野之執行成效與多語布局」，並備質詢。請繼續往下閱讀... 民進黨立委林楚茵質詢指出，她於日前隨立法院長韓國瑜出訪英、法等國時發現，有海外台僑社團遭滲透，將僑團名單洩漏給中國。林楚茵表示，中共近年鎖定「台派」團體，藉由金錢利益收買，甚至以「翻群」手段將創辦人逼走、扶植代理人。她已接獲來自各地台僑、台商的連署支持，呼籲僑委會務必捍衛台灣的海外草根力量。徐佳青回應表示，有關歐洲僑團遭滲透並洩漏名單一事「已有聽說，並在調查中」。徐佳青指出，隨著中國「民族團結進步促進法」實施，跨國鎮壓形勢愈發嚴峻，僑委會必須持續深入第一線布建人脈與掌握資訊，若只坐在辦公室，是尸位素餐。林楚茵指出，網路出現針對徐佳青的「假考察、真旅遊」AI深偽影片帶風向，背後亦是認知戰的一環，意圖透過政治攻擊逼使僑委會不敢走出國門。她強調，外交不限於外交部官方層面，立法院具有國會外交功能，而僑委會則肩負鞏固民間力量的重任，絕不能因抹黑而卻步。徐佳青表示，近期持續收到海外僑團詢問如何應對中共打壓情勢，僑委會將持續與各主權國家建立司法聯繫，並協助僑界提升對認知作戰與深偽技術的識讀能力，全力捍衛海外台僑權益。傳明起又要出國27天 徐佳青：無可奉告不是開玩笑的 另外，對於媒體披露徐佳青明日起將展開長達27天的海外行程。徐佳青接受媒體堵訪追問表示，首長出國都不可以講任何訊息，這是基於國家安全的因素，所以她說「無可奉告」，不是開玩笑的，是基於權責與規定。
title: 林楚茵曝海外僑團名單遭滲透洩露中國 徐佳青證實：調查中 - 政治 - 自由時報電子報
movement_title: 台湾侨委会证实海外侨团遭渗透并启动调查
movement_abstract: 【台湾中央社报道】台湾立法院外交及国防委员会举行会议，邀请外交部长林佳龙、侨务委员会（侨委会）委员长徐佳青报告外交与侨务协同成效。民进党籍立委林楚茵质询指出，中共持续对台进行渗透与收买，锁定海外‘台派’团体，通过金钱利益收买或‘翻群’手段扶植代理人。林楚茵揭露，其随立法院长出访英法期间发现，有海外台侨社团遭渗透，将侨团名单泄露给中国。徐佳青证实已听闻欧洲侨团遭渗透及名单泄露一事，目前正在进行调查。徐佳青表示，随着中国实施‘民族团结进步促进法’，跨国镇压形势严峻，侨委会将深入一线布建人脉，并协助侨界提升对认知作战与AI深伪技术的识读能力。针对近期出现的针对徐佳青的AI深伪影片，林楚茵指出这是认知战的一环，意图通过政治攻击迫使侨委会停止海外活动。此外，针对媒体披露徐佳青将展开长达27天海外行程一事，徐佳青回应称基于国家安全与权责规定，对行程细节无可奉告。

content: Without adequate defenses, AI technology could undermine social trust and democratic institutions, making it critically important to strengthen whole-of-society defense resilience. That came from Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) at the opening ceremony of this year’s Taiwan AI Academy Annual Conference on Tuesday, August 18. Hsiao said that AI sovereignty cannot be built on hardware advantages alone, but must also include data governance and cultural values. Towards that goal, the government is advancing the Ten Major AI Infrastructure Projects, which focus on computing power, data governance, talent cultivation, and innovation ecosystems, as well as future-looking technologies like quantum computing, silicon photonics, and intelligent robotics. Hsiao added that the Cabinet is actively cataloging corpora and datasets that reflect Taiwan’s values for use in training sovereign AI. In addition, it is also improving data governance and supporting open data initiatives in business, technology, humanities, public administration and healthcare. Hsiao said that AI brings both convenience and challenges, like disinformation, deepfake technology, cognitive warfare, and cyberattacks. She said: "If a country lacks the capacity to prevent AI from generating massive amounts of disinformation and deepfakes used in cognitive warfare, or cyberattacks targeting infrastructure, then even the most advanced technology can become a double-edged sword eroding social trust and democratic systems. This is why the president has emphasized whole-of-society resilience." Hsiao said the government has incorporated information, communications, and infrastructure resilience into its whole-of-society defense resilience framework. It is also advancing trustworthy AI development that is human-centered and protects human rights, balancing innovation and security under the Artificial Intelligence Basic Act.
title: Vice president highlights AI technology risks, calls for societal resilience - Rti
movement_title: 台湾副总统萧美琴提出构建全社会AI防御韧性体系
movement_abstract: 【台湾中央社8月18日报道】2026年8月18日，台湾副总统萧美琴在台北举行的台湾人工智能学院年度会议开幕式上发表讲话。萧美琴指出，若缺乏充分防御，人工智能技术可能削弱社会信任及民主制度，强调必须加强全社会防御韧性。她提出，人工智能主权不能仅依赖硬件优势，必须包含数据治理与文化价值观。为此，台湾政府正推进“十大人工智能基础设施计划”，重点涵盖算力、数据治理、人才培养、创新生态及量子计算、硅光子、智能机器人等前瞻技术。行政机构正积极梳理反映台湾价值观的语料库与数据集，用于训练主权人工智能，并改善数据治理，支持商业、科技、人文、公共行政及医疗领域的开放数据倡议。萧美琴警告，人工智能带来便利的同时也伴随虚假信息、深度伪造、认知战及网络攻击等挑战。若国家缺乏防止AI生成大规模虚假信息或针对基础设施网络攻击的能力，先进技术将侵蚀社会信任。因此，政府已将信息、通信及基础设施韧性纳入全社会防御韧性框架，并在《人工智能基本法》下推动以人为本、保护人权且兼顾创新与安全的人工智能发展。

content: A policy panel of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party has approved a proposal to overhaul Japan’s intelligence system that calls for criminal penalties against illicit foreign interference, broader intelligence-gathering powers and an independent foreign intelligence agency. “With foreign espionage activities intensifying, the need (for a stronger intelligence system) is growing,” Akihisa Shiozaki, an LDP lawmaker and secretary-general of the party’s intelligence panel, told reporters after the meeting on Tuesday. The proposal is the next stage of reforms launched in May, when parliament enacted legislation to create a National Intelligence Council chaired by the prime minister and upgraded the Cabinet Intelligence and Research Office into a National Intelligence Bureau. Due to launch on July 31 with about 700 personnel, the new bureau will coordinate and analyze information gathered across the government. The latest recommendations focus more on collection and counterintelligence, areas long seen as fragmented and legally under-equipped. Japan, for instance, has no comprehensive espionage law targeting activity conducted for a foreign power. Authorities instead rely on separate laws covering designated state secrets, corporate trade secrets, illegal computer access and confidentiality obligations. Those laws can punish the theft and disclosure of protected information, but may not cover the recruitment of operatives, the transfer of sensitive but unclassified material or covert attempts to shape elections, public debate or government policy. In 2020, a former SoftBank employee who passed internal documents to a Russian diplomat was indicted and sentenced to two years in prison, suspended for four years, and fined ¥800,000 ($4,890) under a trade-secret law rather than treated as an espionage offense. The Russian diplomat fled the country before he could be detained for questioning. To close those gaps, the LDP panel calls for a foreign interference prevention law that would criminalize covert activities carried out for foreign powers, such as disinformation campaigns intended to influence Japanese politics or public opinion. It separately proposes requiring individuals and organizations acting on behalf of foreign powers to register under a system overseen by the National Public Safety Commission. The proposal calls for heavier penalties when offenses involve ties to foreign powers, while stressing that definitions must be clear enough to avoid discouraging legitimate diplomacy, journalism and other lawful activity. On signals intelligence, it recommends expanding the scope of offenses currently covered under the existing communications interception legislation. It also proposes a separate intelligence collection law to intercept communications to identify the activities of foreign organizations on national security grounds. Legal experts have argued that such a system would raise constitutional issues, as Article 21 of the Constitution protects the secrecy of communications. Existing powers to intercept communications are principally tied to criminal investigations. The proposal says any new intelligence-gathering powers should include limits on their scope, rules for retaining and deleting information as well as independent reviews, and complaint procedures. To strengthen human intelligence, the LDP proposes establishing an independent foreign intelligence agency by the end of fiscal 2027. One option would be to place it under the purview of the foreign minister, with its remit expanding as Japan develops specialist personnel. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has herself advocated revamping what has often been seen as one of the weaker parts of Japan’s security architecture. At a news conference Monday, Takaichi said “threats are already taking shape in Japan,” citing leaks of advanced technology to foreign intelligence services, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns. “Responding to cyber threats, cognitive warfare and economic domain is a pressing need,” she stressed. The LDP’s proposal also calls for stronger parliamentary scrutiny and an independent oversight body to examine classified operations, assess their legality and proportionality, and address privacy and human-rights concerns.
title: LDP eyes new tools to counter foreign spies and disinformation
movement_title: 日本自民党通过情报改革方案拟设独立对外情报机构
movement_abstract: 日本执政党自由民主党政策小组于周二批准一项情报体系改革提案，旨在应对日益加剧的外国间谍活动。该提案建议制定《外国干涉预防法》，将代表外国势力进行的秘密活动（如影响日本政治的虚假信息运动）定为刑事犯罪，并要求相关个人及组织在公安委员会监督下注册。针对现行法律在招募特工、转移敏感未公开材料及干预选举等方面的漏洞，提案主张加重涉及外国势力的处罚力度。在信号情报方面，建议扩大通信拦截立法范围并制定独立的情报收集法，同时设立独立审查与申诉机制以符合宪法对通信秘密的保护。为强化人力情报，提案计划于2027财年末前设立独立的外国情报机构，可能隶属外务省管辖。首相高市早苗强调，针对技术泄露、网络攻击及认知战等威胁的应对已迫在眉睫。此外，改革方案还要求加强议会监督，设立独立监督机构审查机密行动的合法性与相称性，以解决隐私与人权关切。

author_name: By Tech. Sgt. William A. O’Brien
content: Under Secretary of the Air Force Matt Lohmeier implored Airmen to pursue continuous personal growth, authentic leadership and intentional intellectual development during a keynote address at the Air Force Sergeants Association Professional Airmen's Conference. Lohmeier turned directly to the leader he would later share the stage with for a question-and-answer session: Chief Master Sgt. of the Air Force David R. Wolfe. As he centered his remarks on the third edition of Wolfe’s "Why Series" essay on deliberate learning, integrating his own thoughts to illustrate why the Chief's message resonated deeply with him. Reading Wolfe’s words aloud to the crowded forum, Lohmeier highlighted a central premise that he believes defines modern military readiness. "The most decisive advantage is no longer just physical or technological; it's cognitive," Lohmeier said, quoting Wolfe's text. "For members of the United States Air Force, the mind isn't simply a supporting asset; it's a primary weapon system, and like any weapon system, it must be deliberately developed, maintained, and strengthened." While acknowledging the military's ongoing efforts to train and adapt to artificial intelligence, Lohmeier put a finer, more human point on the cognitive domain. "AI will soon do things that even some of our best minds cannot," Lohmeier said. "But your minds, your values, and your psyche should be capable of doing things that AI will never accomplish. If we fail to do that, then we are failing as an Air Force, as an institution, and as human beings." Lohmeier’s insights are informed by his routine of breaking bread with frontline Airmen during installation visits. Meeting small groups of junior enlisted members for a lunch or breakfast session allows him to use those forums to gather feedback to carry back to the senior leadership team in the Pentagon. "Overwhelmingly, I have received positive feedback from our youngest Airmen about the NCOs that they work with, our senior NCOs, and their chain of command," Lohmeier shared. "One of the things I’ve learned in my time meeting with these Airmen is that they resonate with authentic leadership. They crave authenticity in the workplace. When they get it, they respond appropriately, and they'll give you everything that they have to solve the tough challenges we’re facing." To illustrate what it means to lead authentically and from the front, Lohmeier—a former fighter pilot and Space Force officer—shared a lighthearted but pointed anecdote from a recent physical training session with student pilots at Vance Air Force Base, Oklahoma. After a PT session, Lohmeier challenged the attendees to face him in a pull-up competition. Knowing he was facing a younger, more fit Airman, Lohmeier humorously admitted that he turned to "psychological warfare." He insisted they both jump onto the bar at the same time, allowing Lohmeier to control the pacing. In Lohmeier’s recounting of the challenge, he described inserting long, agonizing pauses in the hang position and asking his competitor mid-pull-up if he could perform behind-the-neck variations to break his opponent's focus. His opponent dropped off the bar just one repetition shy of the Under Secretary. "I share that to say that I think they're inspired by your examples," Lohmeier told the conference attendees. "Our Airmen do best when they're led by NCOs and senior NCOs who are out leading in the front. You need to hold them accountable to the standards that we've set. It has to do with leaders and how they lead, serve, and set an example." Reading as an act of service A self-described avid reader, Lohmeier joked that younger Airmen are "big video gamers, but they're not big readers." He challenged the audience to reframe reading from a passive, box-checking activity into a critical component of combat readiness and moral character. He argued that intellectual discipline is directly tied to the Air Force's first core value: Integrity First. "Without this disciplined effort to read deeply, it's not entirely possible to become the most authentic version of yourself," Lohmeier explained. "If you've not accomplished the work that is necessary to fully develop yourself and fully discover and ground yourself in the values that define you, how can you ever truly have integrity? Rigorous study isn't just about intellectual stimulation; it's about values, about character development, and about pursuing the best version of yourself as you lean forward and serve others." Lohmeier emphasized that this intellectual preparation is the foundation of military resilience, providing the mental clarity required to withstand disinformation campaigns from adversaries who seek to exploit fear, anger, and historical ignorance. "As leaders, our job is to foster a culture that values and makes room for continuous learning," Lohmeier said. "Organizations that encourage Airmen to invest in their cognitive readiness create a force that is agile, innovative, and prepared—transforming learning from an individual effort into shared strength." Following his prepared remarks, Lohmeier was joined on stage by Wolfe for a fireside chat, during which, Wolfe tacked onto the theme of reading, officially announcing the release of his latest reading list, the . Lohmeier closed his remarks by giving the conferencegoers a reminder of their influence on the future of the force. "You are the beating heart of the Air Force," Lohmeier said. "If I questioned it before this job—and I really didn't, because I was a squadron commander once too, I truly do believe that you are the beating heart. Your leadership is important, and your personal development is absolutely important as we try and shape the minds and hearts of those that you lead and serve."

movement_title: 美国空军副部长强调认知优势与真实领导力建设
movement_abstract: 美国空军副部长马特·洛迈尔在空军军士协会专业空军人员会议上发表主旨演讲，强调认知能力已成为现代军事准备的决定性优势。洛迈尔引用空军首席军士长戴维·沃尔夫的论述，指出人的思维是主要武器系统，必须像装备一样进行刻意开发和维护。尽管人工智能将承担部分任务，但人类价值观与心理韧性是 AI 无法替代的核心能力。洛迈尔通过基层走访反馈指出，年轻空军人员渴望真实领导力，领导者需以身作则并建立问责机制。他呼吁将阅读从被动任务转化为战斗准备和道德品格的关键组成部分，认为智力纪律是践行‘诚信第一’核心价值观的基础。通过深度阅读和持续学习，空军人员可提升抵御敌方虚假信息的能力，增强组织韧性。会议期间，沃尔夫正式发布了最新阅读书单，旨在推动全军范围内的认知准备与文化转型。

author_name: By John Murray, Dr. Elise Annett, and Dr. James Giordano
content: We previously noted that a central challenge of cognitive warfare is governing the relationship between institutional cognition and an operational environment in which informational, behavioral, and social dynamics evolve continuously and often independently of military decision timelines. To meet this challenge, we propose that future command architectures should emphasize and integrate mechanisms for the adaptive synchronization of human judgment, AI, and the cognitive ecosystem being engaged. This approach augments extant theories of command by recognizing that operational advantage emerges from maintaining temporal alignment between institutional decision-making and the environment in which decisions are executed and incur effects. One method of constructing such an architecture is to reconsider the roles of humans and AI across the decision cycle. If a temporal gap arises because human-paced observation, decision, and execution cannot keep pace with an environment that continues to evolve in the interim, the relevant question becomes which functions must remain human and which can be delegated to AI systems better capable of synchronizing with the cognitive environment. This reframing shifts the challenge from one of tempo alone to one of function reallocation. We posit that the resulting approach entrusts speed-bound functions to AI systems operating under human direction while preserving human judgment, accountability, situational interpretation, and . . This figure consists of two panels depicting a decision cycle along a left-to-right temporal axis. Red segments denote machine-executed functions and blue segments denote human judgment and authority. Dotted vertical lines mark points of ecosystem sampling and downward arrows indicate human discretion exercised over machine-executed functions. The current model (top) confines machine execution to the front and back ends of the cycle, whereas the proposed model (bottom) relocates the human to a supervisory position above the cycle. Figure 2 illustrates both a current and proposed model of human-machine teaming with two panels depicting a decision cycle (i.e., observe, orient, decide, act) along a temporal axis. In doing so, Figure 2 contrasts the current distribution of engagement with the proposed reallocation of human and machine function across the decision cycle. In the regnant loop, machine systems perform the front-end functions of the observe and orient stages by analyzing the operational environment and processing the resulting data for human interpretation. At the back end of the decision cycle, they execute the functions of the action stage by implementing orders issued by human decision-makers. Between these nodes, humans sustain a continuous arc of involvement. Consequently, ecosystem sampling occurs only at the boundaries of these stages, such that institutional understanding is dependent upon a small number of episodic observations acquired early in the cycle. As the cycle advances at human tempo, assessments generated upon initial observation risk losing relevance before decisions can be executed. The proposed model addresses this misalignment by relocating human involvement from within the decision cycle to a supervisory position across it. Here, the human directs and bounds machine systems that execute functions at a tempo the human observer could not achieve unaided. As noted, the vertical arrows indicate how human discretion is exercised continuously over machine function by establishing command intent, parameters, and engagement criteria within which sensing, orientation, and execution proceed. Because these functions are no longer rate-limited by human throughput, the cognitive ecosystem is sampled at a higher frequency, as indicated by the increased density of sampling lines beneath the observe, orient, and act stages. Institutional understanding under this model thereby tracks the evolving environment rather than capturing a series of static snapshots. Decision authority, however, remains a wholly human function in both configurations. As illustrated in the lower panel of Figure 2, the reintroduction of direct human control at the decisional point functions as a guardrail, preserving human judgment, accountability, and responsibility for the use of force even as other functions are executed at machine speed. Delegation of the decisional point to machine interfaces would achieve synchronization at the cost of accountability for the use of force, which we regard as an . The operational implications of this analysis extend beyond the optimization of decision speed and refinement of existing C2 processes. Cognitive environments should therefore not be regarded as static operational conditions to be episodically observed and acted upon. Instead, the object of decision evolves continuously through (1) persistent human interaction, (2) algorithmically mediated information exchange, and (3) increasingly autonomous computation. The operational relevance of any decision is therefore determined both by its velocity and by the extent to which institutional cognition remains synchronized with the evolving . Consequently, temporal synchronization should stand as a complementary principle of military decision theory that extends Boyd's OODA construct. Whereas Boyd demonstrated that adaptive orientation and competitive tempo are central to operational advantage, we argue that this understanding should be broadened to recognize cognition as a biopsychosocial and institutional process in which operational consequences recursively shape future decision-making. Within this framework, the ongoing evolution of the cognitive ecosystem during the execution of each decision cycle emerges as an additional operational variable. Decisional superiority will thus depend increasingly upon preserving coherence between institutional understanding and an operational environment in constant flux. AI assumes importance within this context because it enables persistent observation, continuous contextual integration, predictive analysis, and adaptive decision support across . Properly governed, these capabilities position human-AI teaming to sustain alignment between evolving operational conditions and institutional understanding while preserving the indispensable human roles of judgment, strategic reasoning, ethical deliberation, accountable command, and missional responsibility. Within this paradigm, human cognition and AI are best regarded and engaged as reciprocally complementary capabilities within an adaptive . More broadly, we perceive that this relationship reflects an evolution in the character of command. As military operations become increasingly data-intensive, distributed, and AI-enabled, command advantage will derive less from accelerating individual decision cycles in isolation than from the sustained governance of cognition across interconnected human-machine . Accordingly, future C2 architectures should increase computational speed while preserving alignment among command intent, institutional understanding, computational processes, and environmental change. We believe that decision superiority in AI-enabled warfare will increasingly depend upon this capacity for synchronized cognition and therefore regard temporal synchronization as an essential element of cognitive governance through which military organizations can integrate and sustain AI while preserving accountable human authority. The views and opinions expressed in this essay are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the United States government, Department of War, or the National Defense University. Mr. John Murray is a Research Intern in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare at the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and a graduate candidate in the Master of Public Administration program at Auburn University. Dr. Elise Annett is a Research Fellow in the Program for Disruptive Technology and Future Warfare of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University. Dr. James Giordano is Head of the Center for Strategic Deterrence and Weapons of Mass Destruction Studies of the Institute for National Strategic Studies at the National Defense University and serves as NDU Special Advisor to the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War (CBRN).

movement_title: 美国国防大学提出人机协同认知同步指挥架构
movement_abstract: 【美国国防大学国家战略研究所】美国国防大学国家战略研究所研究人员约翰·穆雷、伊莉丝·安内特和詹姆斯·吉奥尔达诺提出，未来指挥架构应强调人类判断、人工智能与认知生态系统的自适应同步。针对认知战中信息、行为和社会动态独立于军事决策时间线演变的挑战，文章主张重构决策周期中人与机器的角色分配。现有模型将机器执行局限于观察、定向和行动阶段的首尾，导致机构理解依赖早期片段化观察，难以跟上环境变化。提出的新模型将人类从决策循环内部移至监督位置，由人类设定意图、参数和交战标准，指挥机器系统以超越人类速度的节奏执行感知、定向和行动功能。该模式通过提高采样频率，使机构理解能够实时追踪动态环境，同时保留人类在决策点的最终控制权，确保武力使用的判断、问责和伦理责任。文章认为，时间同步应作为军事决策理论的补充原则，扩展博伊德的OODA循环，将认知视为生物心理社会及机构过程。在人工智能赋能的战争中，决策优势将取决于维持机构理解与不断变化的作战环境之间的一致性，而非单纯加速单个决策周期。
