content: Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer for Global Reach and family representative for former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, details the ‘psychological warfare’ Gilman was subjected to while he was wrongfully detained in Russia for 1,666 days. Kieran Ramsey, the chief investigative officer for Global Reach, detailed the horrific conditions U.S. Marine veteran Robert Gilman experienced while wrongfully detained by Russia and urged the immediate release of five other Americans held in Russia in an interview with Fox News Digital. Ramsey, who worked with U.S. authorities to secure Gilman's release after 1,666 days in a Russian prison, praised President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Gilman's return on humanitarian grounds. "Mr. Gilman's home, no doubt, because of the leadership from President Trump. He made a full court press with his senior most team requesting that the Russians release him on a humanitarian basis, which is exactly what happened. MARINE VETERAN ROBERT GILMAN RETURNS TO US SOIL AS TRUMP ADMIN FULFILLS REQUEST: 'NO AMERICAN LEFT BEHIND' "And no doubt it was the work of some good, quiet diplomacy on the part of people like Steve Witkoff, his special envoy, and Secretary Rubio and even the CIA director was involved," Ramsey told Fox News Digital. Gilman was released to U.S. authorities Tuesday after Russian police arrested him in the city of Voronezh in 2022 after he made an unplanned diversion to Russia on his way to a new teaching job in Moldova. Ramsey detailed the circumstances that led to his arrest. "The start of this horrific nightmare comes from the fact that he was actually transiting Moscow. He never intended to stay or visit Russia. He was en route to a new teaching job in Moldova. And while en route, he became really sick. He had to stay and recuperate. And he does have some extended family in Russia. "His father had emigrated from Russia years ago. So, after he recuperated to where at least he thought he was well enough, he decided to go to the U.S. Embassy in Moscow to renew his passport. "But, again, en route to the embassy, he became violently ill, and that's where Russian police came upon him, thought he was drunk, assaulted him, said that he assaulted them, and then it just snowballed from there," Ramsey revealed. Ramsey also revealed the treatment Gilman received while in a Russian prison, which included an extensive campaign of beatings and apparent psychological torture. "Never have we seen the treatment that Mr. Gilman suffered as bad as anybody else. He was provoked in prison. He was beaten in prison, He was forced to exercise, he was forced to fight and then he was told just some crazy things like, you know, there was a hit team to go assault his father in Boston. "And things like that, when they're all together, and you're cut off from the outside world, and you have no idea if there's any hope, you can imagine how that compounds on somebody," Ramsey explained. AMERICAN EX-MARINE FEARED NEAR DEATH AFTER WEEKS IN CATATONIC STATE IN RUSSIAN PRISON When asked if there was any legitimacy to the Boston hit team, Ramsey said, "Totally psychological mumbo-jumbo disinformation campaign to make him feel awful." Gilman, Ramsey told Fox News Digital, is now recuperating in a U.S. hospital alongside family, and while he "still has a long road to go," he was able to receive immediate medical care thanks, in part, to the State Department designating him as a wrongful detainee. U.S. special envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, center, and deputy assistant to the president Sebastian Gorka, right, greeted Robert Gilman, left, upon his arrival in the U.S. after his release from Russia. (SEPeaceMissions/X.com) Global Reach is representing five other Americans detained in Russia who Ramsey argues also deserve that status and have yet to receive it. "All five of those we would assert are wrongfully detained do meet the criteria under the Robert Levinson Hostage-Taking and Accountability Act," Ramsey told Fox News Digital, referencing the 2020 bill that grants the president "visa- and property-blocking sanctions against any foreign person responsible for or complicit in the unlawful or wrongful detention of a U.S. national abroad." FREED MARINE RETURNS HOME 'VERY FRAIL' AFTER RUSSIAN 'NIGHTMARE' AS FAMILY ADVOCATE URGES TRUMP TO FREE OTHERS But Ramsey also detailed the political hurdles that may prevent the U.S. from immediately recognizing the detainees as wrongfully detained. "There's been a policy debate inside the State Department as to whether classifying them or categorizing them as wrongfully detained will raise the price in that diplomacy or that hostage diplomacy negotiations with the Russians to get their release," he explained. Ramsey then told the stories of his five clients, each facing debilitating health conditions in their imprisonment. Alexander Antonov, the first of Ramsey's clients he described to Fox News Digital, is an international businessman from California. "He's a proud husband and father. He's an international businessman. He had business interests in Russian-occupied Crimea and Ukraine," Ramsey explained. Antonov was on his way home from a business trip from Ukraine and transited through Russia, "which obviously is a risky venture," Ramsey said. Former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman, who serves a prison sentence for assaulting a Russian police officer in 2022, attends a court hearing in Voronezh, Russia, April 6, 2026. (Reuters/Vladimir Lavrov/File Photo) Russian authorities stopped him and found his U.S. passport, and "immediately he became a target for them," Ramsey also said. Antonov is now sitting in a Russian prison and was recently violently assaulted by another inmate, Ramsey said, adding that he continues to hear reports that Antonov's being harassed simply for being an American. IRAN JAILS PSYCHOLOGIST OVER TRUMP PLEA AS REGIME DEMANDS HE MAKE AMERICANS ‘LOOK STUPID’: FAMILY Antonov was detained just over a year ago, Ramsey told Fox News Digital. He then detailed the case of David Barnes, a Texas native who traveled to Russia to retrieve his children after his Russian ex-wife fled and took them to Russia. Barnes was involved in a contentious custody battle with his ex-wife, Ramsey explained, in which she allegedly made unsubstantiated claims about him. "Mr. Barnes went to Russia to recover his children, and his ex-wife yet again made claims of criminality against him. And the Russians acted upon it. And he's been sitting in a prison now for over four years, and he's got his own health issues," Ramsey explained. Olga Jezler, a 36-year-old green card holder who lived in New York, is another detainee Ramsey represents who was taken after flying to Russia to take care of her sick sister. Trump) After flying to Russia to take care of her sister with cancer, Russian authorities detained her because she was carrying CBD oil, which Ramsey said was legal in Russia. "Nevertheless, the Russians saw an opportunity, and they charged her with drug trafficking. And today she still sits in a Russian prison," he told Fox News Digital. Jezler has significant health issues and is at risk of losing her ability to have children, Ramsey said. The condition she has is easily treatable in the U.S., he explained. Andre Khachatoorian is yet another case of somebody who was not supposed to be in Russia, Ramsey said. Khachatoorian was traveling through Russia to reach Armenia while transporting a rifle, Gilman said. He allegedly had all the proper paperwork. Khachatoorian also has an autoimmune disease that continues to get worse while he has been sitting in a Russian prison for more than four years, Ramsey said. UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC Ramsey also named Chuck Zimmerman, who Russian authorities nabbed in international waters. Secretary of State Marco Rubio listens during a hearing of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs on Capitol Hill May 21, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) "Chuck Zimmerman is originally from Virginia. He set sail on his lifelong dream with his life savings to sail around the world and end up in New Zealand, where he was planning to be a master electrician," Ramsey detailed. Zimmerman, Ramsey told Fox News Digital, had planned to travel through the Red Sea to reach his final destination, but he rerouted after the war in Iran began. "He could even hear the bombs from his sailboat where he was at the time. So, he decided to divert to the Black Sea. While in the Black Sea, in international waters, the Russian Navy approached him and told him, ‘Under threat of force, you will follow us to the Russian port of Sochi or we will sink you,’" Ramsey told Fox News Digital. Zimmerman had a gun aboard his vessel, leading Russia to charge him with international arms trafficking, Ramsey told Fox News Digital. He has been in a Russian prison for over a year. "He has very serious medical issues. We've consulted medical authorities even recently who have told us he either needs to be treated for a bleeding gastric ulcer or perhaps something worse. But at this time, as we sit here, he's unable to eat without having to throw up immediately after. He's losing weight at a very rapid pace. And, quite honestly, he's losing hope that he's ever gonna make it out of there," Ramsey said. RUBIO UNVEILS VISA RESTRICTIONS TARGETING CYBERCRIME NETWORKS Ramsey again iterated the urgent need for the U.S. to designate his five clients as wrongful detainees. "We don't want to lose momentum right now," he said. "Seeing Mr. Gilman come home was fantastic. And I've been asked, 'Well, you guys should be, you know, patting yourselves on the back or people should be celebrating.' Well, no. It's fantastic. Mr. Gilman's in a hospital in the U.S. with his family right now. "But we alone have five other families that are going, 'When can we expect the same for our loved one?' And we have to keep the pressure up everywhere we can to make sure people know these folks' names and have an expectation that the U.S. government is going to do everything they can to convince the Russians to let these people go." movement_abstract: 【美国福克斯新闻网数字版2026年8月报道】美国福克斯新闻网数字版2026年8月报道，Global Reach首席调查官基兰·拉姆齐（Kieran Ramsey）披露，美国前海军陆战队员罗伯特·吉尔曼（Robert Gilman）在被俄罗斯非法拘押1666天后获释返回美国。吉尔曼于2022年在俄罗斯沃罗涅日（Voronezh）被捕，当时他正前往摩尔多瓦任教途中因突发疾病在莫斯科转机，前往美国大使馆更新护照时遭俄警方误认为醉酒并遭殴打，随后被指控袭警。拉姆齐称吉尔曼在狱中遭受严重殴打及心理折磨，包括被迫进行无意义体能训练及被切断与外界联系。吉尔曼获释后正在美国医院接受康复治疗。拉姆齐同时呼吁美国政府依据《罗伯特·莱文森人质劫持与问责法》将另外五名被俄非法拘押的美国公民认定为非法拘押者，以推动其释放。这五人包括：加州商人亚历山大·安东诺夫（Alexander Antonov），因在克里米亚和乌克兰有商业利益，2025年被捕，在狱中遭其他囚犯暴力袭击；德州居民大卫·巴恩斯（David Barnes），为争夺子女抚养权赴俄，被前妻指控犯罪，已拘押四年；纽约绿卡持有者奥尔加·耶兹勒（Olga Jezler），因携带合法CBD油探望患癌姐姐被控贩毒，面临丧失生育能力风险；亚美尼亚裔安德烈·哈恰托良（Andre Khachatoorian），途经俄罗斯前往亚美尼亚时因携带步枪文件问题被拘押四年，患有自身免疫疾病；弗吉尼亚州居民查克·齐默尔曼（Chuck Zimmerman），在红海航行途中因伊朗战争改道黑海，在公海被俄海军以武力威胁带至索契港，被控国际军火走私，已拘押一年多，患有严重胃溃疡。拉姆齐指出，国务院内部存在政策辩论，担心认定非法拘押身份会提高与俄谈判的代价，但强调必须保持压力以促成释放。

content: 行政院政務委員陳時中透露疫情期間中共疑似刻意介選，和台灣在野黨一同攻擊政府。（記者于安亭攝） 日前慈濟遭詐10.6億元事件爆發，還給時任中央流行疫情指揮中心指揮官陳時中公道、證明當時是力勸慈濟不要被騙；許多網友也感嘆，陳時中當時應開放科興、國藥等中國疫苗，讓想打中國疫苗的人自行接種，但陳時中表示，政府保護人民、不會放任防疫崩潰。陳時中接受本報《官我什麼事》節目專訪，他談及過去防疫期間及參選台北市長時遭受的各項抹黑與攻擊，以他個人想法，認為各種攻擊背後既有本土政治利益的考量，也有外力與認知作戰的干擾。請繼續往下閱讀... 他坦言，面對這些不實打擊，防疫團隊與他心裡當然會痛，但不會唉聲嘆氣，堅持把事情做好，但這在防疫團隊與大家心中都留下了傷口，只是眾人不願講出來，包含自己在內，許多人都認為「有功只是在盡責」、「國家有難、義無反顧」的精神。他也談及2021年本土疫情期間，BNT疫苗採購合約受阻與疫苗進口爭議，陳時中指出，當時便能明確察覺外力干擾，當年透過全球疫苗取得機制（COVAX）洽購疫苗時，供應方曾反應「壓力極大」，甚至連協助COVAX營運的組織最終都不願協助運輸疫苗至台灣，「這事敢說沒有外力嗎」？背後恐又與中國有關。他認為，初期針對疫情指揮中心的相關人員進行人格打擊，到了隔年，攻擊和抹黑則顯然轉化為選舉利益，而認知作戰更是早已無所不在、且手段日益嚴峻。記者也問到，慈濟遭詐事件爆發後，各方還給陳時中公道，也調侃「當年陳時中最大的錯誤，就是沒開放中國科興與國藥疫苗，讓想打的人去打」。對此，陳時中明確表示，政府施政是以保護人民為前提，「不會因為民眾不了解狀況，就放任大家去試」。他以智利廣打中國疫苗為例，智利人口、教育與經濟水準與台灣相當，早期大量施打中國的科興與國藥疫苗，最終卻導致防疫崩潰，證明無效疫苗無法鬆綁防疫政策，他強調，在缺乏科學證據的情況下，無論是受認知作戰干擾還是真有需求的聲音，政府都絕不會因此放棄保護任何一位國人。

movement_title: 台湾陈时中称防疫期间遭受中共认知作战干扰与政治攻击
movement_abstract: 【台湾中央社报道】台湾行政院政务委员陈时中接受媒体专访，回顾2021年本土疫情及2022年台北市市长选举期间遭受的攻击与抹黑。陈时中指出，防疫团队及他个人在疫情期间面临本土政治利益考量与外力认知作战的双重干扰。他提及2021年通过全球疫苗取得机制（COVAX）洽购疫苗时，供应方反映压力极大，甚至不愿协助运输疫苗至台湾，认为背后存在外力干扰，恐与中国有关。针对慈济遭诈10.6亿元事件及当年未开放科兴、国药等中国疫苗的争议，陈时中表示，政府以保护人民为前提，不会因民众不了解状况而放任试错。他以智利大量施打中国疫苗导致防疫崩溃为例，强调在缺乏科学证据情况下，无论是受认知作战干扰还是真有需求，政府都不会放弃保护任何一位国人。陈时中坦言，面对不实打击，防疫团队虽受伤害，但坚持尽责，认为国家有难应义无反顾。

content: Researchers at Monash University have published a capacity maturity model for assessing how prepared a country is to defend itself against disinformation campaigns, backed by a 103-page white paper that lays out the reasoning behind it in far more depth than the university’s public summary of the project disclosed. The model and white paper were released this month by Carlo Kopp, a lecturer in Monash’s Department of Software, Systems and Cybersecurity, with the model itself co-authored by Callum Jones. The project was funded in part by the Oceania Cyber Security Centre, according to the white paper. Kopp is also a longtime defense analyst and co-founder of the Air Power Australia think tank. A related conference paper on measuring the effects of disinformation attacks, authored by Kopp, appeared in a Springer volume on human aspects of information security in 2025. The model is structured on the Cybersecurity Capacity Maturity Model developed by the Global Cyber Security Capacity Centre at the University of Oxford, which governments already use to benchmark their readiness against cyber threats. The white paper argues that framework cannot be applied to disinformation without modification, because the two threats differ at a basic level: cyberattacks target computer systems, while disinformation targets human belief and, through it, human behavior. The white paper works from a specific definition: disinformation is any deception, by any means, intended to implant or reinforce a false belief in a target population to advance an attacker’s agenda, often as part of a sustained campaign. That definition deliberately includes cases where the person spreading the falsehood, a “proxy,” has no knowledge that it is false and no intent to deceive anyone. The paper distinguishes disinformation from misinformation (false content shared without harmful intent) and malinformation (true content shared specifically to cause harm), following a framework published by the Council of Europe. Proxies get an extended treatment in the paper. People pass along disinformation for reasons that have little to do with the attacker’s original agenda, according to the white paper, including maintaining social status within a group, aligning with a preexisting belief, chasing engagement or advertising revenue, or being paid to do so without regard for accuracy. The paper adds newer categories to that list: a proxy can also be a fake online identity operated by the source of the disinformation, or an AI chatbot that was trained, deliberately or through negligence, on contaminated data. Much of the paper concerns how disinformation exploits ordinary human cognition rather than any technical vulnerability. Drawing on the Boyd observation-orientation-decision-action cycle, it describes how a piece of disinformation that contradicts a person’s existing mental model produces cognitive dissonance, which people resolve either by rejecting the new information or by adjusting their beliefs to accommodate it, sometimes incorporating the false belief permanently. The paper lists confirmation bias, the Dunning-Kruger effect, motivated cognition, illusory superiority, false consensus and self-deception among the specific errors that disinformation is designed to exploit, and links group-level dysfunctions such as groupthink and polarization to the same underlying mechanisms, amplified by the connectivity of digital social networks. Citing prior modeling work by Kopp and colleagues, the paper notes that even a small share of a population producing or spreading deception can disrupt cooperation across an entire society. The white paper devotes a separate section to Russian “Reflexive Control” doctrine, a Soviet-era concept in which disinformation is used to shape an adversary’s own decision-making in the attacker’s favor, which the paper treats as a specific instrument within the broader category NATO calls cognitive warfare. It cites the contested debates over the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 and the origins of SARS-CoV-2 as recent examples of adversaries exploiting genuine uncertainty about the facts to sustain competing narratives. Artificial intelligence gets its own section, describing a new problem the paper’s cited sources call “slopaganda,” unwanted AI-generated content spread to manipulate beliefs for political ends. The white paper walks through the taxonomy of AI “hallucinations,” false but fluent outputs that resemble the cognitive errors seen in humans, and cites research finding large language models can display overconfidence more often than humans do, along with confirmation bias toward their own prior outputs. As an illustration, it cites a Russian party’s stated plan to build a chatbot trained on the speeches of a deceased ultranationalist politician to generate ongoing political commentary. On policy, the paper notes that a 2023 U.S. executive order on AI safety mentioned disinformation only once, in passing, before being revoked in January 2025, and it says the EU’s AI Act, while more developed than the U.S. approach, still has significant limitations for addressing disinformation directly. The white paper organizes countermeasures into four categories. Degradation strategies aim to reduce a disinformation source’s reach, through methods such as jamming hostile broadcasts, denial-of-service attacks on servers hosting disinformation, or flooding an audience with competing, truthful messages, though the paper notes that direct attacks on infrastructure may be unlawful in many jurisdictions. Corruption strategies expose an attacker’s false messages, primarily through fact-checking. Denial strategies block an attacker’s access to distribution channels. Immunisation strategies teach potential victims to recognize deception techniques themselves. To illustrate how national policy actually looks in practice, the white paper compares four cases. Australia relied on a voluntary industry code of practice adopted in 2021, then twice attempted stronger legislation, in 2023 and 2024, that would have given the media regulator power to compel platforms to address misinformation; both bills stalled, with the second withdrawn in November 2024 after the Law Council of Australia warned the legislation was overly broad and risked serious unintended consequences. Sweden took a different path, standing up a dedicated Psychological Defence Agency with separate operations and capability-development arms, explicitly framing disinformation defense as a whole-of-society responsibility shared by government, industry and individual citizens. The United States, the paper says, currently lacks a robust government mechanism: the State Department’s Global Engagement Center, the country’s main counter-disinformation body, was closed in late 2024, a Department of Homeland Security disinformation board set up in 2022 was suspended amid criticism of its scope, and the paper notes the U.S. Agency for Global Media’s move to shut down Voice of America and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, both long used to counter foreign propaganda, has drawn legal challenges. The European Union, by contrast, has built a transnational structure dating to a 2018 European Commission communication, running through a voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation and the Digital Services Act; the white paper notes that framework had only limited success interdicting Russian war propaganda in March 2022, and cites the EU’s November 2025 “European Democracy Shield” white paper, which proposed a new European Centre for Democratic Resilience to coordinate detection and response across member states. Among its conclusions, the white paper argues that any capacity maturity model must hold government entities to the same standard as the private sector and civil society when it comes to producing or distributing disinformation, stating that governments are not implicitly immune to the same problems they are being asked to police in others. It also warns against building an overly prescriptive model, since countries will inevitably choose different strategies depending on their legal systems and political cultures, and against assuming that fact-checkers themselves are infallible arbiters of truth. Kopp said the next step for the research is practical application: using the model to evaluate individual countries’ disinformation defense capacity and identify specific gaps in their policy, institutional and technical preparedness. The white paper and the capacity maturity model document are both published through Monash University’s research repository.
title: 莫纳什大学发布虚假信息防御能力成熟度模型评估各国防御准备
movement_title: 莫纳什大学发布虚假信息防御能力成熟度模型评估各国防御准备
movement_abstract: 【澳大利亚莫纳什大学网站2026年8月报道】澳大利亚莫纳什大学软件系统与网络安全系讲师Carlo Kopp与Callum Jones共同发布103页白皮书及虚假信息防御能力成熟度模型，该研究获大洋洲网络安全中心部分资助。白皮书指出，现有网络安全能力成熟度模型无法直接适用于虚假信息防御，因网络攻击针对计算机系统，而虚假信息针对人类信念与行为。研究将虚假信息定义为旨在植入或强化虚假信念以推进攻击者议程的欺骗行为，并区分了代理人传播、AI生成内容等新型威胁。白皮书分析了虚假信息利用确认偏误、达克效应等认知偏差及群体极化机制，探讨了俄罗斯“反射控制”学说及AI“幻觉”在认知战中的应用。针对防御措施，研究提出降级、腐蚀、否认和免疫四类策略。通过对比澳大利亚、瑞典、美国及欧盟四国政策实践，指出各国在立法、机构设置及执行层面存在显著差异与局限。研究强调政府实体在虚假信息治理中应遵循与私营部门相同的标准，并警告避免过度预设模型，下一步将利用该模型评估各国具体防御能力缺口。

content: A Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) Facebook page on July 24 posted a video titled “It’s Out of Your Control” (油不得你) that allegedly used an artificial intelligence (AI)-generated imitation of President William Lai’s (賴清德) voice. The post was edited twice after it was published, but it was not until 1:05pm that a note was added stating that “the audio and some footage in this video were produced using AI. Please do not assume they refer to any particular individual.” However, the video itself, which received many views and was widely circulated online, contained no warning that it included AI-generated content, deepfake technology or fabricated material. The video began with a first-person account before cutting to footage of a Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) spokesperson, making it easy for viewers to draw their own connections between the two. If this was merely educational content, why the rush to add an AI disclaimer after the fact? And if there was truly no intention to mislead, why wait until controversy erupted before attempting to make amends? Even more troubling is that the video directed virtually all of its criticism at the central government, deliberately overlooking the fact that the Act Governing Food Safety and Sanitation (食品安全衛生管理法) explicitly stipulates that local governments also bear responsibility for food safety inspections, sampling, testing and management. If the video were truly educational, it would provide a comprehensive explanation of systems and regulations rather than selectively presenting information that serves a political agenda. When a video is packaged as informational content while selectively presenting facts, and even pairing it with footage of political figures, it goes beyond simple commentary and amounts to politically motivated propaganda. In the past, online parody videos were mostly exaggerated or satirical enough that viewers could easily recognize them as independent creations. However, generative AI can be used to closely mimic real people’s voices and speech patterns. If an AI disclaimer is deliberately omitted from such a video, many could mistake the content as an authentic official statement. Information warfare has never been an abstract or distant concept — it is a genuine security threat facing democratic countries. A seemingly entertaining deepfake video, if circulated at a particular moment, could lead the public to draw false conclusions, trigger social panic and even undermine the government’s credibility. In the early stages of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, deepfake technology was used to fabricate a video purportedly depicting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy calling for surrender in an attempt to undermine the morale of the military and civilians. For former military personnel in Taiwan, a broadcast by the commander-in-chief represents an order from the commander to the entire armed forces. If someone were to use AI to fabricate the voice of a head of state and distribute it widely online, video platforms or other media platforms, the harm could not be dismissed by posting a simple disclaimer after-the-fact saying: “Please do not assume this refers to any particular individual.” Democratic societies guarantee freedom of speech and allow criticism of the government, but that freedom should not be built on sophisticated, misleading deepfake technology. If the KMT continues to defend its video as informational, it would not only fail to address public doubts about information integrity, but would also raise concerns about whether it is blurring the line between democratic politics and cognitive warfare — a line that must never be crossed. Elliot Yao is a reviewer. Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
title: 台湾国民党发布赖清德AI合成视频引发认知安全与虚假信息争议
movement_title: 台湾国民党发布赖清德AI合成视频引发认知安全与虚假信息争议
movement_abstract: 【台湾中央社报道】台湾国民党脸书页面于7月24日发布题为《油不得你》的视频，使用人工智能生成技术合成台湾地区领导人赖清德的声音。视频发布后经过两次编辑，直至下午1点05分才添加免责声明，称音频及部分画面由AI生成，请勿假设指向特定个人。然而，视频在广泛传播期间未包含任何关于AI生成内容、深度伪造技术或虚构材料的警示，且内容结构将第一人称叙述与民进党发言人画面剪辑结合，易使观众产生关联联想。该视频主要批评中央政府，却未提及《食品安全卫生管理法》中关于地方政府在食品安全检查、采样、检测及管理方面的责任。分析指出，若视频旨在教育，应全面解释制度与法规，而非选择性呈现信息以服务于政治议程。当前生成式AI可高度模仿真实人物语音与说话模式，若缺乏明确标识，公众可能误认为官方声明。此类深度伪造内容在特定时间点传播，可能引发社会恐慌并削弱政府公信力。参考俄乌冲突初期，俄方曾利用深度伪造技术制作乌克兰总统泽连斯基呼吁投降的虚假视频，试图打击军民士气。在台湾，若有人利用AI伪造国家元首声音并广泛传播，仅事后添加免责声明不足以消除影响。民主社会虽保障言论自由，但不应成为滥用深度伪造技术的借口。国民党若继续将该视频定性为信息内容，不仅无法消除公众对信息完整性的疑虑，更可能模糊民主政治与认知作战的界限。

content: Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. It’s August, and everyone is in vacation mode, but we’ve still got plenty of national security news for you this week. Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: The Iran war continues to reveal U.S. weaknesses ,Ukraine once again displays its drone prowess , and hackers target U.S. water supplies . Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. It’s August, and everyone is in vacation mode, but we’ve still got plenty of national security news for you this week. Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: The Iran war continues to reveal U.S. weaknesses ,Ukraine once again displays its drone prowess , and hackers target U.S. water supplies . Much has been said about how the Russian military’s strength was vastly overinflated prior to its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Iran is striking a similar tone now with regard to U.S. military strength, months into a war that has become a quagmire for the Trump administration. Iranian Brig. Gen. Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a top advisor to the leader of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),said in a recent interview with PBS News Hour that “the American military is weaker than what we perceived.” While many might dismiss Naqdi’s comment as propaganda or psychological warfare, there’s also no doubt that the Iran war has exposed serious vulnerabilities for the United States. Seeking new friends. For starters, the war has greatly undermined the notion that partnering with the United States can serve as a strong security guarantee. Countries across the Middle East have for years hosted U.S. troops as an insurance policy in an often-volatile region, believing that doing so would deter attacks from adversaries. But when the war began in late February, Iran quickly began targeting U.S. bases—as well as civilian infrastructure—in countries across the region. Iran has continued to do so in the months since, leading Persian Gulf countries to reassess the value of hosting U.S. troops and seek new alliances. Last week, for example, Saudi Arabia joined a NATO-like mutual defense pact with Turkey and Pakistan. Gulf states have also sought help from Ukraine in shoring up defenses against drones (as the United States has simultaneously struggled to defend against Iranian drones ). Missile math. Much like the Russia-Ukraine war, the United States’ fight against Iran has also once again shown how a weaker adversary can leverage asymmetric warfare to undermine a far more powerful military. Despite repeated U.S. and Israeli strikes, Iran retains many military capabilities and remains a threat to its neighbors, U.S. forces in the region, and shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, its strikes with one-way attack drones and missiles have dwindled vital U.S. munitions and weapons stockpiles that are costly and take significant time to replace. The United States has reportedly used 1,500 Patriot missile interceptors during the war and has around 1,700 remaining. Patriot interceptors cost roughly $4 million and take more than two years to build. Reports also suggest that the U.S. military has also burned through close to 80 percent of its THAAD interceptors; used “ virtually all ” of its long-range precision missiles; and lost roughly a quarter of its MQ-9 Reaper drones (which, at $30 million to $50 million apiece, aren’t exactly cheap). Though the administration publicly denies that there are missile shortages, the apparent stockpile concerns reportedly led President Donald Trump to lash out at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during a recent meeting at Camp David—and seemingly contributed to the president’s decision to call off another large-scale attack on Iran. The clock is ticking. The war was launched with a confusing array of objectives, ranging from destroying Iran’s ballistic missile program to preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. But the war is now primarily a fight for dominance over the Strait of Hormuz. The crucial waterway was open when the conflict began but has been largely closed for months now, with devastating impacts on global energy markets and rippling economic consequences. Meanwhile, Trump continues to undermine the United States’ credibility by painting a picture of the war that’s completely at odds with reality. In just the latest example, Trump has claimed in recent days that the United States is in control of the strait, but ship traffic through Hormuz dropped near a three-month low this week. There’s no peace deal in sight, and Trump appears to be unwilling to cut his losses and agree to Tehran’s hard-line demands—believing that Iran will eventually cave to a campaign of economic pressure. But maintaining the status quo carries considerable risks, including further exposing U.S. vulnerabilities that could be exploited by Tehran and other adversaries. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will be leaving her role at the end of the month to spend more time with her family, Trump announced in a Truth Social post , adding that she will continue to be one of his “top outside advisors.” Leavitt posted on X that serving as press secretary has been “the honor and adventure of a lifetime” and that she “relished holding the liberal media accountable.” Trump nominated Julia Nesheiwat , a former State Department and homeland security official who is married to U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz, to the newly created position of ambassador-at-large for the Arctic. Iran majorly shook up its military leadership,naming former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei as secretary of the country’s Supreme National Security Council and elevating six other individuals seen as more hard-line than previous leadership to top positions. What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already. Ukraine’s drone domination. Ukraine keeps reminding the world that it is now an elite fighting force—in real as well as simulated battlefields. The Ukrainian military on Tuesday conducted successful drone and missile strikes on Russian naval infrastructure in the Black Sea, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed in a post on X, adding that it recorded confirmed hits on “defense positions, piers, and seaport infrastructure.” Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Ukrainian drone operators easily defeated U.S. troops in a military exercise in Germany earlier this year. Water wars. Hackers are increasingly going after U.S. water supplies, with cyberattacks suspected to have been carried out by Iran compromising water utilities in possibly as many as a dozen U.S. states over the past month. While no major disruption to households and businesses was reported, the spate of hacks serves as a reminder of how particularly vulnerable water is, as Rishi and our FP colleague Christina Lu outline in their latest piece . Soldiers load supplies onto a military truck with its lights off during a night tactical exercise in Tainan, Taiwan, on Aug. 12. Cheng Chia Huang/Getty Images 12— the number of airplanes that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has purchased in the past year, most of which it said would be used for deportations but are either sitting idle or being used for travel by Trump administration officials. “We do not feel the need to engage in needless, loud, rhetorical provocations to prove our resolve.” —U.S. Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby in a speech in the Philippine capital of Manila on Monday. Iran has unleashed another round of meme warfare in response to the Washington Post ’s reporting that Trump hid in a catering truck to secretly switch planes from Air Force One to a military aircraft over an alleged Iranian assassination threat. Multiple Iranian embassies—including the ones in Armenia and South Africa —shared artificial intelligence-generated images of Trump in the truck, with the latter referring to the U.S. president as a “coward.” This post is part of FP’s ongoing coverage . Read more here .
title: The Iran War Has Left the U.S. Dangerously Exposed
movement_title: 伊朗战争暴露美军弱点，乌克兰展示无人机战力，黑客攻击美国供水系统
movement_abstract: 【美国《外交政策》网站8月16日报道】美国《外交政策》网站8月16日报道，伊朗战争持续暴露美国军事弱点，伊朗伊斯兰革命卫队高级顾问纳克迪称美军实力弱于预期。战争削弱中东国家对美军安全保证的信心，沙特阿拉伯与土耳其、巴基斯坦签署类似北约的相互防御条约，海湾国家寻求乌克兰协助加强无人机防御。美军在战争中消耗约1500枚爱国者导弹拦截器，剩余约1700枚，消耗近80%的萨德拦截器及几乎所有远程精确制导导弹，损失约四分之一MQ-9死神无人机。特朗普政府否认导弹短缺，但库存压力导致总统取消对伊朗大规模攻击。霍尔木兹海峡航运量降至三个月低点，特朗普声称控制该海峡但实际交通受阻。白宫新闻秘书卡罗琳·莱维特月底离职，特朗普提名朱莉娅·内谢瓦特为北极事务特使。伊朗调整军事领导层，任命前伊斯兰革命卫队指挥官穆森·雷扎伊为最高国家安全委员会秘书。乌克兰展示无人机战力，成功打击俄罗斯黑海海军基础设施，并在德国军事演习中击败美军。黑客疑似伊朗背景攻击美国多达12个州供水系统，未造成重大中断。美国国土安全部过去一年采购12架飞机，部分闲置或被官员用于公务旅行。美国国防部政策副部长埃尔布里奇·科尔比在菲律宾马尼拉发表演讲，强调避免无谓挑衅。伊朗大使馆发布特朗普藏身餐车的AI生成图像进行模因战。

content: ◎ 衛重華 2026年「漢光42號」演習於8月5日至14日展開。（國防部提供） 近日中共官媒《環球時報》海外版刊出〈 「漢光演習」把台灣城市變戰場，最終代價由誰承擔？〉一文，藉台灣漢光演習批評政府將城鎮納入防衛作戰準備，聲稱「一旦戰爭真的來臨，首當其衝的一定是台灣百姓」，又說「台灣的土地，是台灣人民生活的家園」。原本企圖以戰爭恐懼對台進行心理施壓，沒想到整篇文章最大的諷刺，恰恰是中共官媒自己的文字，再次暴露北京政治宣傳與客觀現實之間的巨大矛盾。因為當中國把自己描述成可能對台採取軍事行動的一方，又把台灣人民描述成承受戰爭的一方時，事實上已經在敘事結構中區分了兩個不同的治理主體 這就出現一個中共始終無法自圓其說的問題。如果台灣真如北京宣稱，是中華人民共和國不可分割的一部分，那麼人民解放軍到底要「統一」什麼？如果台灣已經是中華人民共和國統治下的領土，又何必跨越台灣海峽進行封鎖、登陸甚至城鎮作戰？更荒謬的是，中共官媒一方面宣稱台灣屬於中國，一方面又警告「台灣城市變戰場」，彷彿造成戰爭的不是揚言動武的一方，而是準備防衛自己家園的人 主權宣稱可以透過政治宣傳重複千遍，但宣稱不等於治理，更不能靠飛彈與軍艦把政治口號變成既成事實。台灣根本不需要透過北京的認證來證明自己的政治現實，我們有自己選出來的總統與國會，政府依法行政，法院獨立審判等。（資料照） 真正值得台灣社會警惕的，反而是中共這種刻意顛倒因果的認知戰。今天讓台灣必須舉行漢光演習的根本原因，不是台灣想把城市變成戰場，而是海峽另一端存在一個從未放棄對台使用武力的政權。沒有中共的軍事威脅，台灣何須演練反登陸、城鎮防衛與關鍵基礎設施防護？不能一手拿著刀逼近別人的家門，一手再責怪屋主裝門鎖、準備滅火器與避難設施。真正降低台海戰爭風險最簡單的方法，從來不是要求台灣解除防衛，而是北京停止武力恫嚇 所以《環球時報》這篇文章最有意思的地方，不是它批判了漢光演習，而是它 無意間替台灣示範了北京論述最大的破綻 中國若堅稱台灣早就是自己的一部分，就請先回答：既然已經是你的，為什麼還需要「統一」？既然台灣人民與城市都在你的統治之下，為什麼還需要解放軍跨海而來？答案其實再清楚不過。台灣與中華人民共和國互不隸屬，是兩岸長期存在的客觀治理現實。真正想改變現狀的，正是企圖以武力把台灣納入中華人民共和國統治的北京當局。中共官媒想用戰爭恐嚇台灣，最後卻被自己的文字戳破了政治宣傳，這才是整篇文章最大的諷刺 movement_title: 台湾自由时报评析环球时报借汉光演习对台施压暴露政治宣传矛盾
movement_abstract: 【台湾自由时报2026年8月报道】2026年8月5日至14日，台湾举行「汉光42号」演习。中共官媒《环球时报》海外版刊文批评台湾将城镇纳入防卫作战准备，称战争代价由台湾百姓承担，试图以战争恐惧对台进行心理施压。文章指出，中共一方面宣称台湾是中华人民共和国不可分割的一部分，另一方面又警告台湾城市变战场，暴露其政治宣传与客观现实之间的巨大矛盾。若台湾早已属于中国，则无需解放军跨海进行封锁、登陆或城镇作战。台湾拥有自主选举的总统与国会、独立司法及国防体系，自1949年以来从未受北京实际统治。文章强调，台湾举行汉光演习的根本原因是应对北京未放弃的武力威胁，而非制造战场。中共官媒的论述逻辑存在加害者悖论，即威胁使用武力者反而置身事外，被威胁者准备防卫却被指责制造冲突。台湾与中华人民共和国互不隶属是两岸长期存在的客观治理现实，真正企图改变现状的是北京当局。

content: A bizarre story is unfolding in Jammu and Kashmir. In a Hindu-majority India, the Kashmiri Pandits, the minority in the Kashmir Valley, continue to face existential threats from Pakistan-sponsored terrorists, three decades after their exodus. As India prepares to celebrate its 80th Independence Day, the occasion offers an opportunity to reflect on India’s long journey since it broke free from British colonial rule in 1947. Yet, amid these celebrations, the painful reality haunts the Kashmiri Pandits, the indigenous Hindu community of Kashmir: Over 3 decades of separation from their homeland. The irony is that India, one of the world’s biggest economies and military powers, has failed to provide one thing that every citizen of the country enjoys: security to the aborigines of the Kashmir Valley. In 1989-90, amid escalating threats and targeted killings, thousands of Pandits fled the Kashmir Valley overnight to save their lives and dignity. It was one of the most painful episodes in Kashmir’s history. Now, adding to the wounds of their painful past, at a time when New Delhi is attempting to resettle a few of them, fresh death threats from Pakistan-linked terrorists are jeopardizing the plan. This time, a terrorist organization—the United Liberation Council (ULC), a shadow front of Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT)—has issued threats against Pandit employees working under the Prime Minister’s Special Employment Package, circulating an online letter containing their names and phone numbers. Reminiscent of 1990, when a similar strategy of public hit lists and targeted profiling was followed to instill terror, these fresh disclosures have once again shaken the community. Fearing for their safety, the J&K government administration has now directed them to work from home and granted administrative leave until August 25. The Unfinished Return Historically, Pakistan has sought to intimidate Kashmiri Pandits and alter the demographic character of Kashmir through multiple means, ranging from propaganda warfare and narrative-building to targeted killings and direct intimidation through its terror networks, separatist ideological elements, and political discourse in J&K, as part of a well-orchestrated strategy directed from Rawalpindi. It has sought to influence the mindset of Kashmiris through state-sponsored propaganda and psychological warfare—engineered by agencies such as the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR)—portraying Kashmiri Pandits as conspirators and suggesting that they were part of an Indian conspiracy. A narrative has been systematically propagated and inculcated that, in 1990, the Pandits were part of a New Delhi plan and that the government orchestrated their mass exodus from Kashmir. Through such alternative narratives, Kashmiri Pandits have been stigmatized in public discourse as untrustworthy collaborators, permanent outsiders, and people who left Kashmir for reasons other than fear and persecution. Pakistan promoted and implanted this narrative, which was then repeated by some so-called Kashmiri professors, thinkers, activists, leaders, and others. Over time, such narratives penetrated sections of Kashmiri society and helped create a distorted understanding of the circumstances surrounding the exodus. By promoting such narratives, Pakistan effectively absolved itself of the crimes and responsibility for the violence, intimidation, and terror that drove the Pandit community from its ancestral homeland. The focus shifted away from the perpetrators and was placed instead on the victims, effectively forcing the Pandits to justify their own displacement and creating the impression that they left for reasons other than fear, persecution, and targeted violence. During this period, there were numerous massacres and targeted killings of Kashmiri Pandits, while harsh and threatening messages were broadcast over loudspeakers, calling upon them to leave the Kashmir Valley. One should keep in mind that nobody would willingly leave their homes, especially when those homes are deeply connected with memories, family history, ancestral property, and everything else that gives a place a sense of belonging, even if they were offered significant material benefits elsewhere. Nobody would do so unless they were so fearful and intimidated that they believed they could be killed. Such was the situation at that time that these Pandits had no option but to leave and save their lives. After their expulsion, many had to live in packed camps and tin sheds, without proper bathrooms, sanitation, or other rudimentary facilities. Who would willingly leave their homes only to live in such conditions? This itself shows that leaving was not a choice but a compulsion driven by fear. Even today, when Kashmiri Pandits return to the Valley and stand before the homes where they were born, where their parents and grandparents lived, and where countless memories of their families remain, they return not as people who willingly abandoned their homes, but as people separated from their homeland by circumstances beyond their control. To see the place that once belonged to them and yet know that they could not live there freely again is a pain that cannot easily be expressed in words. This pain is not only the loss of a home; it is the loss of a connection to a land that has been central to the community’s history, culture, and civilizational identity for centuries. If Kashmir’s culture has survived, a noteworthy contribution goes to them; from the enduring legacy of Kashmiriyat to the sacred traditions of Herath and the historic shrines like Mata Kheer Bhawani. Kashmir’s identity remains incomplete unless they are fully, safely, and permanently reintegrated into Kashmir. When you define Kashmir, it is not possible to define it without the Kashmiri Pandits. They are the original inhabitants of the Valley and remain an integral, irreplaceable part of its history and culture. The name Kashmir itself is also believed to have ancient origins associated with the Vedic sage Rishi Kashyapa, from whose name terms like Kashyapa-mar (the abode of Kashyapa) or Kashmiram originated, signifying the draining of the primordial lake Satisar to create the Valley. Some of the most famous scholars of Kashmir’s history were Kashmiri Pandits, such as Kalhana, who wrote Rajatarangini (The River of Kings) in the 12th century, establishing the foundational chronological historical record of the region’s ancient dynasties. They also birthed the profound philosophical school of Kashmir Shaivism, pioneered by master thinkers like Abhinavagupta and Utpaladeva, alongside the iconic mystical poetry of Lal Ded, which shaped the region’s spiritual consciousness. International Media’s Double Standard Many international media and some human rights organizations, which often appear to cover stories immediately when it suits their agenda, particularly when it comes to India and Kashmir, have also remained largely silent on the plight of the Pandits and on how an entire community was uprooted from its homes. Their reporting on Indian Kashmir often appears agenda-driven, repeatedly focusing on barbed wires, troop deployments, security forces, protests, and other images that shape a particular narrative about the region. Global networks like BBC, Al Jazeera, and CNN give extensive coverage to such issues and often arrive quickly whenever an incident occurs, but the decades-long plight of the Kashmiri Pandits rarely receives comparable attention. Wire agencies like Reuters ensure political standoffs become breaking global feeds, yet there are no major stories or headlines commensurate with the magnitude of this tragedy. In tandem, prominent global watchdogs like Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, which routinely issue exhaustive, urgent statements on civil liberties and state actions, show a glaring lack of institutional urgency when it comes to the systematic displacement and targeted terror campaigns against this indigenous minority. There have been some stories and sporadic reports on the issue, but by and large, the international media and human rights groups have not given the plight of the community the space, advocacy, and sustained attention it deserves. It is as if the Pandits have become invisible in the very Kashmir whose story they are an inseparable part of. When international outlets and international monitors do touch upon the subject, they often dilute the horror of events like the 1990 exodus or the 2022 targeted killings of employees by framing them through the sanitized lens of “communal migration,” local administrative shifts, or generic local violence rather than recognizing it as a targeted campaign of ethnic cleansing. Radicalization of Kashmir and the Roots of the Pandit Exodus It was from the 1980s onward, when jihadi groups, with Pakistan’s active support and assistance from the CIA and funding from several Arab countries, saw the success of their jihad against the Soviet Union in Afghanistan, that they gained confidence and a moral boost. Pakistan’s generals, especially under General Zia-ul-Haq, saw an opportunity to replicate the Afghan model in Kashmir, believing that the availability of local manpower, combined with Pakistan’s military, logistical, ideological, and training support, could be used to build a similar insurgency against India. Under this covert strategy, often referred to as Operation Topac, Pakistan sought to support, train, and facilitate terror groups, even though some of these groups later developed their own agendas and, in certain cases, became increasingly independent of Pakistani control, as demonstrated by the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP). At that time, jihadi thinking, radicalization, and communal attitudes were indoctrinated and inculcated through brainwashing, selective quotation of Quranic verses and Hadith, and, strategically and systematically, by infiltrating their agenda and radicalized thinking into Kashmiri civil society, media, educational institutions, textbooks, journalism, schools, teachers, professors, and other institutions. They infiltrated the broader ideological base, and this radicalized mentality and terror ecosystem subsequently began to take root. Under this radicalization, Kashmiri Pandits were increasingly portrayed as kafirs and as enemies who could be targeted, threatened, or driven out, and who had to be “taught a lesson.” Those who say that India’s alleged rigging of the 1987 elections, in which the Muslim United Front faced defeat against the National Conference-Congress alliance, was the primary cause of the beginning of terrorism are, in effect, downplaying or absolving Pakistan of its responsibility. Elections have been rigged, manipulated, or bitterly contested in many parts of India, but people did not take up an armed insurgency against the Indian state on that basis. Importantly, Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) have also experienced severely compromised electoral systems, including stringent constitutional preconditions under the 1974 Interim Constitution, such as the mandatory oath of allegiance to, and accession to, Pakistan. The developments that followed the 1987 elections must therefore also be viewed against the backdrop of the ideological and psychological environment. In colleges, through the media, through Jamaat-e-Islami (JeI) propaganda, sermons, and literature, stories and narratives were repeatedly presented to the people of Kashmir, and many came to believe these propaganda narratives without having a broader understanding of the regional geopolitics. The environment subsequently became poisonous and communal in parts of the Valley, and narratives against the Pandit community—labeling them as conspirators and portraying them as part of an Indian conspiracy—began to spread. Eventually, this contributed to the atmosphere of fear, insecurity, and persecution that preceded and accompanied their exodus. This represented a direct assault not only on the Kashmiri Pandit community but also on Jammu and Kashmir’s centuries-old tradition of communal harmony, coexistence, and shared cultural heritage. The tragedy of the Kashmiri Pandits is therefore not merely a story of displacement. It is a story of a community that was uprooted from its ancestral homeland through fear, violence, intimidation, and targeted persecution and has still not been able to return fully after more than three decades. Their return and dignified reintegration into Kashmir should not be viewed merely as a political demand but as an essential part of restoring the Valley’s pluralistic cultural and civilizational identity. The OPED is written by a prominent Jammu and Kashmir-based journalist and has requested anonymity due to security reasons.

content: 육·해·공군과 활발히 협력해 ‘제4군 과학사령관’으로 불린 이광형 전 KAIST 총장이 국방대학교 명예 군사학 박사 학위를 받았다. 국방대가 명예 군사학 박사를 수여한 것은 2015년 백선엽 장군에 이어 두 번째다. KAIST는 13일 이 전 총장이 국방대 창설 71주년 기념식에서 명예 군사학 박사 학위를 받았다고 밝혔다. 국방대는 이 전 총장이 KAIST 총장 재임 기간 과학기술과 국방·안보를 잇는 교육·연구 체계를 구축하고, 민·군 협력을 확대해 국가 안보 역량 강화에 기여한 점을 높이 평가했다. 2021년 총장에 취임한 그는 KAIST 안보융합원을 중심으로 AI(인공지능)와 사이버 보안, 우주, 양자 등 첨단 과학기술을 군과 안보 분야에 접목하는 데 힘썼다. 2022년부터 올해 6월까지 군·국방부 관계자 약 3000명과 경찰 관계자 약 1000명 등 4000여 명을 대상으로 첨단 과학기술 교육을 진행했다. 군 장병 SW(소프트웨어)·AI 교육과 군인 가족 자녀 과학 캠프까지 포함하면 교육 인원은 약 1만1200명에 달한다. 이 전 총장은 육군미래혁신연구센터와 육군 인공지능센터 협력사무소를 KAIST에 유치해 대학과 군이 국방 기술을 공동 연구할 수 있는 기반을 마련했다. 군·산·학·연 전문가가 미래 안보와 첨단 기술을 논의하는 ‘문지포럼(안보·국방 과학기술 미래전략포럼)’을 창설했고, 가짜 뉴스나 선전 등으로 상대의 판단과 여론을 흔드는 ‘인지전(認知戰·Cognitive Warfare)’과 사이버 안보 등에 대응하는 연구 기반도 구축했다. 이처럼 육군과 해군, 공군은 물론 해병대까지 폭넓게 협력하면서 군 안팎에서는 이 전 총장을 비공식적으로 ‘제4군 과학사령관’이라고 부르기도 했다. 이 전 총장은 “과학기술이 국가 안보와 국방력을 결정하는 핵심 자산이 되는 시대에 뜻깊은 학위를 받게 돼 큰 영광”이라며 “대한민국의 과학기술 역량이 국가 안보와 국민의 안전에 실질적으로 기여할 수 있도록 힘을 보태겠다”고 했다.

movement_title: 韩国KAIST前校长获国防大学荣誉学位表彰军民科技融合贡献
movement_abstract: 【韩国KAIST网站8月13日报道】韩国科学技术院（KAIST）前校长李光炯于8月13日在国防大学建校71周年纪念仪式上获颁荣誉军事学博士学位，成为继白善烨将军后第二位获此殊荣者。国防大学表彰其在任期内构建科技与国防安全衔接的教育研究体系，推动军民科技融合及国家安全能力建设。李光炯自2021年任校长以来，依托KAIST安全融合院推进人工智能、网络安全、太空及量子等前沿技术在国防领域的应用。2022年至2024年6月，面向约4000名军警人员开展高科技教育培训，含军人家属子女科学营在内累计培训约1.12万人。其推动陆军未来创新研究中心与陆军人工智能中心合作办公室落户KAIST，建立军民联合研究机制，并创立“文智论坛”（安全·国防科学技术未来战略论坛），组织军、产、学、研专家研讨未来安全与科技议题。此外，构建应对认知战、虚假信息及网络安全的科研基础，因与陆海空三军及海军陆战队广泛合作，被非正式称为“第四军种司令官”。李光炯表示，在科技成为国家安全核心资产的时代，将致力于提升韩国科技实力，为国家安全和国民安全作出实质贡献。

content: Data Cutoff: August 10, 2026 The Korean Peninsula Update is a joint product of the American Enterprise Institute (AEI) and the Institute for the Study of War (ISW). It supports the AEI–ISW Coalition Defense of Taiwan project’s broader mission to strengthen a de facto coalition to deter and contain China and North Korea in the Indo-Pacific. This update tracks and analyzes political, military, and security developments on the Korean Peninsula—centered on the North Korean threat and evolving dynamics on the peninsula, South Korean responses, and broader US strategy in the Indo-Pacific. Toplines North Korea is escalating its support for Russia’s war in Ukraine and will likely aid Russian efforts to intensify ballistic missile attacks against Ukraine. Increased Russian demand for North Korean missiles and manpower could open new opportunities for North Korea to benefit from its strategic partnership with Russia. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on August 8 that North Korea is preparing to deploy between 30,000 and 50,000 personnel to Russia at an unspecified time.[1] Reuters reported on August 5 that a Ukrainian Main Military Intelligence Directorate (GUR) Spokesperson stated that North Korea has begun deploying a missile unit equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers to Russia’s 112th Missile Brigade in Voronezh Oblast.[2] This deployment is the first such North Korean deployment to Russia. ISW has assessed that Russia is increasing the intensity of its ballistic missile strikes against Ukraine to capitalize on Ukraine’s shortage of ballistic missile interceptors.[3] Ukraine’s Strategic Communications Center reported on August 8 that Russia is preparing to conduct a major strike campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure in the coming weeks.[4] The North Korean missile unit and its ballistic missiles will likely support Russia’s missile campaign against Ukraine by allowing Russia to increase the number of ballistic missiles in each strike or sustain smaller strikes for a longer period.[5] North Korean manpower may also enable Russia’s ground campaign against Ukraine. North Korea sent around 15,000 infantry, sappers, and construction workers to Kursk Oblast in late October 2024, which aided Russia’s counteroffensive in the area, of which around 10,000 remain in Russia.[6] An estimated additional deployment of between 30,000 and 50,000 personnel would mark a significant escalation in North Korean support for Russia and may allow North Korean forces to take over rear-area and border defense roles to free up Russian personnel for advances in Eastern Ukraine, although the purpose of the prospective deployment has not been specified at the time of writing. North Korea will likely benefit significantly from frontline combat experience and increased Russian demand for missiles and manpower. ISW-CDOT has previously assessed that North Korea may be able to integrate Russian technical improvements and tactical innovations displayed in Russia’s long-range strike campaign to improve the efficacy of its own missile forces.[7] North Korean ground forces will likely also develop an improved understanding of modern combat, including unmanned systems warfare, by deploying alongside Russian forces. North Korea could also leverage its equipment and personnel commitments to demand further economic and military support from Russia. North Korean efforts to develop a military reconnaissance satellite network and a large surface fleet, in particular, would benefit from Russian equipment and expertise.[8] South Korea is unlikely to provide Ukraine with direct military support in Ukraine’s war with Russia to prioritize maintaining engagement prospects with North Korea, despite Ukraine’s calls for air defense cooperation. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on August 8 that Ukraine is in contact with South Korea to expand bilateral cooperation in air defense systems and drones.[9] The South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) responded to the statement on August 10 that its provision of defense equipment to foreign countries must comply with South Korean domestic laws, reaffirming its policy of not providing lethal weapons to Ukraine.[10] Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha previously expressed Ukraine’s interest in purchasing air defense systems from South Korea during his visit to South Korea in June 2026, but the visit did not result in a meaningful arms deal.[11] South Korean President Lee Jae Myung appears less willing to provide direct military assistance to Ukraine than former South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol. The South Korean ruling Democratic Party (DP) alleged that the Yoon administration indirectly provided Ukraine with 500,000 rounds of 155mm artillery shells through the United States.[12] Yoon stated in November 2025 that South Korea would not rule out providing weapons to Ukraine following North Korea’s deployment of troops to Russia.[13] The Lee administration, on the other hand, has pledged to improve relations with “four major neighboring countries” — including Russia — as part of its effort to resume dialogue with North Korea.[14] Russia said in February 2026 that Russia-South Korea relations depend on whether South Korea provides weapons to Ukraine.[15] The Lee administration is thus unlikely to expand cooperation with Ukraine, considering that it believes improving relations with Russia would lead to engagement opportunities with North Korea. Key Takeaways North Korean Military Deployments: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated on August 8 that North Korea is preparing to deploy between 30,000 and 50,000 personnel to Russia, although the purpose of the deployment has not been revealed at this time. North Korea will likely aid Russian efforts to intensify ballistic missile attacks against Ukraine and seek new opportunities to financially and militarily benefit from its cooperation with Russia. South Korea-Ukraine Relations: South Korea is unlikely to provide Ukraine with direct military support despite Ukraine’s calls for air defense cooperation. South Korea likely assesses that cooperation with Ukraine could harm its prospects for engagement with North Korea due to North Korea’s alliance with Russia. North Korean Domestic Politics Nothing significant to report. North Korean Military Developments See topline. North Korean Foreign Relations Nothing significant to report. North Korean Cognitive Warfare North Korea seeks to justify its military development by accusing the US-South Korea-Japan trilateral relationship of regional destabilization. An unnamed North Korean military commentator claimed in North Korean state media on August 4 that combined US-South Korea military exercises constitute a new security threat to the Asia-Pacific region.[16] North Korean state media criticized the recent US-South Korea Buddy Squadron combined air exercise, US-South Korea Combined Joint Sustainment Training, and the Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC) multinational naval exercise and characterized them as US “war rehearsals.”[17] Workers’ Party of Korea (WPK) General Secretary Kim Jong Un’s sister Kim Yo Jong also issued a statement on August 5 regarding the July 29 Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force’s test launch of Tomahawk cruise missiles, describing the launch as the “military expansionist ambitions of a war-criminal state.”[18] Kim Yo Jong further criticized the United States for its support of Japan’s recent military build-up.[19] South Korean media outlet Kyunghyang Shinmun reported that North Korea issued six distinct statements criticizing US-Japan-South Korea trilateral cooperation since July 9.[20] North Korea’s statements likely implicitly referenced North Korea’s commitments to reinforcing its nuclear arsenal amidst its adversaries’ cooperation.[21] North Korea’s short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) launch on August 6 was likely intended to protest recent trilateral cooperation, Japan’s missile launch, and the upcoming annual US-South Korea Ulchi Freedom Shield combined military exercises.[22] North Korea could seek to enhance its own trilateral alignment with Russia and the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to counter the US-South Korea-Japan coalition. Inter-Korean Relations South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urged the South Korean Ministry of Unification (MOU) to temper its conciliatory policies towards North Korea, likely to minimize domestic political discontent and secure support from moderate voters amid Lee’s declining approval ratings. Lee responded to South Korean Minister of Unification Chung Dong-young’s August 5 briefing by saying that Chung should be “cautious” when enacting his North Korean coexistence policy initiative.[23] Lee expressed his concern over the MOU’s initiative to change the official terminology used to refer to North Korea, which could result in domestic political controversy and partisan disputes.[24] Chung responded that changing the terminology serves as the initial step toward advancing “peaceful coexistence.”[25] The MOU began pursuing this terminology shift in earnest after Chung addressed North Korea by its official title and preferred terminology, “Joseon,” in March.[26] ISW-CDOT assessed that the MOU’s attempt to change the terminology was intended as a sign of respect towards Pyongyang and part of the MOU’s efforts to facilitate inter-Korean dialogue.[27] Lee expressed skepticism regarding the MOU’s conciliatory unilateral trust-building measures at an August 5 briefing.[28] Chung also proposed during the briefing that the MOU should facilitate a dialogue for “peace on the Korean Peninsula” with key regional stakeholders during the upcoming United Nations (UN) General Assembly and Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.[29] South Korean Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun also dismissed Chung’s proposal as unrealistic during an August 5 press conference.[30] Lee’s statements could reflect his intention to decelerate the pace of the MOU’s preemptive conciliatory policies, as they thus far lack tangible returns and could risk worsening Lee’s approval ratings.”[31] Lee is likely seeking to preemptively block controversies that South Korean opposition parties could exploit amid a sharp increase in his disapproval ratings. South Korean polling agency Realmeter reported on August 10 that Lee recorded his highest disapproval rating since his inauguration in June 2025.[32] Lee earned a 53 percent disapproval rating in the first week of August, compared to a 41 percent disapproval rating the first week of June.[33] Realmeter attributed this decline in Lee’s popularity to real estate policies, criminal law revisions, Lee’s recent statements on the Korean Military Academy, and economic instability.[34] Lee appears concerned about how his North Korea policies are being viewed by moderate voters. The Lee administration also appears to face ongoing internal policy misalignment regarding its specific North Korean policy approaches. MOFA and the MOU disagreed over North Korean policy jurisdiction in December 2025, prompting Lee to intervene directly to settle the dispute by expanding the MOU’s authority.[35] The MOU has engaged in multiple disputes with MOFA and the South Korean National Security Council over issues such as UN resolutions on North Korean human rights.[36] Lee may seek to reduce or pause the MOU’s conciliatory activities toward North Korea while strengthening defense cooperation with the United States as he attempts to increase his political support. Lee may aim to minimize what he assesses as unnecessary public criticism of his administration. Lee will also likely seek to resolve internal jurisdictional disputes between MOFA and the MOU and enhance coordination with Washington on prospects for United States-North Korea dialogue. Lee will not completely abandon his “peaceful coexistence” policy, however. The South Korean MOU may participate in Russia’s Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok in September, likely to urge Russia to help facilitate inter-Korean dialogue. South Korean Minister of Unification Chung Dong-yong said on August 5 that Russian President Vladimir Putin may attend the annual EEF and thus advocated for South Korea’s attendance of the forum to improve Russia-South Korea bilateral relations.[37] South Korean media outlet News1 reported on the possibility of WPK General Secretary Kim Jong Un also attending the EEF.[38] Chung added that South Korea needs to maintain independent relations with Russia despite North Korea’s likely opposition to improving South Korea-Russia relations. Former South Korean presidents Park Geun-hye and Moon Jae-in attended the EEF in 2016 and 2017, respectively. South Korea sent high-level officials to the forum each year until the COVID-19 pandemic postponed the 2020 EEF to 2021. South Korea has not attended the EEF since. South Korean Minister of Foreign Affairs Cho Hyun said on August 5 that MOFA has not yet reviewed Chung’s proposal to attend the EEF and added that attendance of the forum falls under MOFA’s jurisdiction.[39] The Lee Jae Myung administration is seeking alternative ways to renew engagement with North Korea amid Pyongyang’s continued rejection of dialogue with Seoul. Chung’s proposal is likely a part of such efforts, as the Lee administration has repeatedly urged foreign countries with amicable ties with North Korea — such as the PRC, Indonesia, Singapore, and Vietnam — to support Lee’s engagement initiative. South Korean efforts to reach North Korea through a third party remain unsuccessful, and Cho expressed skepticism on August 5 towards such an approach. The United States and Ukraine are unlikely to welcome South Korea’s participation in the EEF, however, which would strengthen Russia’s demand that South Korea should reject Ukrainian requests for air defense cooperation. Russian Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrey Rudenko said in May 2026 that the Lee administration has not shown efforts to normalize bilateral trade and economic relations, despite having “considerable potential,” while warning that Russia would retaliate if South Korea sent direct military support to Ukraine.[40] The MOU’s potential participation in the EEF is unlikely to change North Korea’s stance on dialogue, however. South Korean Domestic Politics Nothing significant to report. Counter-North Korean Coalition Building Efforts The Donald Trump administration is considering using South Korean shipyards for the construction of four vessels as part of a broader push to loosen regulations on overseas construction of US naval ships, presenting a possible solution to US shipbuilding undercapacity. The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) proposed to the US Congress that the US Navy must build at least four vessels at overseas shipyards to address shipbuilding backlogs, utilize advanced shipbuilding capabilities overseas, and encourage foreign direct investment in US domestic shipyards.[41] The Trump administration seeks to build two surface combatant vessels and two non-combat auxiliary vessels at foreign shipyards, although US laws prevent the construction of naval vessels overseas.[42] South Korean media outlet Newsis and US media outlet USNI News reported that the Trump administration is considering using South Korean or Japanese shipyards and designs if the US Congress approves.[43] Cooperation with South Korean shipyards presents a possible solution to addressing the capacity and capability gaps in meeting US Navy shipbuilding goals.[44] South Korea and Japan both operate guided-missile destroyers that implement US-designed Aegis combat systems and US AN/SPY-1 radars as core components of their surface fleets.[45] The US government has previously issued Requests for Information (RFIs) to HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Hanwha Ocean on their ability to construct guided-missile destroyers and fleet replenishment ships, with Samsung Heavy Industries and two other South Korean shipbuilders receiving a separate RFI for medium-sized fleet oilers.[46] This proposed cooperation follows remarks by US Forces Korea (USFK) Commander General Xavier Brunson, who discussed the possibility of making South Korea a “regional sustainment hub” for US military logistics cooperation, which could feature shipbuilding as part of a broader US-South Korean cooperation.[47] This proposed cooperation with South Korea is preceded by a 2025 agreement by the US Coast Guard and a Canadian shipbuilder on the construction of two Arctic Security Cutter designs for a new class of medium US icebreakers and follow-on ships in shipyards in Finland and the United States, dubbed the “Finland model” by OMB director Russ Vought.[48] The United States, South Korea, and several US partners and allies are expanding cooperation to deter and counter North Korean cyber operations. An unnamed spokesperson for North Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs dismissed a joint advisory issued by 11 nations on North Korean information technology (IT) workers as “a groundless accusation and a hostile act from the United States and its allies” on August 3.[49] The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), which includes security agencies from 11 participating nations, issued a warning on July 31 that North Korean IT personnel are infiltrating Western IT sectors through deceptive employment schemes.[50] ISW-CDOT previously assessed that North Korea leverages advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and other technologies, along with illicit identity forging, to secure employment at Western IT and cryptocurrency firms and transfer corporate financial assets to fund North Korean military development.[51] North Korea also reportedly disseminates malicious code across online open-source websites to compromise the personal data of individual users.[52] North Korea denied its involvement in cyber threats on May 3, characterizing the allegations as a “political ploy” by the United States to slander Pyongyang.[53] The US Department of State emphasized on May 8 that North Korea uses illicit cybercrime revenues directly to fund its weapons of mass destruction (WMD) and ballistic missile programs.[54] US-based security firm Kumio revealed on August 6 that North Korean-affiliated hackers regularly gain unauthorized access to internal corporate networks and employ other deceptive recruitment tactics against job seekers in so-called “contagious interviews.”[55] Kumio secured five terabytes of North Korean data from 1,640 companies across 57 targeted countries.[56] Approximately 700 to 800 firms suffered critical security compromises, including breaches in administrator authorities and leaks of private cryptocurrency keys.[57] North Korean hackers have targeted Western local governments, cryptocurrency firms, tech agencies, and civilian infrastructure.[58] The United States and South Korea are strengthening multilateral cyber defense cooperation as North Korean cyber threats expand across multiple domains. The South Korean Ministry of National Defense announced on July 27 that the South Korean Cyber Operation Command will participate in the US-led “Cyber Flag” exercise alongside 25 other nations.[59] The US-South Korea-Japan diplomatic working group also agreed in June to bolster trilateral cooperation against North Korean cyber threats.[60] US allies are accelerating combined diplomatic, military and technical countermeasures as North Korea diversifies and enhances its cyber tactics. movement_title: 朝鲜向俄罗斯增派3万至5万人员及导弹部队强化对乌军事支持
movement_abstract: 【美国企业研究所与战争研究所网站8月10日报道】美国企业研究所与战争研究所联合发布的朝鲜半岛动态更新显示，朝鲜正升级对俄罗斯在乌克兰战争的支持。乌克兰总统泽连斯基于8月8日表示，朝鲜正准备向俄罗斯部署3万至5万名人员。路透社8月5日报道称，乌克兰军事情报总局发言人证实，朝鲜已派遣一个装备120枚弹道导弹和6枚发射器的导弹部队至俄罗斯沃罗涅日州第112导弹旅，这是朝鲜首次向俄罗斯部署此类部队。分析认为，朝鲜此举旨在利用俄罗斯对导弹和人力需求，获取战略利益及实战经验。此前朝鲜已于2024年10月向库尔斯克州派遣约1.5万名步兵、工兵及建筑工人，目前约有1万人滞留俄罗斯。新增部署可能使朝鲜部队接管俄后方及边境防御任务，释放俄军兵力投入乌克兰东部攻势。朝鲜可能借此提升自身导弹部队效能及无人系统作战能力，并寻求俄罗斯在军事侦察卫星网络及水面舰艇建设方面的技术支持。韩国方面，总统李在明政府倾向于维持与俄罗斯关系以推动对朝对话，因此不太可能向乌克兰提供直接军事援助，尽管乌克兰方面呼吁加强防空系统合作。韩国外交部重申遵守国内法律，不向乌克兰提供致命性武器。美国特朗普政府正考虑利用韩国或日本船厂建造4艘舰艇以缓解美国海军造船产能不足，包括2艘水面战斗舰和2艘非战斗辅助舰，但受限于美国法律。此外，11国组成的多边制裁监测团队警告朝鲜IT人员通过欺诈手段渗透西方IT部门，朝鲜否认指控并指责美国抹黑。美国国务院强调朝鲜利用网络犯罪所得资金资助大规模杀伤性武器及弹道导弹项目。韩国网络安全司令部将参与美国主导的“网络旗帜”演习，加强美日韩三方网络防御合作。

content: Information Integrity Is a National Security Must Much of today’s conversation surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) centers on the models themselves. Organizations worry about prompt injection, model theft, jailbreaks, insider threats, and the growing sophistication of AI-enabled cyberattacks. While these are legitimate concerns deserving attention, there may be a more consequential risk beneath the model itself – the integrity of the information that drives Large Language Models (LLM). LLMs do not think independently; they operate and generate responses based on enormous volumes of information collected from books, websites, academia, research, government documents, news reporting, and other digital sources. If these sources become corrupted, manipulated, or intentionally poisoned, AI-generated outputs inherently become increasingly unreliable. This doesn’t just represent an AI problem but a cybersecurity problem, and as recent reporting shows, a potential national security problem, as well. Information Has Become the New Attack Surface While cybersecurity has traditionally focused on protecting networks, endpoints, etc., over the past ten years or so, data and information have been progressively weaponized to further state interests. With more public and private institutions embracing AI, this technology has introduced a new attack surface that has received little attention – information integrity. Instead of compromising a model through traditional cyber means, adversaries can manipulate the information ecosystem surrounding it to amplify disinformation, misinformation, and influence operations. If enough “false narratives,” fake stories, and manipulated documents are injected into the digital environment, future AI systems may absorb that data and accept it as legitimate knowledge. Recent reporting suggests Russia is expanding its disinformation campaigns beyond influencing public opinion and toward contaminating the online information environment consumed by AI systems. The main goal is not to trick people with lies. Instead, the goal is to make future AI models learn these lies and share them quickly all over the world. That represents a significant evolution in information warfare. From Disinformation to Cognitive Warfare Traditionally, influence operations sought to manipulate people. Now, AI changes the equation, as adversaries have the opportunity to manipulate both human decision-makers and the machines that support those decisions. An ambitious state could execute coordinated campaigns that generate thousands of fake technical articles, scientific studies, altered historical or current events, geopolitical analysis, and even cybersecurity reports. Sure, it’s possible that discerning human readers could recognize and dismiss many of them, but AI systems may not. As organizations continue to rely on retrieval-augmented generation ( RAG ), enterprise knowledge bases, and continuously updated information sources,poisoned information can become operational knowledge. Disinformation seeks to influence beliefs; information poisoning looks to influence future machine reasoning. The distinction is important to highlight because it potentially represents an advancement of cognitive warfare not seen before. The Enterprise Risk Organizations view AI as a productivity enhancer; however, productivity without trustworthy information can lead to poor decision-making. Several notional examples underscore this implication: 1) a security analyst receiving AI-generated threat intelligence based upon manipulated reporting; 2) a software developer unknowingly incorporating bad code recommendations from poisoned repositories; and 3) a financial institution basing and/or recommending investment decisions on AI-generated market analysis tainted by economic disinformation. In each instance, the AI model did not have to be compromised to achieve the objective. The model performed as designed only with invalid information. Security practitioners have long championed the CIA Triad of confidentiality, integrity, and availability as the foundation of cybersecurity. Now with AI, integrity takes on an even greater importance. Why This Matters for U.S. National Security The implications extend far beyond private industry and into national security. AI is being integrated across the U.S. national security apparatus, supporting key functional areas like intelligence analysis; military planning; logistics; cyber operations; and critical infrastructure protection, to name a few. Recognizing this reality, and keeping consistent with the Administration’s goal of making the United States an AI leader, the president issued a Presidential Memorandum on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the National Security Enterprise , directing agencies to fast-track the deployment of secure and reliable AI across defense and intelligence with appropriate cybersecurity considerations in place. But making the actual models secure is not enough. If adversary nations successfully pollute the global information ecosystem, they can subtly influence the content that the knowledge AI systems ingest. While this could cause disruption or failure (depending on the attackers’ intent), data integrity degradation would be a far more insidious attack that could affect the interpretation, analysis, and assessment of the information. Unlike traditional malware, which can generally be detected or at least leaves some digital artifact behind, this hidden threat gives no warning sign. It changes the data itself, so you cannot see it. The victim ultimately unknowingly makes decisions based on the faulty information. This type of attack is perfect for nation-states as an inexpensive, difficult-to-attribute, and scalable option that can be executed during peacetime and conflict situations. Over the next several years, expect influence operations to evolve beyond targeting human perception toward targeting machine cognition. Nation-state adversaries, particularly Russia and China, understand that future geopolitical advantage will depend not only on building more capable AI systems, but also on shaping the information those systems trust. Protecting the information supply chain is now essential, requiring companies to treat information integrity with the same security considerations they regard software integrity. When it comes to supply chains, upstream compromises create downstream victims, and the information supply chain is no different. Source validation, digital authenticity, and verification must become core parts of responsible enterprise AI development, deployment, and management. Moreover, information integrity needs to be recognized as a strategic national asset. The United States must protect its digital knowledge ecosystem with the same urgency and attention it applies toward critical infrastructure and software/hardware supply chains. In the end, winning the AI race may not be only about developing and supplying the world’s most capable AI models; it could very well rest in how the United States ensures that the models are learning from information worthy of the trust we place in them and on which we rely. movement_title: 美国情报界警示信息完整性受损将威胁国家安全与人工智能决策体系
movement_abstract: 【美国OODA Daily Pulse网站2026年8月报道】美国战略情报分析师Emilio Iasiello指出，当前人工智能安全讨论多集中于模型本身，但更深层风险在于驱动大语言模型的信息完整性。随着人工智能系统依赖海量数字来源生成响应，若信息生态被敌对国家蓄意污染，将导致AI输出不可靠，进而影响国家安全决策。文章强调，信息已成为新型攻击面，俄罗斯等国正通过大规模虚假信息、伪造技术文章、篡改历史与地缘分析报告等手段，试图污染AI训练数据，使未来AI系统内化错误知识并广泛传播。这种从‘影响人类认知’转向‘污染机器认知’的演变，标志着认知战进入新阶段。美国已将人工智能纳入国家安全体系，总统发布备忘录要求加速部署安全可靠的AI系统，但仅保障模型安全不足够，必须同步保护信息供应链。敌对国家可利用低成本、难归因方式在和平或冲突时期实施信息投毒，造成隐蔽且长期的战略影响。文章呼吁将信息完整性视为战略国家资产，要求企业与政府将信息验证、数字真实性与溯源机制纳入AI开发与部署核心流程，确保AI系统基于可信信息运行，以维护美国在人工智能领域的竞争优势与国家安全。

共產黨將巴夫洛夫的研究發現應用在傳統操控思想的方法上，這在許多認為自己冷靜客觀、實事求是的人的眼裡，似乎是撞見了一種無堅不摧的策略。共產主義者發現科學就跟火一樣，用於破壞遠比用於建設來得容易，於是決定將它用來摧毀心智。{"type":"general","targeting":{"advertising":["0"],"sponsor":["0"],"paid":["0"],"page_key":["article"],"page_name":["article"],"cabinet":["1157910","a2636dd5-62e4-4529-be20-b6b174b0f327"],"tag_key":["3258","3953","6934","85927","243437","376427","421038","421039","421040"],"tag_name":["\u5171\u7522\u9ee8","\u51b7\u6230","\u6d17\u8166","Edward 這導致許多人出現了悲觀的心態，提出類似這樣的問題：「既然每個人都有極限，我們什麼也做不了，不是嗎？」這種態度往往被冠上值得尊敬的稱號，說是「客觀」、「中立」，甚至是「獨立思考下的產物」，但其實這種態度就是失敗主義，而且是共產黨軟化、削弱人心計畫的一環。共產黨透過爭辯、暗示或例子，永無止境地重複著那「絕望感與必然性」的說法。不論是在蘇聯的監獄裡還是國際會議上，這種說法永遠存在。它就像中世紀的毒藥一樣，能將人的道德血脈稀釋成水。共產黨以一種矯揉造作的謙遜，將他們的勝利歸功於辯證唯物論，並以此作為證據宣示反抗他們的意志是無用的，而且他們終將取得勝利。他們所謂的辯證唯物論，歸根結底不過是披著神祕外衣的唯物主義，宣揚著透過持續不斷的鬥爭達成永恆變化的信條，並宣稱共產主義永遠是衡量真實與善惡的唯一標準。這種政治信仰不承認任何結論，除了它自己的。這便是共產黨所謂的「科學」。其寓意似乎是：共產黨員遲早會得到他們想要的。他們擁有成功施展拖延戰術所需的耐心、冷酷與狹隘思維。他們不斷對那些尚未屈服的人說：「聰明點，趁現在還有機會，加入勝利的一方吧。」這句話的說法會隨不同的心理層次與社會階層而調整。他們從未停止反覆重申這句話，就像一句神奇的咒語。{"type":"general","targeting":{"advertising":["0"],"sponsor":["0"],"paid":["0"],"page_key":["article"],"page_name":["article"],"cabinet":["1157910","a2636dd5-62e4-4529-be20-b6b174b0f327"],"tag_key":["3258","3953","6934","85927","243437","376427","421038","421039","421040"],"tag_name":["\u5171\u7522\u9ee8","\u51b7\u6230","\u6d17\u8166","Edward
